40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Advanced React APIs
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Advanced React APIs
Advanced React APIs covers the React hooks and APIs you don’t reach for daily, but need in your toolbelt for specific scenarios: consolidating sprawling component state, sharing values app-wide, rendering UI outside the DOM tree, computing layout before paint, exposing imperative methods through refs, forcing synchronous re-renders for focus management, and syncing with state that lives outside React.
Each topic below has its own note with an API reference (from react.dev) and a Real-World Scenarios section researched from how other developers actually use it in production.
Topics

useReducer — Complex State Management
use and createContext — Context
createPortal — Portals
useLayoutEffect — Layout Computations
useImperativeHandle — Imperative Handles
flushSync — Focus Management
useSyncExternalStore — Sync External Store


My Additional Angles
The common thread: these are all “escape hatches”
Every API here exists because React’s default model (declarative render, automatic batching, one virtual tree) occasionally isn’t enough: useReducer escapes scattered setState calls into one controlled transition function; useImperativeHandle/flushSync escape into imperative DOM territory; createPortal escapes the DOM tree structure; useSyncExternalStore escapes React’s own state model to sync with the outside world. Reaching for any of them is a signal you’re at a genuine boundary — not a default tool.
use unifies two previously separate mental models
Before use, “read context” (useContext) and “read async data” (manual useEffect + loading state, or a data-fetching library) were unrelated patterns. use collapses both into “unwrap this thing” — a context value or a Promise — and because it isn’t bound by the Rules of Hooks, it composes naturally with conditionals in a way no other Hook does.
flushSync and useLayoutEffect solve the same category of problem from different angles
Both exist because “the DOM hasn’t caught up yet” — useLayoutEffect handles the read-measure-before-paint half (so a layout calculation never gets painted with wrong data), while flushSync handles the force-a-write-then-act-imperatively half (so code right after it can trust the DOM reflects the latest state). Seeing them as two sides of the same synchronous-DOM-timing problem makes it easier to recall which one a given bug needs.
Server rendering shows up twice, not once
useSyncExternalStore’s getServerSnapshot and context’s default value (used when no Provider wraps a server-rendered subtree) are both instances of the same requirement: anything read outside a normal client re-render needs an explicit “what do I return when there’s no real browser/store to ask” answer.

Hello World in JS
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Hello World in JS

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Before touching React, this exercise builds “Hello World” using nothing but the raw DOM APIs — the same primitives React itself is built on top of.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why doesn’t document.createElement alone put anything on the page?
A: This is a general fact about the DOM API, independent of any framework: createElement only builds a node in memory — it isn’t attached to the visible document tree until it’s explicitly append-ed (or insertBefored, etc.) to a node that’s already on the page. That imperative create → mutate → append sequence is exactly the tedium that any declarative UI library, React included, exists to hide behind a simpler API. In our example, element only becomes visible after the final rootElement.append(element) call — the two lines before it just built it in memory.
const element = document.createElement('div') // built in memory only
element.textContent = 'Hello World'            // still not visible
rootElement.append(element)                    // now it's on the page
Q: Why use textContent instead of innerHTML when setting text?
A: This is a security-relevant DOM API distinction that applies anywhere user or dynamic content is rendered: textContent never parses its input as HTML, so a malicious string like <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> is inserted as inert, literal visible text rather than becoming a live, executable element — while innerHTML would parse and run it, opening the door to XSS. This is the same underlying distinction behind why React escapes every string it renders by default and gates raw HTML injection behind the deliberately alarming dangerouslySetInnerHTML name. In our example, element.textContent = 'Hello World' is what keeps this safe by default, with no framework involved yet.
Q: Is there anything special about a “root” DOM node?
A: No, and this holds for any UI framework mounted into the DOM: a “root” is just a regular DOM node, created and appended exactly like any other element — frameworks don’t have privileged access to some special container, they’re just consistently automating the same createElement/append calls you’d otherwise write by hand. In our example, the “Generate the Root Node” step creates <div id="root"> itself and appends it to document.body, proving there’s nothing pre-existing or magical about it.
Hello World in JS

Lesson

const rootElement = document.getElementById('root')
const element = document.createElement('div')
element.className = 'container'
element.textContent = 'Hello World'
rootElement.append(element)

💬 Creating an element with document.createElement only builds it in memory — it isn’t on the page until you explicitly append it to something that already is on the page. This imperative, step-by-step nature (create → mutate → append) is exactly the tedium React’s declarative API exists to hide.


💬 Notice this uses textContent, not innerHTML. textContent never parses its input as HTML — a string like <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> just becomes literal visible text, not a live element. That’s the same reason React escapes every string it renders by default, and why injecting raw HTML requires the deliberately alarming-looking dangerouslySetInnerHTML escape hatch. The safety isn’t a React invention — it’s this same DOM-level distinction, just made the default.

Generate the Root Node

Lesson

Rather than relying on a <div id="root"> already in the HTML, create the root itself and append it to document.body:
const rootElement = document.createElement('div')
rootElement.id = 'root'
document.body.append(rootElement)
 
const element = document.createElement('div')
element.textContent = 'Hello World'
rootElement.append(element)

💬 This is purely to drive home that there’s nothing magic about a “root” element — it’s just another DOM node created and appended like any other. Libraries like React aren’t doing anything you couldn’t do by hand; they’re just doing a lot of it, consistently, for you.

Raw React APIs
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Raw React APIs

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

React ships as two packages for the web: React (creates React elements — components, hooks, the declarative API) and ReactDOM (renders those elements to the actual DOM — the web-specific renderer; React also has renderers for native, VR, and even the terminal). This exercise uses both directly, with no JSX yet, to see what a “React element” actually is before the syntactic sugar is added.
Interview Q&A
Q: What does createElement actually return, and why does that matter?
A: In general, React’s rendering model is built on “virtual DOM” — every createElement(type, props, ...children) call returns a lightweight plain JS object describing what should be on screen, not an actual DOM node. This is what lets React diff two renders cheaply (comparing objects) before touching the real, expensive-to-mutate DOM. In our example, createElement('div', { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' }) returns a descriptor like { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } } — nothing is on screen yet until it’s passed to a renderer.
const element = createElement('div', { className: 'container' }, 'Hello World')
// element is roughly: { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } }
Q: What’s the difference between React and ReactDOM, and why are they separate packages?
A: React is split into a renderer-agnostic core (creating elements, managing components/hooks/reconciliation) and one or more platform-specific renderers, so the same component model can target different environments — ReactDOM for the browser, React Native for mobile, react-three-fiber for WebGL, even terminal renderers exist. This separation is what makes “learn React once, write anywhere” possible. In our example, react.js provides createElement while react-dom/client.js provides createRoot(...).render(...), the step that actually turns element objects into real DOM nodes.
Q: Are React elements mutable?
A: No, generally React elements are meant to be treated as immutable snapshots — a component re-renders by creating brand-new element objects rather than mutating old ones, which is central to how React’s diffing/reconciliation can trust that a previous render’s objects won’t change out from under it. In our example specifically, TypeScript and a dev-mode Object.freeze both guard against reassigning element.props after creation.
Q: Why are key and ref handled specially in createElement/JSX?
A: Generally, key and ref are reserved props React itself needs to read (for list reconciliation and imperative DOM/instance access, respectively) — if they were passed through like any other prop, a component could never define its own key/ref-named prop without ambiguity, and libraries wrapping components could accidentally leak them. React solves this by stripping them out of props before a component ever sees them. In our example, that means createElement('li', { key: 'a' }, ...) never has a key in the resulting element.props — key only shows up in React’s internal bookkeeping.
const el = createElement('li', { key: 'a', className: 'item' }, 'Ham')
// el.props is { className: 'item' } — no `key` in there
Q: What is JSX’s relationship to createElement?
A: JSX in general is purely syntactic sugar — a build step (Babel/TypeScript/etc.) compiles JSX tags into nested createElement (or the newer jsx/jsxs runtime) calls; there’s no special JSX runtime behavior beyond that transformation. In our example, hand-writing the nested createElement calls in “Deep Nesting Elements” below is exactly what a JSX compiler automates — see Using JSX for the same UI written with the sugar.
// This JSX...
<div className="container"><span>Hello</span></div>
// ...compiles to this:
createElement('div', { className: 'container' }, createElement('span', null, 'Hello'))
Create React Elements

Lesson

import { createElement } from '/react.js'
import { createRoot } from '/react-dom/client.js'
 
const element = createElement('div', { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' })
createRoot(rootElement).render(element)

💬 createElement(type, props, ...children) doesn’t create a DOM node — it creates a plain JS object (a React element), essentially a UI descriptor: { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } }. createRoot(...).render(...) is the step that actually turns that description into DOM nodes. children is just a prop — you can pass it in the props object, as extra arguments to createElement, or as an array.


💬 Two more things worth knowing about that descriptor object: it’s immutable — React elements are meant to be created fresh on every render, not mutated in place, and TypeScript (plus a dev-mode Object.freeze) will stop you from reassigning element.props after the fact. And key and ref, if you pass them, are not part of props — React strips them out before your component ever sees them, specifically so they can’t collide with a key/ref a component might otherwise want to define itself as a regular prop. key gets its own dedicated exercise later in Rendering Arrays.

Nesting Elements

Lesson

const element = createElement(
  'div',
  { className: 'container' },
  createElement('span', null, 'Hello'),
  ' ',
  createElement('span', null, 'World'),
)

💬 Arguments after the props object all become children. A plain string doesn’t need createElement — React turns it into a text node automatically. The explicit ' ' string between the two spans matters because, unlike raw HTML source, there’s no whitespace between these createElement calls for the browser to collapse.

Deep Nesting Elements

Lesson

const element = createElement(
  'div',
  { className: 'container' },
  createElement('p', null, "Here's Sam's favorite food:"),
  createElement(
    'ul',
    { className: 'sams-food' },
    createElement('li', null, 'Green eggs'),
    createElement('li', null, 'Ham'),
  ),
)

💬 createElement calls compose arbitrarily deep — this is the exact mechanism JSX compiles down to. Once nesting gets a few levels deep, hand-written createElement calls become hard to read, which is precisely the motivation for Using JSX.

React Fundamentals
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Fundamentals
Notes from Kent C. Dodds’ EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop. It builds React up from first principles — starting at the raw DOM and raw createElement calls, through JSX, custom components, TypeScript, styling, forms, error boundaries, and the key prop — so that by the end, nothing about React’s core API feels like magic.
Exercises

Hello World in JS — DOM basics before any React: creating and appending nodes by hand.
Raw React APIs — createElement and createRoot, with no JSX: what a React element actually is.
Using JSX — JSX as sugar over createElement; interpolation, spread props, nesting, fragments.
Custom Components — the real definition of a component, built up in four small steps.
TypeScript with React — typing props, narrowing, deriving types, defaults, satisfies.
Styling — className vs style, and wrapping a native element in a styled Box component.
Forms — action, method, encType, FormData, and React’s function-valued action prop.
Inputs — checkboxes, selects, radios, hidden inputs, and the value/defaultValue distinction.
Error Boundaries — catching render errors declaratively with react-error-boundary.
Rendering Arrays — why arrays of elements need a key, and what goes wrong without one.


My Additional Angles
The whole workshop is really one long “de-sugaring” exercise
Every exercise strips away one more layer of convenience to show what’s underneath it: the DOM under createElement, createElement under JSX, plain functions under components, native input behavior under React’s defaultValue. Understanding React deeply mostly means being able to mentally compile forward and backward between each of these layers — especially JSX ↔ createElement, which pays off constantly when debugging.
key and Error Boundaries are the same kind of “leak”
Both the key prop and Error Boundaries exist because React’s declarative model has a genuine gap it can’t paper over: React can’t infer array diffs without help (Rendering Arrays), and it can’t try/catch around code that hasn’t run yet at JSX-authoring time (Error Boundaries). Both are places where you have to hand React explicit information (a key, a boundary component) that it structurally cannot derive on its own.
TypeScript’s role here mirrors “props are just an object”
Because a component actually is just a function, there’s no special “React way” to type one — TypeScript with React is just ordinary TypeScript (union types, typeof/keyof, Record, satisfies) applied to a function’s parameter. The one genuinely React-specific type that shows up repeatedly is React.ComponentProps<'div'> (used in Styling) for borrowing a native element’s full prop type when wrapping it.
This workshop deliberately stops short of state
useState shows up exactly once, unexplained, as scaffolding in Rendering Arrays — every other exercise renders purely from props, with nothing remembered between renders (see the aside in Custom Components about components being re-invoked from scratch every render). That’s not an oversight; it’s the boundary of this workshop. The natural next step is EpicReact’s “React Hooks” workshop, where components stop being purely a function of their props and start holding on to values across renders.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
TypeScript with React

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.


“TypeScript is not making your life terrible. It’s just showing you how terrible your life already is.” — Kent C. Dodds

Since a React component is just a function, typing one is no different from typing any other function — the challenge is really (1) getting better at TypeScript generally and (2) learning React’s specific types (like React.ReactNode).
This exercise progressively types a Calculator component through six steps.
Interview Q&A
Q: Should you type React function components with React.FC?
A: As a general modern TypeScript+React recommendation, no — React.FC implicitly adds an optional children prop even to components that never accept one, and makes generic components (function List<T>(...)) awkward to express, since React.FC isn’t itself generic-friendly. Typing the props parameter directly covers every case React.FC does, with none of the downsides. In our example, Calculator is typed as function Calculator({ left, operator, right }: CalculatorProps) rather than const Calculator: React.FC<CalculatorProps> = (...) => ....
Q: Why use a union of string literals instead of string for a prop like operator?
A: This is a general TypeScript narrowing technique, not React-specific: a plain string type accepts any string, including invalid values that compile fine but blow up at runtime because nothing handles them; a literal union narrows the type to exactly the valid set and gives editor autocomplete for free. In our example, operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/' rejects a typo like '**' at compile time instead of only failing when Calculator actually runs.
type CalculatorProps = { left: number; operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'; right: number }
Q: What’s the difference between typeof and keyof when deriving a type from an object?
A: Generally, typeof pulls a type out of a runtime value (turning a JS object into its TS shape), and keyof then extracts a union of that type’s own key names — chaining them (keyof typeof obj) is a common way to avoid hand-duplicating a union that already exists as an object’s keys. In our example, keyof typeof operations derives Operator ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/') straight from the operations object, so adding a new operator to that object is the only change needed instead of also updating a separately hand-written union.
const operations = { '+': (l: number, r: number) => l + r, /* ... */ }
type Operator = keyof typeof operations // '+' | '-' | ...
Q: What does satisfies give you that a type annotation doesn’t?
A: As a general TypeScript rule, annotating a value with a type (const x: T = value) widens its inferred type to exactly T, discarding narrower literal information the value actually had; satisfies instead checks that the value is compatible with a wider type while leaving its own inferred type untouched (still narrow). In our example, operations satisfies Record<string, OperationFn> validates every function matches OperationFn while operations keeps its narrow, literal keys ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/') so keyof typeof operations still works — combining the safety of Reduce Duplication with the narrow-key derivation of Derive Types.
Q: What’s the difference between React.ComponentProps<'div'> and ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'>?
A: More generally, ComponentProps<T> gives you the full prop type of a JSX element or component (including ref), which is convenient for typing a wrapper component — but a plain function component can’t actually receive a ref without forwardRef (or React 19’s ref-as-prop support), so including it can be misleading. ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T> is the same shape minus ref, and is the safer default when a component wraps a native element without specifically handling ref forwarding. In our example (see Styling), Box is typed with React.ComponentProps<'div'> since it doesn’t forward a ref at all — ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'> would be the more precise choice there.
Props

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = { left: number; operator: string; right: number }
 
function Calculator({ left, operator, right }: CalculatorProps) {
  /* ... */
}

💬 Without this, someone could pass left={"2"} and the compiler wouldn’t catch it — only a runtime bug would reveal it. Naming the props type (CalculatorProps) vs. inlining it ({ left, operator, right }: { left: number; ... }) is purely a style choice; both work identically.


💬 You’ll often see React.FC<CalculatorProps> (or React.FunctionComponent) used for the component’s type instead of typing the parameter directly, especially in older code and tutorials. It’s generally discouraged today: it implicitly adds an optional children prop even to components that never accept one, and it makes generic components (function List<T>(...)) awkward to express. Typing the props parameter directly — the way every example in this note does — is the currently recommended approach and works for every case React.FC does.

Narrow Types

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = {
  left: number
  operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'
  right: number
}

💬 A plain string type for operator allows any string — including '**', which would compile fine but blow up at runtime because there’s no handler for it. A union of literal strings narrows the type to exactly the valid values, which also unlocks editor autocomplete for free.

Derive Types

Lesson

const operations = {
  '+': (left: number, right: number) => left + right,
  '-': (left: number, right: number) => left - right,
  '*': (left: number, right: number) => left * right,
  '/': (left: number, right: number) => left / right,
}
 
type Operations = typeof operations
type Operator = keyof Operations // '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'

💬 Hand-listing '+' | '-' | '*' | '/' separately from the operations object duplicates the same information in two places — add a new operator to one and forget the other, and you get either a silent runtime gap or a spurious type error. typeof pulls a type out of a runtime value; keyof then extracts a union of that type’s keys. Deriving Operator from operations this way means adding an operator to the object is the only change needed.

Default Props

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = { left?: number; operator?: Operator; right?: number }
 
function Calculator({ left = 0, operator = '+', right = 0 }: CalculatorProps) {
  /* ... */
}

💬 ? on a type property makes it optional (allows undefined); the destructuring default (= 0) supplies the runtime fallback when the caller omits it. Both pieces are needed — the ? alone would leave left typed as number | undefined inside the function body.

Reduce Duplication

Lesson

type OperationFn = (left: number, right: number) => number
type Operator = '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'
 
const operations: Record<Operator, OperationFn> = {
  '+': (left, right) => left + right,
  '-': (left, right) => left - right,
  '*': (left, right) => left * right,
  '/': (left, right) => left / right,
}

💬 Every operation function has the identical shape (number, number) => number — repeating that signature on each one is its own duplication. Record<Operator, OperationFn> types the whole object as a map instead. The catch: this reintroduces the earlier problem — Operator now has to be listed by hand again, because you can’t derive a key union from a value you’re still in the middle of typing (a circular dependency). Deriving from a Record-typed object also loses per-key literal narrowing.

Satisfies

Lesson

const operations = {
  '+': (left: number, right: number) => left + right,
  '-': (left: number, right: number) => left - right,
  '*': (left: number, right: number) => left * right,
  '/': (left: number, right: number) => left / right,
} satisfies Record<string, OperationFn>
 
type Operator = keyof typeof operations

💬 Casting a value to a type (const x: T = value) widens the value’s type to exactly T, losing narrower literal information. satisfies checks that the value is compatible with a wider type, without widening the value’s own inferred type. So operations still has its narrow, literal keys ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/' inferred directly from the object), while TypeScript still verifies every value matches OperationFn — the best of both the Derive Types and Reduce Duplication approaches, without either one’s downside.


💬 One more React-specific type worth knowing, used in Styling: React.ComponentProps<'div'> includes a ref in its type, but a plain function component can’t actually receive one without extra work (forwardRef, or React 19’s ref-as-prop support). React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'> is the same prop set minus ref — the safer default to reach for when wrapping a native element in a component that doesn’t specifically handle forwarding a ref.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Lifecycle

Summary of the YouTube video “The React Lifecycle: Simply Explained!” by Darius Cosden.


Interview Q&A
Q: What are the three stages of a React component’s lifecycle?
A: Mount (the initial render, happens exactly once when the component first appears), Update (a re-render triggered by a state change, new props, or a context change — can repeat any number of times), and Unmount (the component is removed from the tree and React frees the memory it was holding). Every class-component “lifecycle method” you may have seen (componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmount) and every hook-based equivalent (useEffect with different dependency arrays) maps onto one of these three stages. In our example, the note’s “Full Client-Side Flow” diagram walks through exactly these three stages end to end, from function call through paint.
useEffect(() => {
  // runs after MOUNT and after every UPDATE where deps changed
  return () => {
    // cleanup: runs before the next UPDATE's effect, and once on UNMOUNT
  }
}, [dep])
Q: Does React re-run the whole component function on every render, or just the changed parts?
A: The entire function body re-executes top to bottom on every single render, mount or update alike — this is true of all function components in React, not just this example; React never partially executes a component or skips lines based on what changed. What is selective is purely on the output side: React diffs the newly-returned JSX (via the Virtual DOM) against the previous snapshot and only writes the minimal set of changes to the real DOM, which is why re-running the whole function is cheap in practice even though it sounds wasteful. In our example, the “Initialize vs. Update” table makes this explicit: const/let values are “evaluated fresh” on every render regardless of stage, while only useState (preserved) and useMemo (conditionally recomputed) get special treatment from React’s internal state store.
Q: Why does useEffect run after the browser paints, and when would you use useLayoutEffect instead?
A: useEffect is deliberately scheduled to run after the browser has painted the committed DOM changes, which is what makes it a “side effect” rather than part of rendering — this keeps expensive or non-visual work (fetching data, logging, subscribing to something) from blocking the user from seeing the UI update. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously before the browser paints instead, which matters when the effect needs to read or mutate the DOM in a way the user must never see flicker (e.g. measuring an element’s size and repositioning something based on it) — the tradeoff is that it can delay the paint since the browser waits for it to finish. In our example, the sequence diagram under “The useEffect timing distinction” shows the exact ordering: function runs → JSX evaluated → Virtual DOM → DOM → browser paint → useEffect fires.
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const { height } = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect() // read before paint, no flicker
}, [])
Q: When does a useEffect cleanup function run, and what values does it see?
A: Generally, a cleanup function returned from useEffect runs in exactly two situations: right before the next time that effect re-runs (so React can tear down whatever the previous run set up before setting up the new one), and one final time when the component unmounts. Because the cleanup function was created during a specific render, it’s a closure over that render’s values — so it always operates on the state/props from when the effect was originally scheduled, not whatever the values are by the time it actually runs; this is the same closure behavior that causes stale-closure bugs elsewhere in React (see React Re-rendering). In our example, the “Between Renders: Cleanup Timing” section diagrams this as Render N effect fires → Render N+1 triggered → Render N cleanup runs (with Render N's values) → Render N+1 runs → Render N+1 effect fires.
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000)
  return () => clearInterval(id) // uses this render's `id`, not a later one
}, [])
Q: How is a Server Component’s lifecycle different from a Client Component’s?
A: A Server Component executes exactly once, on the server, has no access to hooks or state, and its output is plain HTML rather than something that participates in a Virtual DOM diff — so there is no mount/update/unmount cycle in the traditional sense at all. Instead of re-rendering in response to state changes, “updates” happen through revalidation: some server action or framework API tells React to re-run the server component function and produce new HTML, which the framework then patches into the page — the component itself has no concept of re-rendering. In our example, the “Server Components — A Different Model” comparison table lays out these differences point by point (hooks, lifecycle, output, Virtual DOM, data fetching), and the “How updates work on the server” section walks through the concrete revalidation flow (revalidatePath('/') in Next.js, then a fresh HTML response).
Core Concept: Components Are JavaScript Functions
Every React component is just a plain JavaScript function. React takes that function and does several things to it behind the scenes:

Adds lifecycle tracking
Enforces hook rules
Runs the function at the right time in each lifecycle stage

This wrapping is why hooks work. useState, useEffect, useMemo, and custom hooks all depend on React executing the function — they aren’t available in plain JS functions because React is the one managing the context around them.
Components can return JSX or null. Returning null is a valid render that tells React to remove that component’s output from the screen.

Only components that are currently active on screen enter the lifecycle. Components on other pages or hidden by conditions are not tracked — they don’t exist in the lifecycle at all.


The Three Lifecycle Stages
Mount → Update (repeats) → Unmount

At every stage, React re-executes the entire function body from top to bottom. The output feeds into the Virtual DOM → real DOM → browser paint pipeline.

Stage 1 — Initial Render (Mount)
Happens once, when the component appears on screen for the first time.
Step-by-step

Run all code in the function body — every line executes top to bottom
Initialize all values

useState(defaultValue) — default value is set and stored in React’s memory
useMemo(fn, deps) — computed immediately and cached
const, let, inline functions — evaluated and held in memory for use in JSX or other functions


Evaluate and return JSX — the returned markup is handed to React
Virtual DOM — React builds an in-memory representation of the component tree; this is React’s working copy used for diffing
DOM update — React compares the Virtual DOM against the real DOM and applies only the necessary changes
Browser paints — the user sees the component on screen
Effects are scheduled — useEffect callbacks are queued to run after the browser has painted

The useEffect timing distinction
useEffect is called a side effect because it runs after the render is committed to the screen, not during it. The sequence is:
function runs → JSX evaluated → Virtual DOM → DOM → browser paint → useEffect fires

If you need code to run before the browser paints (e.g. measuring DOM layout), use useLayoutEffect instead — it blocks the paint until it completes. This can cause visible delays, so it should only be used when strictly necessary.

Stage 2 — Update (Re-render)
Triggered whenever something affecting the component changes: state update, new props from a parent, context change, or an external store update.
Step-by-step

Run cleanup functions — any useEffect that returned a cleanup function runs now, with the values from the previous render (not the new ones). This cleans up subscriptions, timers, or listeners set up in the last effect.
Run all code in the function body again — the entire function re-executes from top to bottom
Update all values

useState — holds its current (updated) value; does not re-initialize from the default
useMemo — recomputes only if its dependencies have changed; otherwise returns the cached value
const, let, inline functions — re-evaluated fresh on every render


Evaluate and return new JSX
Virtual DOM diff — React compares the new Virtual DOM snapshot against the previous one and calculates the minimal set of DOM changes needed
DOM update — only the changed parts are written to the real DOM
Browser repaints — the user sees the updated UI
Effects are scheduled — useEffect callbacks whose dependency arrays include changed values are queued to run after paint

Initialize vs. Update























StageuseStateuseMemoconst/letMountSet to default valueComputed and cachedEvaluated freshUpdateHolds current valueRecomputed only if deps changedEvaluated fresh
The function always re-runs completely — React does not skip lines. The difference is that React’s internal state store preserves useState values across renders; only useMemo and derived values are recomputed conditionally.

Between Renders: Cleanup Timing
The cleanup function returned from useEffect runs in two situations:

Before the next update — right before the component re-renders, React runs the cleanup from the previous render’s effect (using that render’s closed-over values), then runs the new effect after the new paint
On unmount — runs one final time when the component leaves the screen

This means cleanup always runs with stale values (the values from when the effect was set up), which is why closures matter in React. The flow looks like:
Render N effect fires
  → Render N+1 triggered
  → Render N cleanup runs (with Render N's values)
  → Render N+1 runs
  → Render N+1 effect fires


Stage 3 — Exit (Unmount)
Happens when the component is no longer needed — the user navigates away, a condition removes it from the tree, or a parent stops rendering it.
Step-by-step

Run cleanup functions — all useEffect cleanup functions fire one last time
Release all values from memory — useState, useMemo, const/let, and everything else held in the component’s memory is freed
Virtual DOM update — React removes the component from its in-memory tree
DOM update — the corresponding DOM nodes are removed
Browser repaints — the user sees the component disappear


Full Client-Side Flow (Visual Summary)
Your function component
        ↓
   React wraps it
        ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  LIFECYCLE                      │
│                                                 │
│  MOUNT          UPDATE           UNMOUNT        │
│  ─────          ──────           ───────        │
│  Run code  →    Cleanup prev  →  Cleanup        │
│  Init vals      Run code         Release mem    │
│  JSX →          Update vals                     │
│  VirtualDOM     JSX →                           │
│  DOM            VirtualDOM                      │
│  Paint          DOM                             │
│  useEffect      Paint                           │
│                 useEffect                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ↓
   Browser (what the user sees)


Server Components — A Different Model
Server components are still JavaScript functions, but they never reach the client and have no lifecycle in the traditional sense.













































AspectClient ComponentServer ComponentHooksSupportedNot supportedLifecycleMount → Update → UnmountRuns once on server, doneOutput to clientJavaScript bundle + JSXPure HTMLVirtual DOMYesNo — HTML goes directly to DOMAsync/awaitNot at top level (use useEffect)Supported nativelyData fetchingVia useEffect after paintDirectly in the function bodyRe-rendersTriggered by state/propsNo concept — revalidation instead
Why server components are faster (and more limited)

No JavaScript is shipped to the client for these components — only HTML
No round-trips: fetch data, render, send HTML in one pass
Trade-off: no interactivity, no hooks, no state

How “updates” work on the server
Since there is no state or re-render concept, updating server-rendered content requires revalidation:

A server action (a function running on the server) runs — triggered by user interaction on a client component, a timer, a webhook, etc.
That function calls something like revalidatePath('/') (Next.js) or an equivalent framework API
React re-executes the server component function, generates new HTML
The new HTML is delivered to the browser via an HTTP response
The framework patches the DOM with the new HTML — the user sees the update

The framework handles all of this automatically once you call the revalidation function. You don’t manage a lifecycle; you just trigger a re-run.

Key Takeaways

The entire function runs on every render — React doesn’t partially execute components; the whole function body re-executes each time
Only active components are in the lifecycle — components not currently on screen don’t exist in React’s memory
useEffect is always post-paint — if you need pre-paint behavior, use useLayoutEffect, but expect potential jank
Cleanup runs with stale values — the cleanup function closes over the values from the render that created the effect, not the new render
useMemo is not free — it recomputes when dependencies change; the cache is per-render, not global
Server components have no lifecycle — they run once, produce HTML, and are done; updates come through framework revalidation
Mix both — use server components for data-heavy, non-interactive UI (better performance); use client components for anything stateful or interactive

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: React Re-rendering
JavaScript Promises
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
JavaScript Promises

Foundational JS — not React-specific — but scoped inside React Suspense/
because the rest of that folder (The use Hook,
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching) leans on exactly the
mechanics documented here. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with
> 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What is a Promise?
A: A built-in JS object standing in for the eventual result of any
asynchronous operation — network requests, file I/O, timers, worker
messages — so you can attach “when this finishes” behavior without knowing
in advance whether or when it’ll actually happen. It’s the foundation
async/await, fetch, and most async Node/browser APIs are built on. In
this note’s examples, getShip(name) returns exactly this kind of value: a
promise standing in for ship data that hasn’t arrived yet.
Q: What states can a Promise be in, and can it change state more than once?
A: Exactly one of pending, fulfilled, or rejected at a time, for any promise
regardless of what async work it wraps. Once it settles (fulfilled or
rejected) that’s permanent — it never transitions again — which is a
general guarantee that makes a promise safe to hand to multiple independent
consumers without them racing or disagreeing about the outcome. In this
folder specifically, Promise Caching leans on that permanence: once a
cached promise settles, every consumer that reads it later gets the same
answer for free.
pending ──resolve(value)──▶ fulfilled
   │
   └──────reject(reason)──▶ rejected

Q: Are .then/.catch callbacks run synchronously?
A: No, never — this is true of every promise in JS, not just ones tied to
network calls. Even an already-settled promise queues its callback on the
microtask queue, which only drains after the currently executing
synchronous code finishes and before the next macrotask (a setTimeout, an
event, I/O). In this note’s Promise.resolve().then(...) example, that’s
why "synchronous code" logs before "promise callback" even though the
promise is resolved instantly.
Q: What’s the relationship between async/await and .then?
A: async/await is just syntax sugar over .then chains, available for
any promise-returning code, not a separate mechanism — an async function
always returns a promise, and a throw inside one (sync or not) becomes
that promise rejecting with the thrown value instead of an uncaught
exception. In this note, the async function getShip example and its
hand-written .then equivalent produce identical behavior:
// async/await
async function getShip(name) {
  const response = await fetch(`/ships/${name}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
 
// equivalent .then chain
function getShip(name) {
  return fetch(`/ships/${name}`).then((response) => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
    return response.json()
  })
}
Q: Why does it matter that a Promise is “just a value”?
A: Because nothing in the language restricts what you’re allowed to
throw — a string, an Error, or a Promise are all fair game, and any
catch block (or React’s internal render loop) that receives one can
inspect it and attach its own .then to find out later when it settles.
This is a general JS fact useful anywhere you want custom control-flow
around thrown values, not something React invented. In our folder, this is
the entire mechanism `use` and Suspense exploit: use
throws a pending promise, React’s reconciler catches it and attaches its
own .then to know when to retry rendering.
The state machine
A promise is always in exactly one of three states:

pending — the initial state; neither fulfilled nor rejected yet.
fulfilled — the operation succeeded; the promise has a value.
rejected — the operation failed; the promise has a reason (usually an
Error).

A promise is settled once it’s fulfilled or rejected. Settling is
one-way and permanent — a promise can only transition out of pending
once, and never changes state again after that. This guarantee is what makes
a promise safe to hand to multiple consumers (like React’s Suspense
machinery) without worrying that its outcome will flip on you later.
pending ──resolve(value)──▶ fulfilled
   │
   └──────reject(reason)──▶ rejected

Creating one: the executor function
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  // this function — the "executor" — runs immediately and synchronously
  doSomethingAsync((err, result) => {
    if (err) reject(err)       // → settles as rejected
    else resolve(result)       // → settles as fulfilled
  })
})

💬 The executor itself runs synchronously the instant new Promise(...) is
called — it’s the resolve/reject callbacks that get invoked later,
asynchronously. This is why you can’t just wrap new Promise(...) in a
try/catch to catch a later rejection: the executor’s synchronous portion
has already returned by the time reject fires.

Consuming one: .then / .catch / .finally
promise
  .then(
    (value) => console.log('fulfilled with', value),
    (reason) => console.log('rejected with', reason), // optional 2nd arg
  )
  .catch((reason) => console.log('shorthand for .then(undefined, onRejected)'))
  .finally(() => console.log('runs either way, for cleanup'))
Each of .then/.catch/.finally returns a new promise, which is what
makes chaining work — if a handler throws, or returns a rejected promise, the
promise returned by that link in the chain becomes rejected too, and the
error propagates down the chain until something’s .catch handles it (or
nothing does, and you get an unhandled rejection).

💬 A promise’s outcome isn’t synchronously inspectable from the outside —
there’s no public .state or .value you can just read. The only way to
learn it is asynchronously, by attaching a .then and waiting for it to
fire once the promise settles. And you can attach more than one: multiple
independent .then calls, from different pieces of code, on the same
promise, don’t interfere with each other — each just gets invoked (in the
order it was attached) once the promise settles. The use Hook leans on
both halves of this fact: it’s why use has to track status/value/
reason manually instead of asking the promise for them, and it’s why
React’s internal pseudocode and use itself can each attach their own
separate .then to the same promise without stepping on one another.

Timing: the microtask queue
.then/.catch/.finally callbacks never run synchronously, even if the
promise is already settled by the time you attach them:
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise callback'))
console.log('synchronous code')
// logs: "synchronous code" then "promise callback"
Promise callbacks are queued on the microtask queue, which the JS engine
drains only after the currently executing synchronous code finishes (and
before it goes on to the next macrotask, like a setTimeout or an event).
This is why a promise resolving doesn’t interrupt whatever’s running right
now — including, as covered in The use Hook, why a component that throws
a pending promise gets to fully unwind first before React’s own .then
handler on that promise ever fires.
async/await is sugar over this
async function getShip(name) {
  const response = await fetch(`/ships/${name}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
is equivalent to:
function getShip(name) {
  return fetch(`/ships/${name}`).then((response) => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
    return response.json()
  })
}
async functions always return a promise, and a throw inside one
(synchronous or not) becomes that promise rejecting with the thrown
value, rather than an uncaught synchronous exception.
The fact the rest of this folder depends on
A promise is just a JavaScript value — an object like any other. Nothing
in the language restricts what you’re allowed to throw. You can throw
a string, a number, an Error… or a Promise. Nobody awaits a thrown
promise, so throwing one doesn’t pause anything by itself — but a catch
block that receives it can inspect it, and in particular can attach its own
.then to it to find out later when it settles. That’s the entire trick
behind React’s use hook and Suspense: see The use Hook for exactly how
React exploits this.
Sources

MDN — Promise
javascript.info — Microtasks

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 1, “Data fetching”), code pulled
directly from the exercise solutions. Companion to The use Hook (the
mechanism that triggers all of this) and Error Boundaries (the general
ErrorBoundary API — composition, showBoundary, resetErrorBoundary,
not repeated here). Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does <Suspense> actually catch, and what’s it generally used for?
A: A thrown pending promise — any component under it that “suspends” (i.e.
throws a not-yet-settled promise, whether from use, a framework’s data
layer, or React.lazy) gets its fallback rendered instead of its children
until that promise settles. It’s React’s general-purpose mechanism for
declaring “this subtree isn’t ready yet” for any async reason — lazy-loaded
code, data fetching, or streaming SSR — not something built only for one
kind of fetch. In our example, ShipDetails throws the in-flight
shipPromise, so <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}> shows the
fallback until that specific promise resolves:
<Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
  <ShipDetails />
</Suspense>
Q: How far up the tree does React look for a Suspense boundary, and why does that matter for layout?
A: As far as it needs to — React walks up to the nearest <Suspense>
ancestor regardless of how deeply nested the suspending component is, and
treats everything under that boundary as one unit (any child suspending
shows the whole boundary’s fallback). This lets you control loading
granularity generally: one boundary around a whole page for an all-or-
nothing spinner, or several nested boundaries for staggered, progressive
reveal. In our example there’s a single boundary around ShipDetails, so
only that piece of UI shows a fallback rather than the whole page.
Q: Why does ErrorBoundary wrap Suspense, and not the other way around?
A: This follows the general rule for any error boundary in React: a
boundary can’t catch an error thrown from within itself, only from its
children. So ErrorBoundary has to sit outside Suspense to also catch
errors from Suspense’s own internal machinery, not just a rejected fetch. In
our example that’s why the JSX nests ErrorBoundary → Suspense →
ShipDetails, not the reverse — a ship-fetch rejection and any hypothetical
Suspense-internals bug both get caught by the same outer boundary.
Q: Is React’s “throw to suspend” mechanism just a teaching simplification?
A: No — it’s close to literal, and it’s the same mechanism regardless of
what triggers the suspend (data fetching, React.lazy, a framework’s
cache). React’s render work loop wraps each unit of work in a real
try/catch; on catch it duck-types the thrown value
(typeof value.then === 'function') to decide whether it’s a suspend
(thenable) or a real error, then walks up the fiber tree to find the
matching Suspense or error-boundary fiber. In our example, that’s
precisely what happens when ShipDetails throws shipPromise versus when
it throws a fetch-rejection Error — same reconciler code path, different
branch.
Q: Why must ErrorBoundary be a class component?
A: This is a general React constraint, not specific to Suspense: the
reconciler’s upward walk for non-thenable errors specifically looks for a
component with getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch, and there’s
no function-component equivalent of those lifecycle hooks — so any error
boundary anywhere in React, including react-error-boundary’s
ErrorBoundary used in our example, wraps a class component under the
hood.
<Suspense> and ErrorBoundary are the declarative shell around
`use`: use throws either a pending promise or a rejection
reason, and these two components are what actually catch those throws and
turn them into UI.
<Suspense fallback={...}>

Lesson video

“Suspending” means a component threw a pending promise. <Suspense> catches
that throw and renders its fallback instead of its children, for as long as
the promise stays pending:
import { Suspense, use } from 'react'
 
function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
      <ShipDetails />
    </Suspense>
  )
}
React looks up the component tree for the nearest <Suspense> ancestor
of whatever suspended — it doesn’t matter how deep the suspending component
is nested, as long as some <Suspense> sits above it. All the boundary’s
children are treated as one unit: if any of them suspends, the whole boundary
shows its fallback until every suspending child is ready. Boundaries can be
nested for progressive/staggered loading — an outer boundary can reveal
its content while an inner one keeps showing its own fallback for a slower
piece of data.
ErrorBoundary, and why it wraps Suspense (not the other way around)

Lesson video

If the promise rejects, use throws the rejection reason instead of the
promise — a real error, not something <Suspense> knows what to do with. An
ErrorBoundary from react-error-boundary
catches that:
import { ErrorBoundary } from 'react-error-boundary'
 
function App() {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<ShipError />}>
      <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
        <ShipDetails />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  )
}
The convention — put ErrorBoundary outside Suspense, not inside — is
the same reasoning as any other error boundary: a boundary can’t catch an
error that happens within itself, only errors from its children. If
Suspense (or its own internal machinery) were to error, only a boundary
sitting above it could catch that. Putting ErrorBoundary outermost means
it covers both “the data fetch rejected” and “something went wrong in the
suspending/loading machinery itself.” (This mirrors general ErrorBoundary
placement rules — see Error Boundaries.)
How React actually implements this (fiber internals)
The use Hook’s pseudocode says “React wraps the rendering of your
component in a try/catch.” That’s not just a teaching simplification — it’s
close to literal. The real mechanism, from React’s fiber reconciler:

There genuinely is a try/catch, just not one you write. React’s
render work loop (renderRootSync for sync work, renderRootConcurrent
for concurrent/transition work) wraps the loop that renders each unit of
work — each fiber, roughly one component — in a real try/catch. Your
ShipDetails function itself never has a try/catch in it; the
reconciler has one around the call to it.
On catch, handleError → throwException inspects what was thrown.
The check is exactly the duck-typing you’d expect from
JavaScript Promises: typeof value === 'object' && typeof value.then === 'function'.
A thrown promise (or anything else “thenable”) is treated as a suspend;
anything else is treated as a real error.
Thenable → find the nearest <Suspense> fiber. React walks up the
fiber tree via each fiber’s .return pointer (getNearestSuspenseBoundaryToCapture)
until it hits a SuspenseComponent fiber, marks it with a ShouldCapture
flag, and calls attachPingListener(root, wakeable, lane) — which is
essentially promise.then(ping, ping). Notice: both the fulfilled and
rejected callbacks are the same ping — either way, it just means “this
fiber’s work is unblocked, try rendering it again.”
Non-thenable → find the nearest error-boundary fiber. Same upward
walk, but this time looking for a class component whose type has
getDerivedStateFromError or whose instance has componentDidCatch.
That’s precisely what ErrorBoundary from react-error-boundary is
under the hood: a class component implementing those two lifecycle
methods. React queues a CaptureUpdate that will call
getDerivedStateFromError(error) to compute the boundary’s next state.
The “unwind” phase turns the mark into a re-render. During
completeUnitOfWork, the ShouldCapture flag becomes DidCapture, and
the matched boundary (Suspense or the error-boundary class component)
re-renders showing its fallback instead of its previous children.
When the ping fires, React retries — from scratch, not from where it
left off. The suspended fiber’s subtree renders again as a fresh render
pass. This is why use(promise) doesn’t need to “remember its place” —
it just re-runs the component, and this time the promise (or the workshop’s
hand-rolled usePromise.status) is settled, so use returns synchronously
or throws the rejection reason — a plain error now, which takes the
non-thenable path above straight to the ErrorBoundary.


💬 This is also why ErrorBoundary has to be a class component (or wrap
one) and can’t be a plain function: getDerivedStateFromError/
componentDidCatch are the actual hooks the reconciler’s upward walk is
searching for. There’s no function-component equivalent — it’s baked into
this fiber-walking mechanism, not a limitation react-error-boundary
could work around.

The workshop’s progression, in real code
The exercise builds this up in five steps, each one a real diff on the same
ShipDetails component. All snippets below are the actual solution code.
1. Throw the promise, add <Suspense>. Remove the await; keep a module-level
promise; if the data isn’t in yet, throw the promise:
let ship: Ship
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then((result) => (ship = result))
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (!ship) throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
<Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
  <ShipDetails />
</Suspense>
2. Handle rejection, add ErrorBoundary. Track the rejection reason
alongside the resolved value, and throw it when present:
let ship: Ship
let error: unknown
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then(
  (result) => (ship = result),
  (err) => (error = err),
)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (error) throw error
  if (!ship) throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ShipError />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
    <ShipDetails />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>
3. Formalize the status. Replace the implicit “is ship set? is error
set?” checks with an explicit, single source of truth:
let ship: Ship
let error: unknown
let status: 'pending' | 'rejected' | 'fulfilled' = 'pending'
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then(
  (result) => { ship = result; status = 'fulfilled' },
  (err) => { error = err; status = 'rejected' },
)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (status === 'rejected') throw error
  if (status === 'pending') throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}

💬 The workshop explicitly cites Kent C. Dodds’ own
“Make Impossible States Impossible”
and “Stop using isLoading booleans”
for this step. The argument: separate booleans (isLoading, isError,
plus the data itself) can be combined into states that shouldn’t be
possible — e.g. isLoading: true and stale data both present at once.
A single status enum with one value at a time makes those combinations
structurally impossible instead of just “shouldn’t happen.” You can still
derive convenience booleans from it (const isLoading = status === 'pending')
without losing the guarantee.

4–5. Extract use, then swap in React’s own. This is exactly the
progression documented in The use Hook — steps 3’s three let variables
and if checks collapse into the hand-rolled use<Value> utility, and the
component becomes:
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  const ship = use(shipPromise)
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
…then the hand-rolled use is deleted in favor of import { use } from 'react'
— identical call site, React’s real implementation underneath.
Sources

react.dev — <Suspense>
Kent C. Dodds — Make Impossible States Impossible
Kent C. Dodds — Stop using isLoading booleans
EpicWeb React Suspense workshop, exercise 01.fetching (all 5 steps)
jser.dev — How does ErrorBoundary work internally in React? —
throwException, getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch lookup,
ShouldCapture/DidCapture flags
jser.dev — How Suspense works internally in Concurrent Mode —
thenable detection, getNearestSuspenseBoundaryToCapture, attachPingListener

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: The use Hook
Promise Caching
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Promise Caching

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Dynamic Promises”). Builds directly
on The use Hook and Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching —
read those first if use(promise) throwing a pending promise doesn’t
already make sense.

Interview Q&A
Q: Why does calling a fetch function directly inside a component body break Suspense?
A: This is a general consequence of how use/Suspense identifies “the same”
async operation across renders: it goes purely by promise object identity,
not by what the promise represents. Every render that calls a fetch function
inline creates a brand-new Promise object, so React has no way to know two
calls are “the same fetch” — every re-render (even one triggered by
unrelated state) re-suspends the component. In our example, calling
getShip(shipName) directly inside ShipDetails on every render was
exactly this trap — clicking an unrelated counter button re-triggered the
ship fetch.
Q: How do you fix it, generally?
A: The general technique — usable for any resource, not just this app’s
ships — is to cache the promise itself, not just the eventual data, so
the same promise object is returned across renders for the same input: a
module-level variable for a single value, or a Map keyed by id/parameter
for parameterized fetches. In our example that’s the shipCache Map:
const shipCache = new Map<string, Promise<Ship>>()
 
function getShip(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const shipPromise = shipCache.get(name) ?? getShipImpl(name)
  shipCache.set(name, shipPromise)
  return shipPromise
}
Q: Why should the caching function not be declared async?
A: This is a general JS fact about async functions, not specific to
React: an async function wraps its return value in a new promise on
every call, even if the underlying work is already cached — so a strictly
correct cache guards the call with a plain (non-async) function to
guarantee one promise object per cache entry. In our example, getShipImpl
is written as a plain async function, but the outer getShip that
actually gets called by components is not async — it just returns
whatever promise is already in (or newly added to) the cache.
Q: Does this pattern handle cache invalidation?
A: No, deliberately — and this is a real limitation of the general
technique, not just this example: it caches forever for the page’s
lifetime, with no notion of staleness. Real invalidation, eviction, and
cache keys are a much bigger topic on their own; in production you’d
typically reach for a data-fetching library (React Query, SWR, or a
framework’s cache) instead of hand-rolling this Map. Our example’s
shipCache explicitly punts on this — refreshing the page is the only way
to clear it.
The problem: a new promise on every render
In the Data Fetching examples, the promise passed to use was created
once, outside the component, so it never changed. But real apps need to
fetch dynamic data — e.g. “whichever ship the user currently has selected.”
The naive way to do that is to call the fetch function directly inside the
component:
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
This looks reasonable, but getShip(shipName) runs on every render of
ShipDetails — and every call creates a brand-new Promise object. use
doesn’t know two promises are “the same fetch,” so:

Clicking an unrelated button that re-renders this component re-triggers
the fetch and re-suspends the component, even though shipName didn’t
change.
React actually detects this pattern and warns about it — creating promises
during render like this is unsupported unless something is caching them
for you.

The fix: cache the promise, not just the data
The trick is to make the fetch function return the exact same promise
object for the same input, so use (and Suspense) can recognize “this is
already in flight / already settled” instead of starting over.
Single value, no parameters — a module-level variable is enough:
let userPromise: Promise<User> | undefined
 
function fetchUser() {
  userPromise = userPromise ?? fetchUserImpl()
  return userPromise
}
 
async function fetchUserImpl() {
  const response = await fetch('/api/user')
  return response.json()
}
The first call creates and stores the promise; every call after that returns
the same cached promise instead of calling fetchUserImpl again.
Parameterized fetches (e.g. fetch by id/name) need a Map keyed by that
parameter instead of a single variable:
const shipCache = new Map<string, Promise<Ship>>()
 
function getShip(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const shipPromise = shipCache.get(name) ?? getShipImpl(name)
  shipCache.set(name, shipPromise)
  return shipPromise
}
 
async function getShipImpl(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/ships/${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
Now ShipDetails can stay simple and dynamic:
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
Every render with the same shipName returns the cached promise, so use
only ever suspends the first time a given ship is requested. Switching
back to a previously-loaded ship is instant, and unrelated re-renders no
longer trigger a fetch at all.

💬 One subtlety worth calling out: getShipImpl above should not be
declared async if you want to be strict about “only creating one promise
object” — an async function returns a new promise wrapper around its
body every time it’s called, even if the body itself resolves instantly.
Since getShip already guards the call with the cache check, this rarely
matters in practice, but it’s the difference between “definitely one
promise” and “one fetch, wrapped in a fresh promise shell each time.”

Cache invalidation is out of scope (on purpose)
This pattern caches forever — for the lifetime of the page. It deliberately
doesn’t address:

What happens when the underlying data changes on the server (stale cache).
Evicting old entries so the Map doesn’t grow unbounded.
Keying on more than one parameter, or partial/derived keys.

Kent C. Dodds calls this out explicitly in the workshop: caching correctly
(invalidation, staleness, cache keys) is a whole topic on its own — see his
talk Caching for Cash. In a
real app you’d typically reach for a data-fetching library (React Query,
SWR, or a framework’s built-in cache) rather than hand-rolling this Map.
This simple pattern exists here purely to make use/Suspense work correctly
with dynamic, parameterized data — not as a production caching strategy.
Sources

EpicReact — Promise Cache (exercise + solution)
Kent C. Dodds — Caching for Cash

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Dynamic Promises”, steps 2–3).
Assumes Promise Caching is already in place — this note is about
smoothing the experience of switching between already-cacheable data,
not about fetching itself.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does useTransition do?
A: It marks a state update as non-urgent/lower-priority rather than the
default “urgent” priority every state update gets. Concretely this means:
React can interrupt or delay that low-priority render if something more
urgent comes in (a keystroke, a click), which keeps the UI responsive
instead of janky/blocking on slow renders; and if the low-priority update
would cause a component to suspend, React keeps the currently-committed UI
on screen instead of tearing it down for a Suspense fallback, giving you an
isPending boolean to show your own lighter-weight loading state instead.
Avoiding the Suspense fallback is one visible consequence of that — the
underlying idea is “this update can wait, don’t block on it.” In our
example, wrapping setShipName in startTransition is what keeps the
previously selected ship visible (dimmed) instead of blanking out for the
fallback while the new ship loads:
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
 
function handleShipSelection(newShipName: string) {
  startTransition(() => {
    setShipName(newShipName)
  })
}
Q: When would you use it, beyond avoiding a Suspense fallback?
A: Generally, any time a state update might cause an expensive re-render or
block the main thread long enough to feel janky — filtering a large list,
switching tabs that re-render a heavy chart, typing into a search box that
triggers a costly re-render on every keystroke (keeping the input itself
“urgent” while the results re-render as a lower-priority transition) — even
when nothing suspends at all. Suspense-avoidance (our example: switching
between already-cacheable ships) is just one common case of a broader
“don’t let this update block more important ones” tool.
Q: Does useTransition prevent the fetch/suspend from happening?
A: No, and this is true regardless of what’s inside the transition — it
never changes what work happens, only how React schedules and displays
it. The underlying use/<Suspense> mechanism, or any expensive
computation, still runs exactly the same; the transition just changes the
priority of the update and, if it suspends, suppresses the fallback UI in
favor of isPending. In our example, getShip(shipName) still actually
fetches — startTransition just changes what the user sees while it does.
Q: Why can transitions still show a flash of loading state, and how do you fix it?
A: This is a general UX problem with any asynchronous pending indicator,
not specific to useTransition: if the underlying work resolves very
quickly, a boolean like isPending can flip true then false fast enough
to register as an ugly flicker rather than useful feedback. The general fix
is to decouple “is it pending” from “should I show a spinner” with a
debounce-like rule — which is exactly what useSpinDelay (from the
spin-delay package) does: only show the pending UI if it lasts longer than
a delay, and once shown, hold it for at least a minDuration, so it never
flashes regardless of how fast the network is. In our example:
const showSpinner = useSpinDelay(isPending, { delay: 300, minDuration: 350 })
The problem: every suspend falls back to the Suspense fallback
With Promise Caching in place, switching to a ship you haven’t loaded
yet still suspends the component — that’s correct, there’s a real fetch
happening. But by default, any suspend bubbles up to the nearest
<Suspense> boundary and swaps the entire UI for the fallback, even for a
quick, minor update like picking a different item from a list. That’s a
jarring flash for what should feel like a small state change.
useTransition: keep the old UI, get an isPending flag instead
useTransition lets you mark a state update as a transition. React then
tries to render the new UI in the background while keeping the old UI (and
all its already-resolved data) visible, instead of tearing it down for the
Suspense fallback. You get an isPending boolean to show your own, more
subtle pending state while that happens:
function ShipPicker() {
  const [shipName, setShipName] = useState('dreadnought')
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
 
  function handleShipSelection(newShipName: string) {
    startTransition(() => {
      setShipName(newShipName)
    })
  }
 
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <ShipDetails shipName={shipName} />
      {/* buttons call handleShipSelection(...) */}
    </div>
  )
}
What actually happens when setShipName runs inside startTransition:

React starts rendering ShipDetails with the new shipName in the
background, without committing it yet.
If that render suspends (the new ship isn’t cached yet), React does
not show the Suspense fallback. Instead, it keeps showing the
previously committed UI and sets isPending to true.
isPending drives your own inline loading treatment — here, just
dimming the details to opacity: 0.6 — instead of blowing away the UI.
Once the new ship’s promise resolves, React commits the new render and
isPending flips back to false.

The only two things that changed versus a plain setShipName(newShipName)
call: wrap the update in startTransition, and use the returned isPending
for a local loading indicator. Everything about use/<Suspense> from
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching keeps working exactly the
same underneath — useTransition only changes what the user sees while a
suspend is happening, not whether it happens.

📜 useTransition docs

The next problem: transitions can flash too
isPending solves the “replace the whole screen” problem, but it introduces
a smaller version of the same issue: if the fetch resolves very quickly
(say, 50ms), the user still sees a brief flicker of opacity: 0.6 and back.
Delaying the pending UI with a CSS transition doesn’t really fix
this — it just moves the threshold at which the flash happens (a request
that takes slightly longer than your CSS delay still flashes).
useSpinDelay: only show pending state if it’s actually worth showing
The spin-delay package solves this with two
rules:

If the pending state resolves in under delay ms, never show a spinner
at all.
If it takes longer than delay, show the spinner for at least
minDuration ms — even if the data arrives right after the delay window,
so the spinner itself doesn’t flash.

import { useSpinDelay } from 'spin-delay'
 
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  const [isTransitionPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  const showSpinner = useSpinDelay(isTransitionPending, {
    delay: 300,
    minDuration: 350,
  })
 
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: showSpinner ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
    </div>
  )
}
With delay: 300, minDuration: 350:

Fetch takes 100ms → showSpinner never becomes true. No flash.
Fetch takes 400ms → showSpinner becomes true at the 300ms mark and
stays true until at least 300 + 350 = 650ms, even though the data was
ready at 400ms. No flash, just a clean, deliberate loading state.

useSpinDelay doesn’t replace useTransition — it just wraps the
isPending boolean useTransition gives you with debounce-like timing
rules, so what the user actually sees stays smooth regardless of how fast
or slow the network happens to be.
Sources

EpicReact — useTransition (exercise + solution)
EpicReact — Pending Flash (exercise + solution)
react.dev — useTransition
spin-delay on npm
