claude/03-prompt-evaluation/07-exercise-.content:
Exercise on prompt evals


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt evaluation — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson is a hands-on exercise where the learner builds a small eval pipeline from scratch, applying everything covered earlier in the module: assembling a test dataset, running a prompt against it, and grading the results with either a model judge or code. The goal is to practice the full loop once, end to end, rather than just reading about each piece separately.
Deep dive
The exact exercise instructions and starter materials for this lesson aren’t available here, so rather than inventing specifics, this section covers what a learner would typically build to practice the concepts from this module, and what a solid outcome looks like.
A realistic practice project. Pick a small, well-scoped prompt task — something like a support-ticket classifier, a data extractor (pulling structured fields out of unstructured text), or a short-summary generator. The task should be small enough to build a dataset and eval loop for in a single sitting, but real enough that grading isn’t trivial. Classification and extraction tasks are good first choices because they support both code-based and model-based grading, so they let you practice both approaches from “Model based grading” and “Code based grading” on the same project.
Step 1: Write success criteria. Before building anything else, write one or two sentences defining what a correct output looks like for your task, following the pattern from “A typical eval workflow.” For a classifier, this might just be “the predicted label matches the true label.” For an extractor, “every required field is present and matches the source text, and no field is fabricated when the source doesn’t mention it.”
Step 2: Build a small dataset. Following “Generating test datasets,” assemble 15–30 test cases. If you don’t have real data handy, prompt Claude to generate synthetic examples with ground-truth labels attached, and deliberately ask for a few ambiguous or edge-case examples in addition to straightforward ones — this is what makes the eval actually informative rather than trivially easy to pass.
Step 3: Write the prompt, and run it against the dataset. Following “Running the eval,” write a short Python script using the Anthropic SDK that loops over your dataset, calls the API for each item, and saves the raw input/output pairs to a file. Set temperature low (e.g., 0) so results are as consistent as possible while you’re iterating.
Step 4: Grade the results. Implement at least one grading method end to end:

If your task has a clear right answer (classification label, required JSON fields), write a small Python grading function per “Code based grading” — exact match or schema validation — and compute a pass rate.
If your task involves any subjective judgment (does the summary capture the key points? is the tone appropriate?), write a judge prompt per “Model based grading,” with the content to grade wrapped in XML tags and a concrete rubric, and have Claude score each output.

Step 5: Look at the failures, not just the score. Whatever your pass rate comes out to, read through the specific cases that failed. Look for a pattern — is the prompt confusing two categories, hallucinating a field, missing an instruction? Make one targeted edit to the prompt to address that pattern, then rerun the exact same eval and confirm the previously-failing cases now pass without the previously-passing cases breaking.
What success looks like: by the end, you should have (1) a saved dataset file, (2) a script that runs a prompt against it and saves raw outputs, (3) a grading function or judge prompt that turns those outputs into a score, and (4) at least one documented iteration where you used a failure pattern to improve the prompt and confirmed the improvement with a rerun of the same eval. The specific accuracy number matters far less than demonstrating the full loop works and that you can trust the score it produces — that loop is the actual skill this module is teaching, and it’s the same one you’d reuse on a real production prompt.
A common trap to avoid during the exercise: don’t tune the prompt by staring only at the two or three examples that failed and rewriting the prompt until just those pass. Always rerun the entire dataset after a change, since a fix targeted too narrowly at specific failures can regress cases that were previously working — this is the overfitting pitfall introduced back in “Prompt evaluation,” and the exercise is a good low-stakes place to notice it happening.
Key takeaways

The exercise is a hands-on rehearsal of the full eval workflow: criteria, dataset, run, grade, revise, rerun.
A small classification or extraction task is a good practice project because it supports both code-based and model-based grading.
Deliberately include a few ambiguous or edge-case examples in the dataset — an eval that’s too easy teaches you nothing.
Success is having a working, reusable pipeline and one verified iteration, not a specific accuracy number.
Always rerun the full eval after a prompt change, rather than checking only the cases you were trying to fix, to avoid overfitting to a handful of examples.

Related lessons
Previous: 06 Code based grading

claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.title: Prompt engineering
claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.content:
Prompt engineering


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt engineering techniques — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Prompt engineering is the practice of carefully crafting the instructions and context you give Claude to reliably get the output you want. It’s the fastest, cheapest lever for improving a model’s behavior on your task — usually much faster to iterate on than retraining or fine-tuning a model — which is why it’s the starting point for almost every application built on the Claude API.
Deep dive
When a model’s output isn’t quite what you want, the instinct might be to assume the model itself needs to change — a bigger model, a fine-tuned model, more training data. In practice, the first and most effective lever is almost always the prompt itself. The same model, given a clearer, more specific, better-structured prompt, will very often produce a noticeably better result. Prompt engineering is the discipline of finding that better prompt deliberately, rather than by luck.
It helps to think of prompt engineering as genuinely iterative, much like the eval workflow from the previous module. You write a prompt, test it against representative inputs, notice where it falls short, and revise — repeating until performance is good enough for your use case. This module introduces the concrete techniques you reach for during that revision step: being clear and direct, being specific, structuring input with XML tags, and providing examples. Each is a distinct lever, and real prompts usually combine several of them at once.
Why prompting works as well as it does. Claude is trained on enormous amounts of text and fine-tuned to follow instructions, but it has no access to your specific intent beyond what’s in the prompt. It can’t read your mind about what “a good summary” means to you, or what tone your brand voice requires, or what output format your downstream code expects to parse. A vague prompt forces the model to guess at all of that, and it will guess reasonably but not perfectly. A well-engineered prompt closes that gap by making the implicit explicit — spelling out exactly what’s wanted so there’s less left to infer.
A quick before/after to set the tone for the module. Consider a prompt meant to generate product descriptions for an e-commerce site:
Before: “Write a description for this product: wireless earbuds, noise cancelling, 30-hour battery.”
After: “Write a 2-3 sentence product description for an e-commerce listing, in an upbeat but not overly salesy tone. Lead with the key benefit for the customer, not a list of specs. Product: wireless earbuds with noise cancellation and 30-hour battery life. Avoid superlatives like ‘best’ or ‘amazing.’”
The underlying model and product haven’t changed at all — only the prompt has become clearer about length, tone, structure, and constraints. That’s the entire premise of this module: small, deliberate changes to how a prompt is written can produce large, measurable differences in output quality, and the coming lessons each isolate one specific way to make that change.
How this connects to prompt evaluation. The previous module covered how to measure whether a prompt is actually good; this module covers concrete techniques for making it better. In practice the two are used together constantly — you apply a technique from this module (say, adding examples), then use the eval workflow to confirm it actually improved the metric you care about, rather than just assuming it helped. A technique that seems obviously better in isolation can sometimes underperform on your specific eval, which is exactly why measurement matters alongside technique.
A note on scope. Prompt engineering is not a substitute for good product design — if a task fundamentally requires information the model doesn’t have (private data, real-time facts), no amount of clever prompting will supply it; that’s a job for providing that data via context, tools, or retrieval, which are covered elsewhere in the broader course. Within this module, the techniques assume the model already has what it needs to succeed, and focus purely on how to ask for it effectively.
The next lesson, “Being clear and direct,” is the foundational technique underlying everything else here: most prompt failures trace back to instructions that were ambiguous or left something to inference that should have been stated outright.
Key takeaways

Prompt engineering is usually the fastest, cheapest way to improve a model’s output on a specific task, before considering fine-tuning or a different model.
It’s an iterative practice: write, test, observe failures, revise — the same loop introduced in the prompt evaluation module.
A vague prompt forces Claude to guess at your intent; a well-engineered prompt makes that intent explicit.
This module’s techniques (clarity, specificity, XML structure, examples) are levers that are typically combined, not used in isolation.
Prompt engineering pairs with evals: apply a technique, then measure whether it actually improved the metric that matters for your task.

Related lessons
Next: 02 Being clear and direct

claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.title: Being clear and direct
claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.content:
Being clear and direct


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt engineering techniques — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Being clear and direct means telling Claude exactly what you want, spelling out steps and expectations rather than hinting at them. Claude follows instructions well, but it can only act on what’s actually written in the prompt — so anything left vague or implied is something it has to guess, and guesses aren’t always the guess you wanted.
Deep dive
A useful mental exercise, and one Anthropic explicitly recommends, is to imagine handing your prompt to a new colleague who has zero context on your task, your company, or your preferences, and who can only do exactly what the prompt says — nothing more, nothing assumed. If that colleague would be confused about what to do, or would have to guess at details you cared about, Claude will face the same gap. This is often called the “golden rule” of prompting: if a smart person reading your prompt cold couldn’t produce the output you want, the prompt needs more clarity.
Before/after: a data-cleaning task.
Vague: “Clean up this customer list.”
A new colleague reading this has no idea what “clean up” means here — remove duplicates? Fix formatting? Remove test accounts? Standardize phone numbers? Claude, given the same vague instruction, has to guess too, and it might guess something different from what you had in mind.
Clear and direct: “Here is a list of customer records. Remove any duplicate rows (same email address). Standardize all phone numbers to the format (XXX) XXX-XXXX. Remove any row where the email domain is ‘test.com’ or ‘example.com’. Leave all other fields unchanged. Return the result as a table with the same columns as the input.”
The second version leaves almost nothing to inference — every action is spelled out, along with the exact criteria for each one and the expected output format.
Before/after: a writing task.
Vague: “Write something for our onboarding email.”
Clear and direct: “Write the body of a welcome email for new users of a project management app. It should: (1) thank them for signing up, (2) point them to one specific first action — creating their first project, (3) mention that support is available via the in-app chat icon. Keep it to 3 short paragraphs. Do not include a subject line, greeting, or sign-off — just the body text.”
Notice what the second version does: it breaks the task into an explicit numbered list of required content, states a length constraint, and — just as importantly — states what not to include. Negative constraints (“do not include X”) are just as much a part of being direct as positive instructions, since Claude otherwise has no way to know that a greeting or sign-off wasn’t wanted.
Where instructions commonly stay too implicit, even from experienced prompt writers:

Output format. “Summarize this” leaves open whether you want bullet points, a paragraph, a specific length, or a particular structure. State it: “Summarize this in exactly 3 bullet points, each under 20 words.”
Scope and boundaries. “Answer questions about our product” doesn’t say what to do when a question is out of scope. State the fallback: “If the question is unrelated to [product], say so and don’t attempt to answer it.”
Sequencing. For multi-step tasks, numbering the steps explicitly (“First do X, then do Y, then do Z”) produces more reliable results than describing the same steps in a single dense sentence, because it removes ambiguity about order and completeness.
Edge cases. What should happen if the input is empty, contradictory, or missing expected information? A prompt that only describes the happy path leaves the model to improvise when reality doesn’t cooperate.

Pitfall: being direct is not the same as being verbose. Padding a prompt with excessive caveats, redundant restatements, or hedging language (“please try to,” “if possible, maybe consider”) doesn’t add clarity — it can actually dilute the instructions that matter by burying them among ones that don’t. The goal is precision, not length. A short, unambiguous instruction beats a long, hedgy one.
This lesson is the foundation the rest of the module builds on. “Being specific” narrows in on one particular dimension of clarity — precision of detail, especially around format and constraints. “Structure with XML tags” and “Providing examples” are both, in a sense, tools for being clear and direct at scale: they’re ways of making instructions and expectations unambiguous when a plain paragraph of prose would get unwieldy or easy to misread.
Key takeaways

Write prompts as if for a new colleague with zero context who can only do exactly what’s written — no assumed background knowledge.
Spell out format, scope, sequencing, and edge cases explicitly rather than leaving them implied.
State what should not be included or done, not just what should — negative constraints matter as much as positive ones.
Numbering steps in multi-step tasks reduces ambiguity about order and completeness.
Clarity is about precision, not length — padding a prompt with hedging or redundant caveats doesn’t make it clearer.

Related lessons
Previous: 01 Prompt engineering
Next: 03 Being specific

claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.filePath: Claude/04 Prompt engineering techniques/03 Being specific.md
claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.title: Being specific
claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.content:
Being specific


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt engineering techniques — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Being specific means replacing general, open-ended requests with precise details about exactly what you want — the exact format, the exact length, the exact criteria for a decision. Where “being clear and direct” is about not leaving things implied, being specific is about how narrowly and concretely you define what you did state, so there’s only one reasonable way to satisfy the instruction.
Deep dive
Clarity and specificity work together but aren’t quite the same thing. A prompt can be direct and unambiguous about what task to do while still being vague about how exactly to do it. Specificity closes that second gap — it’s the difference between “format this as a list” and “format this as a numbered list with no more than 5 items, each a single sentence under 15 words.”
Before/after: specificity in output format.
General: “Give me the key points from this meeting transcript.”
This could reasonably produce three sentences or thirty, a paragraph or a list, formal or casual language — all technically valid ways to satisfy the request.
Specific: “Give me the key points from this meeting transcript as a bulleted list of exactly 5 items. Each bullet should be a single sentence, start with an action verb where the point involves a decision or task, and be no longer than 20 words. Order the bullets by importance, most important first.”
Now there’s essentially one shape the correct answer can take, which makes the output far more predictable and far easier to consume programmatically or drop directly into a report.
Before/after: specificity in criteria.
General: “Tell me if this email sounds urgent.”
“Urgent” is doing a lot of unstated work here — urgent to whom, based on what signals?
Specific: “Classify this email’s urgency as HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW. Use HIGH if it mentions a deadline within 24 hours, a system outage, or uses words like ‘immediately’ or ‘ASAP’. Use MEDIUM if it requests a response but has no explicit deadline. Use LOW for informational messages that don’t require action. Respond with only the single word HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW.”
Defining the exact criteria for each category, and constraining the output to one of three fixed words, removes almost all room for the model (or a human reviewer checking its work) to disagree about what counts as urgent.
Specificity around numbers and constraints. Vague quantity words — “a few,” “some,” “brief,” “concise” — mean different things to different readers, and the model has to pick an interpretation. Replacing them with actual numbers removes that guesswork: “a few examples” becomes “3 examples”; “keep it brief” becomes “under 100 words”; “a short list” becomes “no more than 5 items.” This is a small change that consistently tightens output variance.
Specificity in defining roles and audience. “Explain this concept” is less specific than “Explain this concept to a high school student with no background in the subject, using one concrete analogy.” The second version tells the model not just what to explain but the register, depth, and rhetorical device to use — all specific parameters that shape the actual content of the answer, not just its format.
How this connects to evaluation. Specificity is exactly what makes code-based grading possible, as covered in the prompt evaluation module. A prompt that outputs “HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW” from a fixed set can be graded with a simple exact-match check; a prompt that vaguely says “tell me if it’s urgent” produces free-text output that can only really be graded by a model judge, which is slower and noisier. Tightening a prompt’s specificity often has the side benefit of making it dramatically easier and cheaper to evaluate later.
Pitfall: over-specifying at the cost of missing the point. It’s possible to be so specific about surface details (exact word counts, exact formatting) that the underlying task quality suffers — for example, forcing a summary into exactly 3 bullet points when the source material genuinely needs 5 to be accurate. Specificity should target things you actually care about controlling; if length is flexible but tone is what matters most, put the specificity budget on tone, not an artificial word cap. As with the previous lesson, more specific isn’t always better — it should be deliberately aimed at the dimensions of the output that genuinely need to be pinned down for your use case.
The next lesson, “Structure with XML tags,” introduces a complementary technique for handling prompts that need to be both clear and specific but also contain multiple distinct pieces of content (instructions, examples, source documents) that could otherwise blur together in a single block of text.
Key takeaways

Specificity narrows down how a task should be done, not just what the task is — format, criteria, and constraints should be spelled out concretely.
Replace vague quantity or quality words (“a few,” “brief,” “urgent”) with concrete numbers and defined criteria.
Defining a fixed output format (like a closed set of labels) makes downstream parsing and code-based grading much easier.
Specifying audience and register shapes not just the format but the actual content of a response.
Aim specificity at the dimensions of output you actually care about controlling — over-specifying irrelevant details can hurt output quality.

claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.content:
Structure with XML tags


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt engineering techniques — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Structuring a prompt with XML tags means wrapping distinct pieces of content — instructions, source documents, examples, output format — in tags like <document>...</document> so Claude can clearly tell them apart. Claude has been specifically trained to pay close attention to XML-tagged structure, so using tags reduces the chance it confuses your instructions with the content it’s supposed to act on.
Deep dive
As prompts grow beyond a single instruction — once they include a document to analyze, a few examples, formatting requirements, and the actual question — plain prose starts to blur together. A wall of unstructured text forces the model (and any human reading it later) to infer where one section ends and another begins. XML tags solve this by making the boundaries explicit and unambiguous.
Before/after: a document analysis prompt.
Unstructured: “Here is a contract: [contract text]. Summarize the payment terms. Also here are two examples of good summaries: [example 1] [example 2]. Keep your summary under 100 words.”
Read closely, this is actually confusing — where does the contract end and the first example begin? Is “keep your summary under 100 words” an instruction for the final answer, or part of the second example? A model has to parse all of this correctly by guessing at boundaries from context, and it’s easy to see how it could misattribute a sentence to the wrong section.
Structured with XML tags:
<contract>
[contract text]
</contract>

<examples>
<example>
[example 1]
</example>
<example>
[example 2]
</example>
</examples>

<instructions>
Summarize the payment terms in the contract above.
Keep your summary under 100 words.
</instructions>

Now every section has an unambiguous boundary. There’s no possible confusion about whether “under 100 words” applies to the task or is quoted text from an example — it’s clearly inside <instructions>, separate from everything else.
Commonly used tag names. There’s no fixed, required vocabulary — you can name tags whatever makes sense for your content — but some conventional, self-explanatory choices show up often: <document> or <source> for reference material the model should read but not treat as instructions, <example> (often nested inside <examples>) for demonstrations, <instructions> for the actual task, <question> for a user query, <format> for output formatting requirements, and <thinking> or <reasoning> for asking the model to work through a problem before giving a final answer. What matters more than the specific names is that they’re descriptive, consistent, and used the same way every time the prompt is reused.
Referencing tags in your instructions. Once content is tagged, you can refer back to it by name, which is itself a form of clarity: “Using only the information in the <document> tags above, answer the question in <question> tags. If the answer isn’t in the document, say so.” This is more precise than “using the above information, answer the question,” because it removes any doubt about which “above information” is meant when there are multiple sections above.
Why this matters for grading, too. XML structure isn’t just useful in prompts you send to Claude — it’s exactly the technique recommended in “Model based grading” for judge prompts, wrapping the content being graded and the rubric in separate tags so the judge model can’t confuse them. The same principle — separate distinct content types clearly — applies whether Claude is the one performing the task or the one grading it.
Pitfalls:

Inconsistent or overlapping tag names. Using <example> to mean two different things in the same prompt, or nesting tags incorrectly (<examples><example>...</examples></example>), reintroduces the exact ambiguity tags are meant to prevent. Keep tag structure clean and properly nested.
Over-tagging trivial content. Wrapping every single sentence in its own tag adds visual noise without adding clarity. Reserve tags for genuinely distinct sections — a whole document, a whole instruction block, a whole example — not every clause within them.
Tags don’t replace clear instructions. Structure organizes content; it doesn’t substitute for the specificity and directness covered in the previous two lessons. A well-tagged but vague instruction inside <instructions> is still a vague instruction.
Untrusted content inside tags. If a <document> tag contains text from an external or user-submitted source, that text could contain something designed to look like an instruction (a prompt injection attempt). Tags help contain this by making clear that content is data, not instructions, but it’s worth explicitly telling the model in your instructions to treat everything inside <document> as content to analyze, never as commands to follow — the same injection concern raised in “Model based grading.”

The next lesson, “Providing examples,” builds directly on this one: examples are almost always most effective when wrapped in their own XML tags, which is why the <examples> structure appears again there in more depth.
Key takeaways

XML tags make the boundaries between distinct prompt sections (instructions, documents, examples, format) explicit rather than inferred from prose.
Claude has been trained to pay close attention to XML structure, making tagged prompts more reliable at scale than unstructured prose.
Tag names aren’t fixed by a spec — use descriptive, consistent names like <document>, <instructions>, <example>, and reference them explicitly in your instructions.
The same tagging technique is used for grading prompts (separating graded content from the rubric) as for task prompts.
Keep tags well-nested and reserved for genuinely distinct sections; over-tagging or inconsistent naming reintroduces the ambiguity tags are meant to remove.

claude/04-prompt-engineering-techniques/.content:
Exercise on prompting


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Prompt engineering techniques — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson is a hands-on exercise where the learner takes a rough, underspecified prompt and improves it by applying the techniques from this module — clarity, specificity, XML structure, and examples — one at a time or in combination. The goal is to build the habit of noticing exactly what’s making a prompt underperform and fixing it deliberately, rather than by trial and error alone.
Deep dive
The exact exercise instructions and starter prompt for this lesson aren’t available here, so rather than inventing specifics, this section covers what a learner would typically practice given the four techniques covered earlier in the module, and what a strong result looks like.
A realistic practice approach: start from a deliberately weak prompt. Pick (or write) a vague, one-line prompt for a task with some real complexity — for example, “Summarize this article” for a task where you actually care about length, tone, what to include, and what to leave out. Run it once and look at the output critically: where did the model have to guess something you actually cared about? Every place it guessed is a place the prompt was under-specified.
Step 1: Apply clarity and directness. Following “Being clear and direct,” rewrite the prompt as if for a new colleague with no context. Spell out the task in full: what exactly should be summarized, what should be excluded, what happens with edge cases (an article with no clear main point, a very short article). Add any negative constraints that matter (“don’t include the author’s opinion, only factual claims from the article”).
Step 2: Apply specificity. Following “Being specific,” replace any remaining vague terms with concrete numbers and criteria. “Keep it short” becomes “3-4 sentences.” “Cover the main points” becomes an explicit list of what a “main point” means for this task (e.g., “any claim the article devotes more than one paragraph to”).
Step 3: Add XML structure. Following “Structure with XML tags,” wrap the source article, the instructions, and (if used) any examples in their own tags, and reference them explicitly in the instructions (“Summarize only the content inside <article> tags”).
Step 4: Add a few examples. Following “Providing examples,” write 2-3 example article/summary pairs that demonstrate the exact length, tone, and level of detail you want, covering at least one straightforward case and one harder or more ambiguous one. Wrap them in <examples> tags as shown in the previous lesson.
Step 5: Compare outputs before and after. Run the original vague prompt and the fully rewritten prompt on the same 3-5 test articles, side by side. Look specifically for the gaps you identified in Step 1 — did the rewritten prompt actually close them? If a particular gap remains (say, length is still inconsistent), figure out which technique should have addressed it and sharpen that part of the prompt rather than adding unrelated changes.
A good stretch goal: connect back to the previous module. If you completed the exercise from “Exercise on prompt evals,” try applying that eval loop here — build a tiny dataset of 10-15 inputs for whatever task you’re practicing, grade the before and after prompts against it (code-based grading works well for something like length compliance or presence of required content; model-based grading works well for tone and coverage), and confirm with an actual score that the rewritten prompt improved on the vague one, rather than assuming it did because it reads better.
What success looks like: a side-by-side comparison of a vague prompt and its improved version, where you can point to specific, identifiable changes and connect each one back to a specific technique (clarity, specificity, XML structure, examples) — not just a vague sense that the second version is “better.” The improved prompt’s output should be noticeably more consistent across repeated runs and across different test inputs than the original, since reducing the model’s need to guess is exactly what consistency depends on.
A common trap to avoid: don’t apply all four techniques simultaneously without noticing which one actually did the work. If possible, make changes incrementally — add clarity first and check the output, then specificity and check again, and so on — so you build an intuition for which technique matters most for which kind of problem. That diagnostic skill (recognizing why a prompt is failing, not just applying every technique reflexively) is the actual outcome this exercise is meant to build.
Key takeaways

The exercise is a hands-on rehearsal of applying clarity, specificity, XML structure, and examples to improve a deliberately weak starting prompt.
Diagnosing exactly where a prompt lets the model guess is the first step, before deciding which technique to apply.
Applying techniques incrementally, one at a time, builds a better intuition for which one addresses which kind of failure than applying all four at once.
Comparing before/after outputs on the same set of test inputs, ideally with an eval-style score, makes the improvement verifiable rather than assumed.
Success is a demonstrated, technique-by-technique improvement in output consistency, not a specific score or a “nicer sounding” prompt.

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/01-introd.content:
Introducing tool use


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Claude can only generate text — it cannot check today’s weather, query a database, or run code on its own. Tool use (“function calling”) is the mechanism that lets you hand Claude a menu of functions it’s allowed to ask for, so it can request the exact information or action it needs, and you run that function on its behalf. This lesson introduces why that matters: it turns Claude from a text generator into something that can act on real, current, external data.
Deep dive
Without tool use, Claude answers purely from what’s in the prompt and what it learned during training — which means it can’t know today’s stock price, can’t query your internal database, and can’t perform precise calculations reliably. Tool use closes that gap. You describe one or more functions (“tools”) to Claude — their names, what they do, and what arguments they take — and Claude decides, based on the conversation, whether it needs to call one to answer the user’s question. Claude never executes anything itself; it only produces a structured request describing which tool it wants and with what arguments. Your code is responsible for actually running that function and feeding the result back.
This is fundamentally different from a normal single-turn API call. A tool-use interaction is a loop: user asks a question, you send it to Claude along with your tool definitions, Claude may respond by asking to use a tool, you execute the tool locally, you send the result back to Claude, and Claude uses that result to either call another tool or produce a final answer. This lesson sets up the mental model for that entire loop before the course dives into implementation.
A minimal skeleton of what’s coming later in the module:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
tools = [
    {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get the current weather in a given location",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"
                }
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
]
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in San Francisco?"}]
)
 
print(response.stop_reason)  # "tool_use" if Claude wants to call get_weather
Three pieces make up every tool-use system, each of which gets its own lesson in this module:

Tool functions — the actual code you write that does the work (e.g. hitting a weather API).
Tool schemas — the JSON Schema description you give Claude so it knows the tool exists and how to call it correctly.
The message loop — reading tool_use blocks from Claude’s response, running the function, and sending a tool_result back.

A common pitfall even at this conceptual stage: assuming Claude “runs” the tool. It does not — Claude only ever emits a request. If you don’t implement the execution and result-sending side, the conversation stalls at stop_reason: "tool_use" with nothing happening. Keeping this client-server split clear (Claude proposes, your code executes) is the foundation for everything that follows in this module, including the hands-on project introduced in the next lesson.
Key takeaways

Tool use lets Claude request that a defined function be called, but Claude never executes code itself — your application does.
A tool-using interaction is a loop, not a single call: request → tool request → execution → result → (repeat or final answer).
Three core pieces make it work: tool functions (your code), tool schemas (what you tell Claude), and the message-passing loop.
This lesson is the conceptual foundation for the whole module, which culminates in a hands-on tool-using project.

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/02-projec.content:
Project overview


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson previews the hands-on project the module builds toward: a working assistant that uses one or more tools to answer questions it couldn’t answer from text alone. Instead of learning tool use as isolated facts, you’ll assemble each concept — schemas, execution, results, multi-turn loops — into a single running program by the end of the module.
Deep dive
Courses that teach tool use conceptually often leave a gap between “I understand what a tool_use block is” and “I can build something that actually works end to end.” This lesson exists to close that gap by framing the rest of the module as one continuous build rather than a series of disconnected demos. Every lesson that follows — tool functions, tool schemas, handling message blocks, sending tool results, multi-turn conversations, multiple tools, forced tool calling, and the built-in text editor and web search tools — adds one more capability to the same underlying project.
The shape of that project follows the standard tool-use architecture you’ll implement piece by piece:

Define one or more tool functions — real Python functions that do the work (e.g. look something up, compute something, edit a file).
Describe each function to Claude as a tool schema using JSON Schema, so Claude knows the tool’s name, purpose, and expected arguments.
Send a user message plus your tools list to the Messages API.
Handle the response: check stop_reason, and if it’s "tool_use", walk the content list for tool_use blocks.
Execute the requested function locally with the arguments Claude provided.
Send the result back as a tool_result content block in a new user message, matching the tool_use_id Claude gave you.
Loop: repeat steps 3–6 until Claude’s stop_reason is no longer "tool_use" — meaning it has everything it needs to give a final, direct answer.

By the end of the module, this loop is extended to support several tools at once (letting Claude pick and even call multiple in parallel), forced tool calling via tool_choice (for cases where you want to guarantee a specific tool gets used, or guarantee exactly one call), and Anthropic’s built-in server-side tools — the text editor tool (str_replace_based_edit_tool) for making edits to files, and the web search tool (web_search_20250305) for pulling in live information from the internet.
A basic client setup you’ll reuse and extend throughout the project:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
 
def run_tool(name: str, tool_input: dict) -> str:
    """Dispatch to the correct local function based on the tool name Claude requested."""
    if name == "get_weather":
        return f"It's 68°F and sunny in {tool_input['location']}."
    return f"Unknown tool: {name}"
This lesson doesn’t introduce new API mechanics on its own — its job is to set expectations and give you a mental map of where each subsequent lesson’s piece fits, so that when you reach “Implementing multiple turns” and “Using multiple tools,” you’re assembling a program you already understand the shape of rather than seeing it for the first time.
Key takeaways

The module builds toward one cumulative project: a working tool-using assistant, not isolated demos.
Each following lesson adds one piece of the standard tool-use pipeline: schema → response handling → execution → result → loop.
The project later grows to include multiple tools, forced tool calling (tool_choice), and Anthropic’s built-in text editor and web search tools.
Understanding this end-to-end shape now makes the later, more mechanical lessons easier to place in context.

Next: 03 Tool functions

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/04-tool-s.content:
Tool schemas


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Claude can’t read your Python code, so you describe each tool to it using a structured format: a name, a description, and a JSON Schema of the expected arguments. This description — the “tool schema” — is how Claude decides whether a tool is relevant and how to call it correctly. A clear, well-written schema is the single biggest factor in getting reliable tool calls.
Deep dive
Every tool you give Claude is a JSON object with three fields, passed in a tools list on the Messages API request:

name — a unique identifier, the string Claude will send back when it wants to call this tool. Must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$.
description — a natural-language explanation of what the tool does and when to use it. This is the field Claude actually reasons over to decide whether to call the tool, so vague descriptions (“does stuff with weather”) lead to Claude either not calling it when it should, or calling it inappropriately. Be specific about what the tool returns and any constraints.
input_schema — a JSON Schema object describing the shape of the arguments the tool accepts: type: "object", a properties map, and a required array.

tools = [
    {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get the current weather in a given location. Returns temperature and conditions.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"
                },
                "unit": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                    "description": "The unit of temperature"
                }
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
]
Key JSON Schema mechanics that carry over directly:

properties supports standard JSON Schema types: string, number, integer, boolean, array, object.
enum restricts a field to a fixed set of values (useful for units, categories, statuses) and meaningfully improves reliability versus a free-text string.
required lists which properties must be present; anything not listed is optional, and Claude may omit it.
Nested objects and arrays of objects are supported, so schemas can describe fairly rich structured input (e.g. an attendees array of email strings, or a nested recurrence object with its own frequency and count fields).
Some SDKs also accept an input_examples field (a list of example input dicts) to further disambiguate how a tool should be called, especially for optional parameters.

You pass the whole tools array on every request in the conversation — including follow-up requests after a tool result has been sent — because Claude needs to see the tool definitions again to potentially call another tool or to know what was available when producing its final answer.
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Tokyo in celsius?"}]
)
Common pitfalls with schemas:

Vague descriptions. The description is Claude’s only window into what the tool does — treat it like documentation for a teammate who can’t see the source code.
Missing or wrong required fields. If a field is actually mandatory for your function to work but isn’t marked required, Claude may omit it, and your function call will fail or behave unexpectedly.
Type mismatches. If your tool function expects an integer but the schema says string, Claude will happily supply a string, and you’ll need to cast/validate it yourself before calling the function.
Overloaded single tools. A tool that tries to do too many unrelated things with many optional flags is harder for Claude to use correctly than several small, clearly-scoped tools — this becomes especially relevant once you get to “Using multiple tools” and “Fine grained tool calling” later in the module.

Getting the schema right is what makes the next lesson — reading the tool_use block Claude sends back — reliable, since a well-constrained schema means the input dict you receive will consistently have the fields your tool function expects.
Key takeaways

Every tool has three fields: name, description, and input_schema (standard JSON Schema).
description is what Claude reasons over to decide whether/how to call a tool — write it precisely.
required and enum meaningfully constrain and improve the reliability of Claude’s tool calls.
Pass the full tools list on every request in a multi-turn tool conversation, not just the first one.

Next: 05 Handling message blocks

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/05-handli.content:
Handling message blocks


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
When Claude wants to use a tool, its response isn’t just plain text — it’s a list of structured “content blocks,” some of which are ordinary text and some of which are tool_use requests. This lesson is about reading that response correctly: checking why Claude stopped, and pulling out the tool name, ID, and arguments it wants to use.
Deep dive
A Messages API response has a content field that’s always a list of blocks, not a single string — even a plain-text reply is a list with one text block. When tools are involved, that list can contain a mix of block types in the same response: Claude often emits a text block explaining what it’s about to do, followed by one or more tool_use blocks.
The top-level stop_reason field tells you why generation stopped. The one to watch for in tool use is "tool_use" — it means Claude has paused specifically because it wants a tool executed before it can continue. (Contrast with "end_turn", meaning Claude finished its answer with no further tool calls needed, and "max_tokens", meaning it was cut off.)
Example response shape:
{
  "id": "msg_01Aq9w938a90dw8q",
  "model": "claude-opus-5",
  "stop_reason": "tool_use",
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "I'll check the current weather in San Francisco for you."
    },
    {
      "type": "tool_use",
      "id": "toolu_01A09q90qw90lq917835lq9",
      "name": "get_weather",
      "input": { "location": "San Francisco, CA", "unit": "celsius" }
    }
  ]
}
Each tool_use block has three fields you need:

id — a unique identifier for this specific tool call (e.g. toolu_01A09q90qw90lq917835lq9). You must echo this back exactly in the matching tool_result’s tool_use_id — mismatches break the conversation.
name — which tool Claude wants to call, matching one of the names in your tools list.
input — a dict of arguments, already validated against your schema’s shape, ready to be unpacked into your tool function.

In Python, handling this means checking stop_reason and then iterating response.content, filtering for blocks where .type == "tool_use":
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in San Francisco?"}]
)
 
if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "text":
            print("Claude said:", block.text)
        elif block.type == "tool_use":
            print("Tool requested:", block.name)
            print("Tool call ID:", block.id)
            print("Arguments:", block.input)
A response can contain more than one tool_use block — Claude is allowed to request several tool calls in parallel within a single turn (this becomes central in “Using multiple tools” later in the module). Your handling code needs to loop over all blocks of type tool_use, not just grab the first one, or you’ll silently drop tool calls Claude expected to be executed.
Common pitfalls:

Assuming content has exactly one block. It’s always a list; treat it as such even when you expect a single text reply.
Only checking the first block. If Claude emits text then tool_use, code that only inspects content[0] will miss the tool call entirely.
Ignoring stop_reason. Some code naively looks for a tool_use block regardless of stop_reason; while it works, checking stop_reason == "tool_use" first is a cleaner, more explicit signal that a tool response is expected next, and it’s what determines whether your multi-turn loop (covered in “Multi-turn conversations with tools”) continues.
Discarding the id. It’s easy to overlook, but it’s mandatory — the next lesson uses it directly to build the tool_result block that gets sent back.

Once you can reliably extract name, id, and input from a response, you have everything needed to actually call your tool function and construct the reply — which is exactly what the next lesson covers.
Key takeaways

response.content is always a list of blocks; tool-use responses often mix text and tool_use blocks together.
stop_reason == "tool_use" signals Claude is waiting on one or more tool executions before it can continue.
Each tool_use block has id, name, and input — all three are needed to execute the tool and reply correctly.
A single response can contain multiple tool_use blocks; iterate over all of them, don’t just take the first.

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/06-sendin.content:
Sending tool results


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Once you’ve run the function Claude asked for, you have to tell Claude what happened. You do this by sending a new message back with a tool_result block containing the output, tagged with the same ID Claude gave the request. This is how the answer from your tool actually makes it back into the conversation.
Deep dive
After you’ve executed a tool function locally (see “Tool functions” and “Handling message blocks”), the result needs to travel back to Claude in a specific format: a tool_result content block, sent inside a new message with role: "user". This might feel counterintuitive — the result of Claude’s own request is sent back as a user message — but that’s the API’s convention: only user and assistant roles exist, and tool results are conceptually “information supplied to Claude,” which the API models as user-turn content.
A tool_result block has two required fields:

tool_use_id — must exactly match the id from the tool_use block you’re responding to. This is how Claude knows which of potentially several pending tool calls this result belongs to.
content — the actual result, typically a string (you can also pass structured content blocks, e.g. for returning images, but a plain string is the common case and is often a JSON-encoded string when the result is structured data).

Critically, the message history you send back must also include Claude’s original assistant turn (the one containing the tool_use block) — you’re not just sending the result in isolation, you’re appending both the assistant’s tool request and your result to the growing conversation:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather in a given location",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "location": {"type": "string", "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"}
        },
        "required": ["location"]
    }
}]
 
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in San Francisco?"}]
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=messages
)
 
if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    tool_use_block = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
 
    # 1. Execute the tool locally
    result = f"It's 68°F and sunny in {tool_use_block.input['location']}."
 
    # 2. Append Claude's turn (including the tool_use block) to the conversation
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
 
    # 3. Append a new user message containing the tool_result
    messages.append({
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": tool_use_block.id,
                "content": result
            }
        ]
    })
 
    # 4. Send the updated conversation back, with the same tools list
    final_response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages
    )
    print(final_response.content[0].text)
A few details that matter: the tools parameter must be included again on this follow-up call (Claude needs it to potentially request another tool call). The content list of the user message can hold multiple tool_result blocks at once if you’re answering multiple pending tool calls in the same turn (see “Using multiple tools”). If your tool execution failed, you can optionally set "is_error": true on the tool_result block alongside a descriptive error string in content, which signals to Claude that the call didn’t succeed so it can adjust its approach rather than treating the error text as a normal result.
Pitfalls to avoid:

tool_use_id mismatches. Sending back the wrong ID, a stale ID from a previous turn, or a typo will cause an API error or a broken conversation. Always pull the ID directly off the tool_use block you’re responding to, never hardcode it.
Forgetting to re-append the assistant’s tool_use message. The API needs the full turn history — skipping the assistant turn that contained the tool_use block breaks the conversation’s structure.
Sending a tool_result with no matching prior tool_use. Every tool_result must correspond to a tool_use block that appeared in the immediately preceding assistant message.
Forgetting tools on the follow-up call. Omitting it doesn’t error, but it does mean Claude can no longer call more tools even if the task requires it.

This single round trip — request, execute, reply — is the atomic unit of tool use. The next lesson, “Multi-turn conversations with tools,” is about repeating this unit in a loop until Claude has everything it needs.
Key takeaways

A tool result is sent as a tool_result content block inside a new role: "user" message.
tool_use_id must exactly match the originating tool_use block’s id.
You must re-include Claude’s assistant turn (with the tool_use block) and the tools list on the follow-up call.
Use "is_error": true on a tool_result to signal a failed tool execution rather than a successful one.

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/07-multi-.content:
Multi-turn conversations with tools


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Answering one question often takes more than one tool call — Claude might need to look something up, then use that result to decide it needs to look up something else, before it can finally answer. This lesson covers why a single request/result exchange usually isn’t enough, and introduces the idea of looping until Claude is truly done.
Deep dive
The previous two lessons covered a single round trip: Claude requests a tool, you execute it, you send the result back, and (in the examples shown) Claude gives a final answer. In practice, that one-shot pattern is the exception, not the rule. Claude frequently needs to chain tool calls: check the calendar, then create an event only if there’s no conflict; look up a customer ID, then use it to fetch their order history; search for a file, then read its contents. Each of these steps is a separate exchange where Claude receives a result, reasons about it, and may decide it needs another tool call before it can respond to the user.
This is why real tool-use code is structured as a loop, not a fixed sequence of steps. The loop condition is simple and important: keep sending requests as long as stop_reason is "tool_use". Only when stop_reason becomes something else (typically "end_turn") does Claude consider itself finished and ready to produce its actual answer to the user.
Conceptual shape of the loop (fleshed out fully in code in the next lesson):
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Check my calendar for next Monday, then schedule a 1-hour planning session if I'm free."}]
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=messages
)
 
while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    # 1. Append the assistant's turn (may contain one or more tool_use blocks)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
 
    # 2. Execute every tool_use block and collect tool_result blocks
    tool_results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            output = execute_tool(block.name, block.input)
            tool_results.append({
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": output
            })
 
    # 3. Send all results back together in a single user message
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})
 
    # 4. Ask Claude to continue — it may request another tool, or finish
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages
    )
 
# Loop exited: stop_reason is no longer "tool_use" — Claude has a final answer
final_text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print(final_text)
Each iteration of the loop grows the messages list — the full history of user turns, assistant turns (including their tool_use blocks), and tool result turns is preserved and resent every time, since Claude has no memory between API calls and needs the entire conversation as context each time. This means message list length, and therefore token usage, grows with every tool round trip — something to be mindful of in longer chains, since it affects both cost and how close you get to the model’s context window.
The most common bug at this stage is writing code that only sends one tool result and then stops, regardless of what Claude does next — effectively hardcoding a “loop” of exactly one iteration. If the task genuinely needs two or three tool calls in sequence, that code will silently return an incomplete or wrong answer after the first tool call, because it never gives Claude the chance to ask for the second one. Another subtle bug is discarding earlier turns from messages to “save space” — doing so breaks the conversation, since tool_result blocks reference tool_use_ids that must still be resolvable within the history Claude sees.
This lesson sets up the concept; the next lesson, “Implementing multiple turns,” turns it into a complete, runnable implementation as part of the module’s project.
Key takeaways

Many real tasks require several sequential tool calls — one round trip is often not enough.
The correct loop condition is: keep calling the API as long as stop_reason == "tool_use".
The full message history (user, assistant with tool_use, and tool_result turns) must be resent on every iteration — Claude has no memory across calls.
A loop that stops after exactly one tool call is the most common implementation bug in multi-step tool use.

Related lessons
Previous: 06 Sending tool results
Next: 08 Implementing multiple turns

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/09-using-.content:
Using multiple tools


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Real assistants usually need more than one capability — checking weather and looking up flights and sending a message, for instance. This lesson covers giving Claude several tools at once, letting it choose which one(s) to use, and how Claude can even call more than one tool in the same turn (parallel tool calls).
Deep dive
Extending from one tool to several is mostly additive: the tools parameter simply takes a longer list, and your dispatch logic (from “Tool functions”) needs to route each tool_use block’s name to the right function. The real complexity is in two behaviors that only show up with multiple tools available: tool selection (which tool, if any, Claude picks) and parallel tool use (Claude requesting more than one tool call in a single response).
tools = [
    {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get the current weather in a given location",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"location": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    },
    {
        "name": "get_stock_price",
        "description": "Get the current stock price for a given ticker symbol",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticker": {"type": "string", "description": "Stock ticker, e.g. AAPL"}},
            "required": ["ticker"]
        }
    }
]
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in NYC and the stock price of AAPL?"}]
)
For a question that needs two independent lookups like the one above, Claude will often issue both tool_use blocks in a single assistant turn — this is parallel tool use, and it’s the default behavior when tool_choice is left at its default ("auto"). Your response-handling code, as covered in “Handling message blocks,” already needs to loop over all tool_use blocks rather than assuming just one, and that’s exactly what makes parallel calls work correctly: you execute each tool, and send back a tool_result for each, all bundled into the same follow-up user message:
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
 
tool_results = []
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        output = execute_tool(block.name, block.input)
        tool_results.append({
            "type": "tool_result",
            "tool_use_id": block.id,
            "content": output
        })
 
# All results for this turn go in one user message together
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})
Sending results in one combined message (rather than one API call per result) matters: Claude expects to see all outstanding tool_use_ids resolved before it continues, and sending a tool_result for only some of them while leaving others unanswered leaves the conversation in an invalid state for the next request.
Parallel tool use is generally beneficial — it reduces the number of round trips and lowers latency for independent lookups — but it’s not always wanted. If you need to guarantee Claude calls at most one tool per turn, you can disable parallel calling explicitly:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice={"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": True},
    messages=messages
)
With disable_parallel_tool_use: True and tool_choice.type: "auto", Claude is limited to at most one tool call per response but can still choose to respond with plain text and no tool call at all. (Forcing tool use itself — as opposed to just limiting parallelism — is the subject of the next lesson, “Fine grained tool calling.”)
Pitfalls specific to multi-tool setups:

Ambiguous or overlapping tool descriptions. If two tools’ descriptions sound similar (e.g. get_price and get_stock_price), Claude may pick the wrong one or hesitate. Keep descriptions distinct and specific.
Only executing the first tool_use block found. This silently drops the second (or third) tool call and leaves the conversation with an unresolved tool_use_id, which will error on the next API call.
Naming collisions. Tool names must be unique within the tools list — reusing a name for two different behaviors makes dispatch ambiguous.
Forgetting order doesn’t matter but completeness does. You don’t have to resolve tool_use blocks in the order they appear, but every single one in that assistant turn must get a matching tool_result before the next API call.

With multiple tools now in play, the next lesson looks at the opposite control: how to force Claude toward (or away from) specific tools using tool_choice, rather than leaving the choice entirely up to the model.
Key takeaways

Multiple tools are just a longer tools list; your dispatch logic routes each tool_use block’s name to the right function.
Claude may request several tools in one turn (parallel tool use) by default when tool_choice is "auto".
All tool_result blocks answering one assistant turn must be sent together in a single follow-up user message.
tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true} limits Claude to at most one tool call per turn while still allowing a plain-text reply.

Related lessons
Previous: 08 Implementing multiple turns
Next: 10 Fine grained tool calling

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/10-fine-g.title: Fine grained tool calling
claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/10-fine-g.content:
Fine grained tool calling


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Sometimes you don’t want to leave it up to Claude whether to call a tool — you want to guarantee it does, or guarantee it calls one specific tool, or guarantee it doesn’t call any tool at all. The tool_choice parameter gives you that control, on top of the default behavior where Claude decides for itself.
Deep dive
By default, when you pass a tools list, Claude decides on its own whether a tool is needed at all — this is tool_choice: {"type": "auto"}, the implicit default if you don’t set the parameter. But tool_choice supports three other modes that force Claude’s hand:

{"type": "auto"} — Claude decides whether to use a tool, and may use zero, one, or (if not disabled) multiple tools. This is the default.
{"type": "any"} — Claude must call some tool from the tools list, but it chooses which one. Useful when you know the user’s request definitely requires a tool and you don’t want Claude to just answer in text.
{"type": "tool", "name": "<tool_name>"} — Claude must call that exact tool. Useful for testing a specific tool in isolation, or when your application logic has already determined which tool is needed and just wants Claude to fill in the arguments.
{"type": "none"} — Claude is prohibited from calling any tool, even if tools were provided; it must respond with text only.

Every tool_choice type also accepts an optional disable_parallel_tool_use boolean. With auto, this caps Claude at at most one tool call (it can still reply with plain text). With any or a specific tool, it forces exactly one tool call:
# Force exactly one call to get_weather, no other tool, no parallel calls
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in San Francisco and New York?"}]
)
# Require some tool call, but let Claude pick which one, and limit it to exactly one
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice={"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": True},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in San Francisco and New York?"}]
)
Practical uses of forced tool calling (“fine grained” in the sense of precisely controlling which tool gets used, rather than trusting the model’s judgment):

Structured data extraction. Defining a single tool whose input_schema represents the exact structure you want back (e.g. a schema for extracting a name, date, and amount from a document) and forcing that tool with {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_data"} is a common pattern for reliably getting structured JSON out of Claude, even when the “tool” isn’t a real action — it’s really being used as an output format contract.
Guardrailing behavior. If your product should never let Claude answer certain kinds of questions without checking a tool first (e.g. always verify an order ID against your system before discussing it), {"type": "any"} prevents Claude from skipping straight to a text answer.
Testing and debugging. Forcing a specific tool during development lets you verify your schema and function work correctly in isolation, without depending on whether Claude decides to invoke it.
Disabling tools mid-conversation. {"type": "none"} is useful if you want to keep the same tools list defined (so schema context/history stays consistent) but temporarily prevent tool use for a particular follow-up turn, e.g. after tools have already run and you just want a final natural-language summary.

Pitfalls: forcing a tool (any or a specific tool) when the tools genuinely aren’t relevant to the user’s request produces a bad result — Claude will call something even though nothing fits, likely with poor or hallucinated arguments, so forced modes should only be used when you’re confident a tool call is actually appropriate. Also, forcing {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} with a name that isn’t in your tools list is a request error, not something Claude works around. And relying on tool_choice alone to guarantee output structure without validating the resulting input against your own schema/types is risky — always validate before executing.
Having covered tool selection, the module now turns to two of Anthropic’s own pre-built tools that plug directly into this same tools/tool_choice mechanism: the text editor tool and the web search tool.
Key takeaways

tool_choice controls whether/which tool Claude must use: auto (default), any (some tool), {"type": "tool", "name": ...} (a specific tool), or none (no tools).
disable_parallel_tool_use: true limits Claude to at most one tool call (auto) or exactly one (any/specific tool).
Forced tool calling is commonly used for structured data extraction, guardrailing required checks, and isolated testing.
Only force a tool call when a tool is genuinely relevant — forcing an irrelevant call produces poor arguments and unreliable results.

Related lessons

Next: 11 The text edit tool

claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/12-the-we.title: The web search tool
claude/05-tool-use-with-claude/12-the-we.content:
The web search tool


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Tool use with Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
The web search tool lets Claude look things up on the live internet — current events, recent prices, anything past its training cutoff — without you writing any search-engine integration yourself. Unlike every other tool in this module, Anthropic runs the actual search on its own servers, so there’s no local execution step for you to implement.
Deep dive
Every tool covered earlier in this module — custom tools, and even the text editor tool — is a client tool: Claude requests it, and your code executes it. The web search tool is different: it’s a server tool. You enable it by adding it to tools, and when Claude decides to search, Anthropic’s infrastructure performs the search and feeds the results back into the same conversation automatically, without a round trip through your code.
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What are the latest developments in fusion energy this year?"}],
    tools=[{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 5}]
)
print(response)
Key parameters on the tool definition:

type — the dated version string, e.g. web_search_20250305.
name — must be "web_search".
max_uses — an optional cap on how many searches Claude can perform while answering a single request, protecting against runaway search loops and controlling cost/latency.
Optional filtering parameters are also supported in the tool definition, such as restricting or excluding specific domains, and constraining results by locale — useful for keeping search grounded in trustworthy or relevant sources.

Because the server performs the search itself, the response you get back can already include the finished answer, with intermediate server_tool_use and web_search_tool_result blocks showing what was searched and what was found, plus citations tied to particular claims in the text. This is a meaningful structural difference from client tools: with get_weather or the text editor tool, seeing a tool_use block means the conversation is paused waiting on you; with web_search, Claude’s turn can complete in one API call because Anthropic already resolved the tool call before returning the response to you. You may still see stop_reason: "tool_use" mid-stream if there are multiple search rounds, but there is no manual “execute and send tool_result” step for you to write, unlike every other tool in this module — the loop still applies conceptually (Claude may search more than once before finishing) but the execution half of that loop is handled for you.
Where the earlier lessons’ concepts still apply directly: web search can be combined with your own custom client tools in the same tools list, and tool_choice still governs it the same way (e.g. {"type": "tool", "name": "web_search"} to force a search). Handling the response for citations and mixed content still means iterating response.content and checking block types, exactly as in “Handling message blocks” — you’ll just see additional block types (server_tool_use, web_search_tool_result) alongside the text and tool_use blocks you’ve already learned to expect.
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)
    elif block.type == "server_tool_use":
        print("Claude searched for:", block.input.get("query"))
    elif block.type == "web_search_tool_result":
        print("Search returned", len(block.content), "results")
Pitfalls: forgetting that max_uses is a real cost/latency control, not a formality — an open-ended research question without a cap can trigger many searches; assuming you need to write execution code for this tool the way you would for a custom tool (you don’t, and trying to intercept and “handle” a web_search_tool_result block as if it were a pending tool_use will misread the conversation state); and not surfacing citations to end users when displaying search-grounded answers, which matters for trustworthiness given the content came from live, unverified web sources rather than the model’s own knowledge.
This closes out the module: starting from the basic mechanics of defining a tool and handling a single round trip, through multi-turn loops and multiple simultaneous tools, to fine-grained control with tool_choice, and finally to Anthropic’s own pre-built client and server tools — the text editor tool and the web search tool — which show the same tools/tool_choice interface extended in two different execution models (client-executed vs. server-executed).
Key takeaways

The web search tool (web_search_20250305, name "web_search") is a server tool — Anthropic executes the search, not your code.
max_uses caps how many searches Claude can perform per request; optional domain/locale filters can further constrain results.
Responses may include server_tool_use and web_search_tool_result blocks with citations, in addition to the usual text/tool_use blocks.
It can be combined with your own custom client tools in the same tools list, and is still governed by tool_choice.

Related lessons
Previous: 11 The text edit tool
