claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/01-intr.title: Introducing Retrieval Augmented Generation
claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/01-intr.content:
Introducing Retrieval Augmented Generation


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a way of giving Claude access to information it wasn’t trained on — like your company’s internal docs — by fetching relevant text and handing it to the model right before it answers. Instead of relying purely on what the model memorized during training, RAG looks things up first, then generates an answer grounded in what it found. This matters because it lets you build assistants that answer accurately about private, large, or constantly changing data without retraining the model.
Deep dive
Large language models like Claude have two structural limitations that RAG addresses. First, their knowledge is frozen at training time — they don’t know about documents created after training, or about private data (your company’s contracts, wikis, support tickets) that was never in the training set at all. Second, even within a single conversation, there’s a limited context window: you can’t just paste your entire 50,000-document knowledge base into every prompt. RAG solves both problems by treating retrieval as a preprocessing step. Instead of asking Claude to “know” everything, you build a search system that finds the small number of relevant passages for a given question, and only those passages get inserted into the prompt.
The basic shape of a RAG system is: a user asks a question, a retrieval system searches an external knowledge store for the most relevant chunks of text, those chunks are inserted into the prompt as context, and Claude generates an answer using both the question and the retrieved context. This is fundamentally different from fine-tuning, which bakes knowledge into the model’s weights through additional training. RAG is often cheaper and faster to update — when a document changes, you just re-index it rather than retraining a model — and it’s more transparent, because you can show users exactly which passages informed an answer (a theme this module returns to later with citations-style grounding).
RAG systems are usually built around a component called a vector database (or vector store) — a specialized index that stores numeric representations of text (embeddings) and can quickly find the passages whose embeddings are most similar to a query’s embedding. This module builds up to that: subsequent lessons cover how to split documents into chunks small enough to embed and retrieve meaningfully (chunking strategies), how those chunks get converted into vectors (embeddings), how the full pipeline fits together end to end (ingest, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, augment, generate), and how to complement vector search with older but still highly effective lexical/keyword search (BM25). The final lesson combines multiple retrieval strategies into a single multi-index pipeline, since production systems rarely rely on just one method.
It’s worth being precise about vocabulary here, since the term “RAG” gets used loosely. Strictly, RAG refers to the pattern of retrieving external context and inserting it into a generation prompt — it doesn’t mandate a specific retrieval technology. You could do RAG with a simple keyword search over a folder of text files; you don’t need embeddings or a vector database to call something RAG. In practice, most modern RAG systems use embeddings because they capture semantic similarity (matching “how do I cancel my subscription” with a document titled “Ending your plan” even though the words don’t overlap), but lexical search remains valuable, especially for exact terms, product codes, or names that embeddings can blur.
A common pitfall when people first hear about RAG is assuming it’s a single tool or API call. It’s actually an architecture with several moving, tunable parts: how you chunk documents, which embedding model you use, how many chunks you retrieve, how you rank and filter them, and how you format them into the prompt. Getting any one of these wrong — chunks too large, too few results retrieved, irrelevant context crowding out the important passage — degrades answer quality even though the “RAG” label technically still applies. The rest of this module walks through each of these decisions in turn, building toward a working pipeline you can implement with the Claude API and a retrieval library of your choice.
Key takeaways

RAG lets Claude answer questions about data it wasn’t trained on by retrieving relevant text and inserting it into the prompt before generation.
It complements the context window limit by only including the small number of passages relevant to a given question, rather than the entire knowledge base.
RAG is distinct from fine-tuning: it updates knowledge by re-indexing documents, not by retraining the model.
The core pipeline is retrieve → augment prompt → generate; vector databases and embeddings are a common but not mandatory way to implement retrieval.
Getting RAG right requires tuning multiple stages — chunking, embedding, retrieval, ranking — not just picking a vector database.

claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/02-text.content:
Text chunking strategies


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Before you can search a document, you have to break it into smaller pieces, or “chunks,” because embedding and retrieving an entire book at once is neither useful nor efficient. Chunking strategy — how big the pieces are, where you cut them, and whether they overlap — has a huge effect on whether your RAG system finds the right answer later. Get chunking wrong and even a perfect retrieval algorithm will return irrelevant or incomplete text.
Deep dive
Chunking is the process of splitting a source document into smaller segments that will each be embedded and stored individually. The reason chunking exists at all is that embeddings work best over focused, semantically coherent spans of text — a single embedding vector for an entire 100-page manual would blur together so many topics that it wouldn’t be similar to any specific query. Conversely, chunks that are too small (a single sentence, or worse, a sentence fragment) lose the surrounding context needed to make sense of them, and can be misleading when retrieved in isolation.
Fixed-size chunking is the simplest strategy: split text every N characters or N tokens, regardless of sentence or paragraph boundaries. It’s fast, predictable, and easy to implement — you just walk through the text with a sliding window. Its weakness is that it doesn’t respect the structure of the content: a fixed-size cut can land in the middle of a sentence, splitting a key fact across two chunks so that neither chunk alone contains the complete idea. This hurts retrieval quality because the embedding of a truncated chunk may not closely match a query about the fact it only half-contains.
Semantic chunking tries to fix this by splitting text at natural boundaries — paragraphs, sections, or points where the topic shifts — rather than at an arbitrary character count. One common approach: split on paragraph or heading boundaries first, and only fall back to size-based splitting for paragraphs that are still too long. A more sophisticated version computes embeddings for consecutive sentences and looks for points where similarity drops sharply, treating those drops as topic boundaries. Semantic chunking usually produces more coherent chunks, but it’s more expensive to compute and the “right” boundary is often ambiguous.
Overlap is a technique used with either strategy: instead of chunk boundaries being back-to-back, consecutive chunks share a bit of text (for example, the last 50–100 tokens of one chunk are repeated as the first 50–100 tokens of the next). This guards against the “split fact” problem — if a sentence spanning a boundary gets cut in chunk A, the overlap ensures it also appears intact, in context, in chunk B. The tradeoff is storage and retrieval overhead: overlapping chunks mean redundant content in your index, more embeddings to store, and a higher chance of retrieving near-duplicate chunks that don’t add new information to the prompt.
Choosing a chunk size is itself a tradeoff. Small chunks (a paragraph or less) tend to produce more precise retrieval — the embedding is a tight semantic fingerprint of one idea — but they can lack context, and you often need to retrieve more of them to cover a topic fully. Large chunks (multiple paragraphs or a full section) preserve more context per chunk, but their embeddings are less specific (an average over many ideas), which can hurt matching for narrow queries, and they eat into the model’s context window faster once retrieved. A frequently cited starting point is chunks of a few hundred tokens with 10-20% overlap, then tuning based on evaluation against real queries — there’s no universally correct size, because it depends on how information is distributed in your source documents (dense reference tables need different treatment than narrative prose).
Chunking also interacts with document structure that shouldn’t be ignored: headings, tables, code blocks, and bullet lists often carry meaning that a naive character-based splitter destroys (e.g., cutting a table in half so rows lose their column headers). Production chunkers frequently use structure-aware splitting — respecting Markdown headers, HTML tags, or code fences — before falling back to size-based rules within a section. Whatever strategy you choose, it’s worth storing metadata alongside each chunk (source document, section title, position) so that later stages of the pipeline can cite sources or re-assemble context, which becomes important once you get to implementing the full RAG flow and to citations later in this course.
Key takeaways

Chunking splits documents into embeddable, retrievable units — the size and boundaries chosen strongly affect retrieval quality.
Fixed-size chunking is simple and fast but can split sentences and facts awkwardly across chunk boundaries.
Semantic chunking respects natural structure (paragraphs, sections, topic shifts) at the cost of more compute and ambiguity about where boundaries belong.
Overlap between consecutive chunks reduces the risk of losing context at a boundary, at the cost of redundant storage and near-duplicate retrieval results.
Chunk size is a tradeoff between retrieval precision (smaller) and preserved context (larger); structure-aware splitting (headings, tables, code) avoids destroying meaningful formatting.

claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/03-text.content:
Text embeddings


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
An embedding is a way of turning a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector) that captures its meaning, so that texts with similar meaning end up with similar-looking vectors. This lets a computer compare “how close” two pieces of text are in meaning using simple math, instead of matching exact words — which is what makes it possible to search a knowledge base by concept rather than by keyword.
Deep dive
A text embedding model takes a string of text — a word, sentence, paragraph, or chunk — and outputs a fixed-length vector of floating point numbers, typically a few hundred to a couple thousand dimensions. The model is trained so that texts which are semantically similar produce vectors that are close together in that high-dimensional space, and texts with unrelated meaning produce vectors that are far apart. Crucially, “similar” here is about meaning, not surface form: “How do I reset my password?” and “I forgot my login credentials, what do I do?” share almost no words but should still embed to nearby vectors, because a good embedding model captures the underlying intent.
“Closeness” between two vectors is usually measured with cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between the two vectors, ranging from -1 (opposite meaning) to 1 (identical meaning), with 0 meaning unrelated. Cosine similarity is popular because it ignores vector magnitude and focuses purely on direction, which tends to correlate well with semantic similarity for text embeddings. Many embedding models (including Voyage AI’s) also normalize their output vectors to unit length, which makes cosine similarity and the plain dot product mathematically equivalent — so you’ll often see dot products used directly for efficiency.
Anthropic doesn’t provide its own first-party embedding model; instead, Anthropic recommends Voyage AI for generating embeddings to use alongside Claude in RAG applications. A minimal example of embedding a set of documents and a query, then finding the closest match with NumPy:
import voyageai
import numpy as np
 
vo = voyageai.Client()  # reads VOYAGE_API_KEY from the environment
 
documents = [
    "To reset your password, go to Settings > Security and click 'Reset Password'.",
    "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days after approval.",
    "Our support team is available 24/7 via live chat.",
]
 
# Embed the documents once, at ingest time.
doc_embeddings = vo.embed(
    documents, model="voyage-4", input_type="document"
).embeddings
 
# At query time, embed the user's question with input_type="query".
query = "I forgot my login credentials, what do I do?"
query_embedding = vo.embed(
    [query], model="voyage-4", input_type="query"
).embeddings[0]
 
# Voyage embeddings are unit-normalized, so dot product == cosine similarity.
similarities = np.dot(doc_embeddings, query_embedding)
best_match_idx = int(np.argmax(similarities))
 
print(documents[best_match_idx])
Note the input_type parameter: many embedding models, including Voyage’s, distinguish between embedding a document (something being indexed) and embedding a query (something being searched for), and use slightly different internal representations for each. Using the wrong input_type — or omitting it — typically degrades retrieval quality, so it’s a common and easy-to-miss pitfall.
A few other practical considerations. Embedding models have a maximum input length (measured in tokens), which is why chunking (the previous lesson) has to happen before embedding — you can’t embed an arbitrarily long document in one call. Different embedding models also produce vectors of different, incompatible dimensionality and semantics; you cannot mix embeddings from two different models in the same similarity comparison, so if you switch models later you need to re-embed your entire corpus. Embedding is also not free: it costs money and time per API call, so production systems typically batch embedding requests and cache results rather than re-embedding unchanged documents on every run.
Once you have embeddings for your chunks, you need somewhere to store and search them efficiently — a vector database (e.g., a specialized store, or a library like FAISS, or an extension on top of a general-purpose database like pgvector) that can perform approximate nearest-neighbor search over potentially millions of vectors without brute-force comparing against every one. That storage-and-retrieval step, plus how embeddings fit into the broader pipeline alongside chunking, prompt augmentation, and generation, is the subject of the next lesson.
Key takeaways

An embedding is a numeric vector representation of text such that semantically similar texts have vectors that are close together.
Cosine similarity (or, for unit-normalized vectors, the plain dot product) is the standard way to measure closeness between two embeddings.
Anthropic recommends Voyage AI for generating embeddings to pair with Claude in RAG pipelines; the voyageai Python client’s embed() method takes a model name and an input_type of "document" or "query".
Using the correct input_type for documents versus queries matters — mismatching it degrades retrieval accuracy.
Embeddings from different models are not interchangeable; switching embedding models requires re-embedding your whole corpus.

claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/04-the-.content:
The full RAG flow


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson zooms out and shows how chunking and embeddings fit together into one continuous pipeline, from raw documents all the way to a Claude-generated answer. Understanding the whole flow — not just its individual pieces — is what lets you debug a RAG system when it gives a wrong or incomplete answer, because you can pinpoint which stage failed.
Deep dive
The full RAG pipeline has two distinct phases that run at different times: an ingestion (offline) phase, which happens once per document or whenever documents change, and a query (online) phase, which happens on every user request.
Ingestion phase:

Ingest — collect raw source documents (PDFs, web pages, database rows, support tickets, wiki pages) and extract their text content.
Chunk — split each document into smaller, semantically coherent pieces using a strategy like the ones covered in the previous lesson (fixed-size, semantic, with or without overlap).
Embed — pass each chunk through an embedding model (e.g., Voyage AI) to get a vector representation, using input_type="document".
Store — save each chunk’s text, its embedding vector, and any useful metadata (source, title, section, position) into a vector store or vector-capable database, so it can be searched later.

Query phase (per user request):
5. Retrieve — embed the user’s question (input_type="query") and search the vector store for the chunks whose embeddings are most similar (highest cosine similarity / dot product), typically returning the top-k results (e.g., top 3-5 chunks).
6. Augment the prompt — insert the retrieved chunks into the prompt sent to Claude, usually as part of the system prompt or as context prepended to the user’s question, often with clear delimiters and instructions like “answer using only the information in the documents below.”
7. Generate — send the augmented prompt to Claude via the Messages API; Claude reads both the retrieved context and the original question and produces an answer grounded in that context.
A minimal illustration of the query-time steps 5-7, assuming chunks and their embeddings are already stored from an ingestion step:
import anthropic
import voyageai
import numpy as np
 
vo = voyageai.Client()
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
# Pretend these were produced during ingestion and loaded from your store.
chunks = [
    "To reset your password, go to Settings > Security and click 'Reset Password'.",
    "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days after approval.",
]
chunk_embeddings = vo.embed(chunks, model="voyage-4", input_type="document").embeddings
 
def answer_question(question: str, top_k: int = 2) -> str:
    # Retrieve
    query_embedding = vo.embed([question], model="voyage-4", input_type="query").embeddings[0]
    scores = np.dot(chunk_embeddings, query_embedding)
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_k]
    retrieved = "\n\n".join(chunks[i] for i in top_indices)
 
    # Augment
    system_prompt = (
        "Answer the user's question using only the information in the "
        "documents below. If the answer isn't in the documents, say so.\n\n"
        f"Documents:\n{retrieved}"
    )
 
    # Generate
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=512,
        system=system_prompt,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
 
print(answer_question("How long do refunds take?"))
A few things go wrong in practice at each stage, and it’s worth knowing where to look. If Claude’s answers are confidently wrong, check retrieval first: are the right chunks even being returned? This can be tested independently of Claude by printing the retrieved chunks for a known question. If retrieval is correct but the answer is still wrong, the issue is often in the augmentation step — the prompt might not clearly instruct Claude to prioritize the provided context over its own knowledge, or the chunks might be too fragmented to answer the question fully (a chunking problem surfacing downstream). If retrieval returns no relevant chunks at all, the problem may be upstream — bad chunk boundaries, wrong input_type, or an embedding model mismatch between ingestion and query time.
It’s also worth deciding upfront what happens when nothing relevant is found — a well-designed prompt should let Claude say “I don’t have information about that” rather than inventing a plausible-sounding but unsupported answer (a form of hallucination that RAG is meant to reduce, but doesn’t eliminate on its own). Later in this module, the “Implementing the RAG flow” lesson turns this end-to-end sketch into working code with a real vector store, and subsequent lessons add BM25 lexical search and multi-index retrieval to make the retrieval step more robust than pure vector search alone.
Key takeaways

The RAG flow splits into an offline ingestion phase (ingest → chunk → embed → store) and an online query phase (retrieve → augment → generate).
Ingestion happens once per document (or whenever a document changes); retrieval and generation happen on every user request.
Augmenting the prompt means inserting retrieved chunks as context, typically with explicit instructions to ground the answer in that context.
Debugging a RAG answer means isolating which stage failed: test retrieval independently before assuming the generation step is at fault.
A robust system prompt should let Claude decline to answer when retrieval finds nothing relevant, rather than fabricating an answer.

claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/06-bm25.content:
BM25 lexical search


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
BM25 is a decades-old keyword search algorithm that scores how well a document matches a query based on the actual words they share, rather than on learned “meaning” like embeddings do. It’s included here because it catches things embeddings often miss — exact terms, codes, names, and rare words — making it a valuable complement to semantic search rather than a competitor to it.
Deep dive
BM25 (“Best Matching 25”) is a probabilistic ranking function used by classic search engines (it’s the default relevance algorithm in Elasticsearch and many other search systems) to score how relevant a document is to a query, based purely on word overlap — no neural network or training required. It’s a refinement of an older idea called TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency), and it’s still highly competitive with modern methods for tasks that hinge on exact terminology.
The intuition behind BM25 has three parts:

Term frequency (TF) — a document that mentions a query word more often is probably more relevant to that word. But BM25 caps the benefit of repetition: the tenth occurrence of a word barely adds more relevance than the ninth, avoiding the situation where a document could game the score just by repeating a word many times.
Inverse document frequency (IDF) — words that appear in most documents (like “the,” “system,” or generic domain words) carry little discriminating power, so they’re downweighted; words that appear in only a few documents (like a specific product name or error code) carry more weight, because matching on them is a stronger signal.
Document length normalization — a long document naturally contains more words and could accumulate spurious term-frequency matches just by being long. BM25 normalizes for document length so that a short, focused document isn’t unfairly penalized relative to a long, sprawling one.

Combined, BM25 produces a score per document for a given query, and documents are ranked by that score — conceptually the same output shape as vector similarity search, just computed a completely different way. That’s what makes it easy to combine with embeddings: both methods produce a ranked list (or score) per document, so a hybrid system can merge or re-weight the two rankings.
Where BM25 wins over embeddings: exact identifiers. If a user searches for an error code like ERR_429_RATE_LIMIT or a specific product SKU, an embedding model may treat it as a near-meaningless token and fail to distinguish it from similar-looking codes, because embeddings are trained to capture semantic meaning and rare, structured strings don’t carry much of that. BM25, by contrast, directly rewards an exact string match and will surface the document containing that exact code very reliably. The same applies to proper nouns, acronyms, and domain jargon that a general-purpose embedding model was never trained to differentiate finely.
Where BM25 loses to embeddings: paraphrase and intent matching. If a user asks “how do I get my money back” and the relevant document says “refund policy,” BM25 finds zero shared terms and scores it as irrelevant, while a good embedding model recognizes the semantic relationship. This complementary failure pattern — BM25 strong on exact terms, weak on paraphrase; embeddings strong on paraphrase, weak on exact terms — is exactly why production RAG systems increasingly run both and combine the results, an approach covered in the next lesson on multi-index pipelines.
A minimal illustration using the popular rank_bm25 Python package:
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
 
documents = [
    "To reset your password, go to Settings > Security and click Reset Password.",
    "Error ERR_429_RATE_LIMIT means you've exceeded the API rate limit.",
    "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days after approval.",
]
 
tokenized_docs = [doc.lower().split() for doc in documents]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized_docs)
 
query = "ERR_429_RATE_LIMIT"
tokenized_query = query.lower().split()
scores = bm25.get_scores(tokenized_query)
 
best_idx = scores.argmax()
print(documents[best_idx])  # Correctly finds the exact error-code document
Notice this example doesn’t call the Claude API or an embedding model at all — BM25 is a self-contained, local, statistical algorithm. That’s actually a practical advantage: it requires no network calls, no per-query API cost, and no embedding model, so it’s cheap to run alongside vector search as a second, independent retrieval signal. The main pitfall to watch for is tokenization quality: BM25’s matching is sensitive to how you split, lowercase, and (optionally) stem words — inconsistent tokenization between indexing and querying (e.g., stemming at index time but not at query time) silently degrades scores.
Key takeaways

BM25 is a statistical keyword-matching algorithm — no training or embeddings required — that scores documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document-length normalization.
It excels at exact-match queries (error codes, SKUs, names) where embeddings often underperform, and struggles with paraphrased or intent-based queries where embeddings excel.
BM25 and vector search fail in complementary ways, which is the main motivation for combining them in a hybrid pipeline.
BM25 runs locally with no per-query API cost, making it cheap to run as a second retrieval signal alongside embeddings.
Consistent tokenization (casing, stemming) between indexing and querying is essential — mismatches silently hurt BM25 scores.

claude/06-rag-and-agentic-search/07-a-mu.content:
A Multi-Index RAG pipeline


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of RAG and Agentic Search — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
A multi-index pipeline runs more than one retrieval method — typically vector search and BM25 keyword search — against the same query and merges their results, instead of relying on a single method. This closes the gaps each method has on its own, giving Claude better, more complete context to answer from, and it’s how most serious production RAG systems are actually built.
Deep dive
The previous two lessons established that embeddings and BM25 fail in complementary ways: embeddings are strong on paraphrase and intent but weak on exact terms, while BM25 is strong on exact terms but weak on paraphrase. A multi-index (or “hybrid”) pipeline runs both retrieval methods against the same query, over the same underlying chunks (each chunk lives in two indexes — a vector index and a lexical index), and combines the two ranked result lists into one.
The most common way to combine rankings is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which avoids the problem of the two methods producing scores on incompatible scales (cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1; a BM25 score is an unbounded, corpus-dependent number). Instead of combining raw scores, RRF combines rank positions: for each chunk, take 1 / (k + rank) from each retrieval method (where rank is that chunk’s position, starting at 1, in that method’s results, and k is a small constant, often 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks), and sum across methods. Chunks that rank highly in either method — or both — bubble to the top of the combined list.
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists: list[list[str]], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    """Each ranked_list is a list of chunk IDs, best match first."""
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked_list in ranked_lists:
        for rank, chunk_id in enumerate(ranked_list, start=1):
            scores[chunk_id] = scores.get(chunk_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
A full hybrid retrieval step, combining the vector store and BM25 index from the previous two lessons:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
def hybrid_search(query: str, vector_store, bm25, chunk_ids: list[str], top_k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    vector_results = vector_store.search(query, top_k=10)
    vector_ranked_ids = [r["chunk_id"] for r in vector_results]
 
    bm25_scores = bm25.get_scores(query.lower().split())
    bm25_ranked_ids = [chunk_ids[i] for i in bm25_scores.argsort()[::-1][:10]]
 
    fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([vector_ranked_ids, bm25_ranked_ids])
    return fused[:top_k]
 
 
def answer_with_hybrid_search(query: str, vector_store, bm25, chunk_ids, chunk_lookup) -> str:
    top_chunk_ids = hybrid_search(query, vector_store, bm25, chunk_ids)
    context = "\n\n".join(chunk_lookup[cid] for cid in top_chunk_ids)
 
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=512,
        system=f"Answer using only these documents:\n\n{context}",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": query}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
Beyond fusing two retrieval methods, “multi-index” often also means indexing on metadata, not just text. Real document collections have structured attributes — document type, date, department, access permissions, language — and a robust pipeline lets you filter the candidate set by metadata before or after the similarity search (e.g., “only search HR documents” or “only documents from the last 90 days”). This is usually implemented as a filtered query against the vector store (most vector databases support attaching metadata to each vector and filtering on it natively) rather than a separate index, but conceptually it’s the same idea: combine multiple signals rather than relying on similarity scores alone.
A further refinement used in production systems is reranking: after hybrid retrieval produces, say, the top 20-30 candidate chunks (a cheap, high-recall step), a separate, more expensive reranking model or a call to Claude itself scores each candidate more precisely against the query, and only the top few (e.g., top 5) survive into the final prompt. Rerankers can consider the full query-document pair jointly (rather than comparing precomputed embeddings independently), which typically improves precision significantly, at the cost of extra latency and compute — which is why reranking is applied to a small shortlist rather than the whole corpus.
The main pitfall in building a multi-index pipeline is over-engineering it before you have evidence it’s needed: hybrid search, metadata filtering, and reranking each add complexity, latency, and cost. It’s worth first measuring where a simpler pipeline (from the “Implementing the RAG flow” lesson) actually fails — using a small set of real or representative queries — before layering in additional retrieval methods. That evaluation-driven approach, rather than assuming a maximally sophisticated pipeline is always better, is what separates a RAG system that’s actually accurate from one that’s merely elaborate. With retrieval this course has covered, later lessons in “Features of Claude” build on top of it — extended thinking, prompt caching, and citations all interact directly with how you structure and reuse retrieved context in your prompts.
Key takeaways

Multi-index pipelines combine vector search and BM25 (and sometimes metadata filters) to cover each method’s blind spots.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines ranked lists from different retrieval methods using rank position rather than raw, incompatible scores.
Metadata filtering narrows the candidate set using structured attributes (date, type, permissions) alongside text similarity.
Reranking applies a more precise, more expensive scoring step to a small shortlist of candidates to improve final precision.
Add hybrid search, filtering, and reranking based on evidence of where a simpler pipeline fails — not by default — to avoid unnecessary complexity and latency.

claude/07-features-of-claude/01-extended.title: Extended thinking
claude/07-features-of-claude/01-extended.content:
Extended thinking


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Extended thinking lets Claude work through a problem step by step in a visible “scratchpad” before giving its final answer, similar to a person sketching out reasoning on paper before writing a clean summary. It’s useful for harder problems — math, multi-step logic, complex planning — where letting the model reason at length before committing to an answer improves accuracy.
Deep dive
By default, Claude produces its response directly, without a separate reasoning phase. Extended thinking changes this by having Claude generate a distinct thinking content block first — its internal reasoning process — before the final text block that’s meant to be shown to the user. This is enabled via the thinking parameter on the Messages API:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2000},
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "A train leaves station A at 60 mph, another leaves station B (300 miles away) at 90 mph toward A. When do they meet?"}
    ],
)
 
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "thinking":
        print("Thinking:", block.thinking)
    elif block.type == "text":
        print("Answer:", block.text)
The budget_tokens field caps how many tokens Claude may spend on the thinking block — a larger budget gives the model more room to work through a harder problem, at the cost of higher latency and token usage. budget_tokens must be less than max_tokens overall (thinking tokens plus the final response tokens both count against the request), so setting a generous thinking budget with a small max_tokens will constrain the final answer. Note that some newer model families have moved to an “adaptive” thinking mode, where Claude decides on its own how much to think rather than a developer specifying a fixed budget (thinking={"type": "adaptive"}); check the specific model’s documentation for which mode it supports, since passing an unsupported budget_tokens value to a model that only accepts adaptive thinking will return an error.
An important behavioral detail: when extended thinking is enabled, the thinking block must generally be preserved and passed back unmodified in multi-turn conversations if you want Claude to continue reasoning coherently across turns — stripping it out or editing it can break the model’s ability to reference its own prior reasoning.
Interleaved thinking is a related, more advanced capability relevant to agentic workflows involving tool use: normally, Claude thinks once, then may call a tool, then responds — but with interleaved thinking enabled (via the beta header interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14), Claude can think again between tool calls, reasoning about the result of one tool call before deciding what to do next. This is useful when a task involves multiple sequential tool calls where the right next action depends on what a previous tool returned:
response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 10000},
    tools=[calculator_tool, database_tool],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the total revenue if we sold 150 units of product A at $50 each?"}],
    betas=["interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14"],
)
 
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "thinking":
        print(f"Thinking: {block.thinking}")
    elif block.type == "tool_use":
        print(f"Tool call: {block.name}({block.input})")
    elif block.type == "text":
        print(f"Response: {block.text}")
With interleaved thinking, budget_tokens represents the total thinking budget across all thinking blocks in a single assistant turn, and — unlike standard extended thinking — it can exceed max_tokens, since the model may think, act, think again, and act again multiple times before its final response.
When should you reach for extended thinking? It helps most on tasks with real multi-step reasoning: math word problems, code debugging, multi-constraint planning, or agentic tool-use sequences where the model benefits from reasoning about intermediate results. It’s generally unnecessary — and adds latency and cost for no benefit — on simple factual lookups, short-form generation, or straightforward formatting tasks, where Claude’s direct response is already reliable. A common pitfall is treating the thinking block as something to show end users verbatim as “the answer” — it’s an internal scratchpad, often exploratory or self-correcting, and should typically be hidden or summarized rather than surfaced raw in a product UI. Another pitfall, covered in more depth in this module’s caching lessons, is that changing thinking configuration (enabling/disabling it, or changing the budget) between otherwise-identical requests invalidates prompt caching for that request, so toggling it carelessly in a caching-heavy pipeline has a real cost impact.
Key takeaways

Extended thinking is enabled with thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N} on messages.create(), producing a separate thinking content block before the final text block.
budget_tokens caps reasoning length and counts toward max_tokens; some newer models instead use thinking={"type": "adaptive"} with no explicit budget.
Interleaved thinking (beta header interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14) lets Claude reason between tool calls in agentic workflows, and its budget can exceed max_tokens since it spans multiple thinking blocks per turn.
Best suited to multi-step reasoning tasks (math, planning, debugging, agentic tool sequences); adds unnecessary latency/cost for simple, direct-answer tasks.
Thinking blocks are an internal scratchpad, not a polished answer — avoid showing them raw to end users, and note that changing thinking config between requests can break prompt cache hits.

claude/07-features-of-claude/02-image-su.title: Image support
claude/07-features-of-claude/02-image-su.content:
Image support


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Claude can see and reason about images, not just text — you can send it a photo, screenshot, chart, or diagram alongside a question, and it will describe, analyze, or extract information from it. This “vision” capability opens up use cases like reading charts, describing photos for accessibility, extracting text from screenshots, or reviewing UI mockups.
Deep dive
Images are sent to Claude as a special image content block inside a message, alongside (or instead of) text blocks. The API supports two ways of providing the image data: base64-encoded bytes embedded directly in the request, or a URL that Claude fetches itself. Supported formats include JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP.
Base64 encoding, useful for local files or images you already have in memory:
import anthropic
import base64
import httpx
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
image_url = "upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/Camponotus_flavomarginatus_ant.jpg"
image_media_type = "image/jpeg"
image_data = base64.standard_b64encode(httpx.get(image_url).content).decode("utf-8")
 
message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "image",
                    "source": {
                        "type": "base64",
                        "media_type": image_media_type,
                        "data": image_data,
                    },
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "What is in the above image?"},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(message.content[0].text)
URL-based, when the image is already publicly hosted and you’d rather not download and re-encode it yourself:
message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "image",
                    "source": {"type": "url", "url": image_url},
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "What is in the above image?"},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
A single message can contain multiple image blocks — useful for comparison tasks (“how do these two screenshots differ?”) or for feeding Claude several pages of a scanned document as separate images. When sending multiple images, it’s good practice to label them with preceding text blocks (e.g., "Image 1:", "Image 2:") so Claude’s response can refer back to them unambiguously:
message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Image 1:"},
                {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png", "data": image1_data}},
                {"type": "text", "text": "Image 2:"},
                {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png", "data": image2_data}},
                {"type": "text", "text": "How are these images different?"},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
Common vision use cases include: extracting structured data from charts and graphs (asking Claude to read off values or trends), transcribing text from screenshots or scanned documents (a lighter-weight alternative to a dedicated OCR pipeline for many cases), reviewing UI or design mockups for feedback, describing photos for accessibility purposes, and classifying or tagging images in a content pipeline. Image content blocks can be mixed freely with tool use and other API features — for example, a tool-using agent could receive a screenshot as part of a tool result and reason about what it shows before deciding on a next action.
A few practical constraints and pitfalls to keep in mind. Very large or very high-resolution images consume more of the context window and cost more, since images are converted into a number of tokens roughly proportional to their pixel dimensions — downscaling oversized images before sending them is a common optimization. There are also limits on image size and the number of images per request, so a workflow processing many images (e.g., every page of a long scanned document) typically needs to batch or paginate rather than sending everything in a single call. As with prompt caching (covered later in this module), image content blocks can themselves carry a cache_control breakpoint, which is worth using if the same image is reused across multiple requests, since re-processing image tokens on every call is otherwise wasteful. Finally, vision is good at general description and reading clearly rendered text, but it isn’t infallible at fine-grained tasks like reading dense small print or precise pixel-level measurements — for high-stakes precision use cases, it’s worth validating outputs rather than trusting them blindly. The next lesson extends this same content-block pattern to PDFs, which Claude can read natively rather than requiring you to convert pages to images yourself.
Key takeaways

Images are sent as an image content block with a source of type "base64" (with media_type and data) or "url" (with url).
Multiple images can appear in a single message; labeling them with preceding text blocks helps Claude reference them clearly in its response.
Supported formats include JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP; image tokens scale with resolution, so downscaling oversized images saves cost and context space.
Common uses: chart/data reading, screenshot or document transcription, UI/design review, accessibility descriptions, and image classification.
Image blocks support cache_control for reuse across requests, and vision output should be validated for high-precision tasks rather than trusted outright.

claude/07-features-of-claude/03-pdf-supp.content:
PDF support


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Claude can read PDF files directly — including their text, layout, tables, and any images or charts on the page — without you having to extract the text yourself first. You just send the PDF as a document content block, and Claude processes both the visual layout and the textual content together, which is more capable than plain text extraction for documents where layout carries meaning.
Deep dive
Before native PDF support, using a PDF with an LLM meant extracting text yourself (often losing table structure, footnotes, or figures in the process) and sending only that text. Claude’s native PDF support instead lets you send the PDF file itself as a document content block, and Claude processes each page combining both its text and its visual layout — meaning it can reason about tables, charts, diagrams, and multi-column layouts that plain text extraction would mangle or lose entirely.
A PDF is provided the same way an image is — base64-encoded data or a fetchable URL — but with type: "document" and media_type: "application/pdf" instead of type: "image":
import anthropic
import base64
import httpx
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
pdf_url = "assets.anthropic.com/m/1cd9d098ac3e6467/original/Claude-3-Model-Card-October-Addendum.pdf"
pdf_data = base64.standard_b64encode(
    httpx.get(pdf_url, follow_redirects=True).content
).decode("utf-8")
 
# Alternative for a local file:
# with open("document.pdf", "rb") as f:
#     pdf_data = base64.standard_b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")
 
message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "document",
                    "source": {
                        "type": "base64",
                        "media_type": "application/pdf",
                        "data": pdf_data,
                    },
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "What are the key findings in this document?"},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(message.content[0].text)
Because Claude processes both text and visual layout, PDF support handles cases plain text extraction struggles with: multi-column academic papers, financial reports with dense tables, forms with checkboxes, and slide-deck-style PDFs where spatial position (not reading order) conveys meaning. Internally, each page is effectively treated similarly to an image plus its extracted text, so — just like image support — larger PDFs consume more tokens roughly in proportion to their page count and visual complexity, and there are practical limits on file size and page count per request, so very long PDFs (hundreds of pages) may need to be split or have irrelevant sections trimmed before sending.
PDF support is also the natural document format for the Files API, which lets you upload a file once and reference it by file_id in multiple subsequent requests instead of re-encoding and re-sending the same base64 blob every time — useful when the same PDF is used across many questions or many users. This pairs directly with the citations feature covered next: PDFs sent with citations enabled let Claude point back to the exact page or passage that supports a claim in its answer, which is much more useful for a long report than a plain text summary with no traceability. The document block also accepts optional title and context fields — title labels the document for Claude and in citation output, and context supplies background information about the document that Claude should use for understanding but should not cite from directly.
A few pitfalls worth flagging. First, scanned PDFs (images of pages with no underlying text layer) rely entirely on Claude’s visual reading of the page, similar to OCR — this generally works well but is not infallible for poor-quality scans, unusual fonts, or handwriting. Second, sending PDFs as raw base64 on every request is simple but wasteful for repeated use of the same document — the “Prompt caching” and “Code execution and the Files API” lessons later in this module both offer better patterns (caching the PDF content, or uploading it once via the Files API) for avoiding that repeated cost. Third, when a PDF contains sensitive information you don’t want reasoned over in full, it’s worth trimming or redacting before sending, since there’s no way to have Claude selectively “not see” part of a document once it’s included in the request.
Key takeaways

PDFs are sent as a document content block with media_type: "application/pdf", using the same base64 or URL source pattern as images.
Claude reads both text and visual layout natively, handling tables, multi-column layouts, and forms better than plain text extraction alone.
Larger and more visually complex PDFs consume more tokens; very long documents may need to be trimmed or split before sending.
The Files API lets you upload a PDF once and reference it by file_id across multiple requests, avoiding repeated base64 encoding and re-transmission.
Optional title and context fields label a document and supply background without making that background citable; scanned PDFs rely on Claude’s visual reading, which isn’t infallible on poor scans.

claude/07-features-of-claude/04-citation.content:
Citations


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Citations let Claude back up its claims by pointing to the exact passage in a source document that supports each part of its answer, instead of just asserting facts. This makes answers verifiable — a user (or your application) can trace any statement back to its original source and check it, which is especially valuable for RAG-style applications built on retrieved documents.
Deep dive
The citations feature is configured per document: you attach a citations: {"enabled": True} flag to a document content block, and Claude’s response will include structured citation objects alongside its generated text, identifying exactly which span of which document supports each claim.
A document can be provided in a few different source forms — as plain text, as base64-encoded PDF data, or as a previously uploaded file referenced by file_id (via the Files API). A plain-text example:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "document",
                    "source": {
                        "type": "text",
                        "media_type": "text/plain",
                        "data": "The grass is green. The sky is blue.",
                    },
                    "title": "My Document",
                    "context": "This is a trustworthy document.",
                    "citations": {"enabled": True},
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "What color is the grass and sky?"},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(response)
A PDF example, combining citations with the native PDF support covered in the previous lesson:
import base64
import pathlib
 
pdf_base64 = base64.standard_b64encode(
    pathlib.Path("/path/to/document.pdf").read_bytes()
).decode()
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "document",
                    "source": {
                        "type": "base64",
                        "media_type": "application/pdf",
                        "data": pdf_base64,
                    },
                    "title": "Document Title",
                    "context": "Context about the document that will not be cited from",
                    "citations": {"enabled": True},
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this document."},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
For a document already uploaded via the Files API, you reference it by file_id instead of re-sending its bytes, using the beta files-api-2025-04-14 header:
cited_response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "document",
                    "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": file_id},
                    "title": "Document Title",
                    "context": "Context about the document that will not be cited from",
                    "citations": {"enabled": True},
                },
                {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this document."},
            ],
        }
    ],
    betas=["files-api-2025-04-14"],
)
Note the difference between title and context on a document block: title labels the document (and appears in citation output so you know which source a citation points to), while context supplies background information for Claude to use when interpreting the document — but explicitly is not citable material itself. This is useful for including instructions like “this document may be outdated” without those instructions themselves showing up as a quoted citation.
Citation objects returned in the response are structured, not just inline footnote markers — for a plain-text or PDF-derived document, a citation looks like:
{
    "type": "char_location",
    "cited_text": "The exact text being cited",
    "document_index": 0,
    "document_title": "Document Title",
    "start_char_index": 0,
    "end_char_index": 50
}
This gives you document_index (which of possibly several documents in the request), the exact cited_text, and character offsets locating it precisely — enough to highlight the source passage in a UI, link back to a specific page, or programmatically verify Claude didn’t misquote the source. Notably, cited_text doesn’t count toward output tokens, since it’s a reference into input the model already received rather than newly generated text.
Citations connect directly back to this course’s RAG module: a RAG pipeline that retrieves chunks and inserts them as one or more cited document blocks gets source attribution essentially for free, turning “trust me” answers into answers a user can independently verify against the retrieved passages. The main pitfall is conflating citations with correctness — citations prove Claude is quoting something it was given, not that the quoted passage is itself true or that the surrounding claim is a fair characterization of it, so citation-backed answers still deserve scrutiny, especially for consequential decisions. It’s also worth noting citations add some latency and response size overhead, so they’re best reserved for scenarios where traceability genuinely matters to the user, not enabled reflexively on every request.
Key takeaways

Enable citations per document with "citations": {"enabled": True} on a document content block; supported sources include plain text, base64 PDFs, and Files-API-uploaded files (file_id).
title labels a document for citation output; context gives Claude background information that is explicitly excluded from being cited.
Citation objects include the exact cited_text and character offsets (start_char_index/end_char_index), enabling precise source highlighting or verification.
Citations pair naturally with RAG: retrieved chunks sent as cited documents give answers built-in source attribution.
A citation proves Claude quoted the source correctly, not that the source or surrounding claim is true — citation-backed answers still need scrutiny.

claude/07-features-of-claude/05-prompt-c.content:
Prompt caching


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Prompt caching lets Claude remember a large, unchanging chunk of your prompt — like a long system prompt or a big reference document — between API calls, so it doesn’t have to reprocess that same content every single time. This makes repeated requests that share a lot of context noticeably cheaper and faster, which matters a lot for applications like RAG or long-document Q&A where the same big context is reused across many questions.
Deep dive
Normally, every API call processes its entire input from scratch, regardless of how much of it is identical to a previous call. If you’re sending a 20,000-token system prompt (say, detailed instructions plus a reference document) with every single user question, Claude re-reads and re-processes that entire prefix every time, even though it hasn’t changed. Prompt caching solves this by letting the API server cache the internal processed representation of a prompt prefix, so a subsequent request that starts with the exact same prefix can skip reprocessing it and instead read from the cache — cheaper and faster than a full pass.
Caching is enabled by inserting a cache_control marker on a content block — this marks a “breakpoint,” telling the API “everything up to and including this block is a candidate to be cached.” The most common setup is caching a long, static system prompt:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
SYSTEM_PROMPT = [
    {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "You are an expert software engineer with deep knowledge of distributed systems...",
        "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
    }
]
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I implement a binary search tree?"}],
)
cache_control can also be placed on content blocks within the messages array, not just the system prompt — useful when the cacheable content is a large document earlier in a conversation rather than the system prompt itself:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "...long system prompt", "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ],
    messages=[
        # ...prior conversation turns...
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Good to know."},
                {"type": "text", "text": "Tell me more about Mars.", "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
            ],
        },
    ],
)
The only cache type currently available is "ephemeral" — a short-lived cache with a time-to-live (TTL). By default this TTL is 5 minutes, refreshed on each cache hit; you can instead request a 1-hour TTL by adding a ttl field to the cache_control object:
"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}
The 1-hour option costs more to write into the cache than the default 5-minute option, so it’s a tradeoff: pay a bit more upfront for a cache entry that survives longer gaps between requests (useful for bursty, spread-out traffic), versus the cheaper default that’s ideal for tight request sequences (e.g., an agentic loop firing several calls in quick succession).
The cost model has two sides. Writing to the cache (the first time a given prefix is seen) costs more than a normal, uncached input token — you’re paying a premium to have that content stored. Reading from the cache (a subsequent request that hits the same cached prefix) costs significantly less than reprocessing those tokens normally — this is where the savings come from. So caching pays off when a prompt prefix will be reused multiple times before its TTL expires; caching a prefix you’ll only ever send once is pure added cost with no payoff. A common pattern for applications with predictable startup traffic is pre-warming the cache — issuing a throwaway request with max_tokens=0 against the cacheable prefix before real user traffic arrives, so the very first real request is already a cache hit:
def prewarm_cache() -> None:
    client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=0,
        system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "warmup"}],
    )
This lesson covers the mechanics of turning caching on; the next lesson goes deeper into the rules that determine whether a given request actually hits the cache — prefix matching and content ordering — which is where most caching bugs and missed savings actually come from in practice.
Key takeaways

Prompt caching stores the processed representation of a prompt prefix so repeated requests sharing that prefix skip reprocessing it, cutting cost and latency.
Enable it by adding "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"} to a content block in system or messages, marking everything up to that point as a cache breakpoint.
The default TTL is 5 minutes (refreshed on each hit); an optional ttl: "1h" extends it at a higher write cost.
Writing to the cache costs more than normal input tokens; reading from a cache hit costs much less — caching only pays off for prefixes reused multiple times before expiry.
Pre-warming the cache with a throwaway max_tokens=0 request before real traffic arrives ensures the first real request is already a cache hit.

claude/07-features-of-claude/06-rules-of.content:
Rules of prompt caching


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Turning on cache_control doesn’t guarantee a cache hit — Claude only reuses cached content when the request matches a previous one closely enough, following specific rules about ordering and exact content. This lesson covers those rules, because misunderstanding them is the most common reason developers enable caching and then don’t see the expected savings.
Deep dive
The core rule underlying prompt caching is prefix matching: a cache breakpoint says “everything from the start of the request up through this content block is cacheable as a unit.” For a later request to hit that cache, its content up to the same point must match exactly — same text, same ordering, same structure. This is why caching works best on genuinely static content placed early in the request: a long system prompt, a fixed set of tool definitions, or a reference document that doesn’t change between calls.
Ordering matters, and it’s fixed. Requests are structured, conceptually, as tools → system → messages, and the cache checks each part in that order. This has a direct practical implication: if you want to cache your tool definitions and system prompt, and only vary the user’s message, that works cleanly, because the varying part (the message) comes after everything you’re caching. But if you insert something variable — like today’s date, or a per-user identifier — into the system prompt before the cache breakpoint, you invalidate the cache on every single request, because the “exact match” requirement fails as soon as one earlier byte differs. The practical fix is to place variable content (dates, user IDs, session-specific instructions) after the cache breakpoint, or in a separate, later block, so the earlier static portion still matches and hits the cache.
Multiple breakpoints are supported and independent. You’re not limited to a single cache breakpoint per request — you can mark, for example, your tool definitions, your system instructions, and a large RAG document each with their own cache_control, so that updating one of them (say, refreshing the RAG document) doesn’t force the others (tool definitions, system prompt) to be invalidated and re-cached too. This modular approach is the recommended pattern for a RAG-plus-tools application: cache what’s stable independently from what changes.
Certain configuration changes invalidate the cache even if the text is identical. The clearest example is extended thinking: modifying the thinking configuration between requests — switching from disabled to enabled, changing budget_tokens, or switching modes — invalidates cached message prefixes, system prompts, and tool definitions, because the thinking configuration is effectively rendered as part of what gets processed. A real before/after from a documented example shows the pattern clearly in the usage field of the response: a first request shows cache_creation_input_tokens: 1370, cache_read_input_tokens: 0 (a fresh cache write); a second, identical request shows cache_creation_input_tokens: 0, cache_read_input_tokens: 1370 (a clean cache hit); a third request with a different thinking budget shows cache_creation_input_tokens: 1370, cache_read_input_tokens: 0 again — the cache was invalidated and rewritten, even though the surrounding prompt text hadn’t changed. This is exactly the usage data you should inspect when debugging why expected cache hits aren’t happening.
Mid-conversation system-message changes are a related pattern: if you need to append new system-level guidance partway through a long conversation, place the cache breakpoint on the last stable content block before that new system message, so the new addition doesn’t invalidate everything that came before it.
Putting the rules together as a practical checklist:

Put the largest, most stable content first (tool definitions, then system prompt, then static reference material), and put anything that changes per-request last.
Mark cache breakpoints at the boundary between “stable” and “variable” content, and use multiple independent breakpoints when different parts of your prompt change on different schedules.
Keep the thinking configuration identical across requests you expect to share a cache; treat any change to it as a deliberate cache-invalidating action.
Check usage.cache_creation_input_tokens and usage.cache_read_input_tokens on responses to verify caching is behaving as expected rather than assuming it silently works.
Remember the TTL from the previous lesson: even a perfectly structured request misses the cache if it arrives after the cache entry (5 minutes by default, or 1 hour with the extended TTL) has expired.

The next lesson walks through applying these rules to a realistic prompt structure — the practical exercise of deciding where breakpoints go in an actual RAG-plus-system-prompt setup.
Key takeaways

A cache hit requires an exact prefix match — same content, same order — up to the breakpoint; any earlier difference (even a timestamp) invalidates it.
Requests are structured as tools → system → messages; put stable content early and variable content after the cache breakpoint to maximize hits.
Multiple independent cache breakpoints let you cache tool definitions, system prompt, and reference documents separately, so updating one doesn’t invalidate the others.
Changing the thinking configuration between requests invalidates cached prefixes even if the surrounding text is unchanged.
Verify caching behavior using usage.cache_creation_input_tokens and usage.cache_read_input_tokens in the response rather than assuming it’s working.

Prompt caching in action


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson is a walkthrough — taking the caching mechanics and the ordering/invalidation rules from the previous two lessons and applying them to a realistic application, rather than introducing new concepts. It’s where the abstract rules (“put stable content first,” “watch for invalidation”) turn into a concrete decision about where to place cache_control breakpoints in a real prompt.
Deep dive
Consider a realistic setup that combines several features covered earlier in this course: a support assistant with a fixed set of tool definitions, a long system prompt describing its behavior, a knowledge base of retrieved RAG documents (per the “RAG and Agentic Search” module), and an ongoing multi-turn conversation with a user. Applying the previous lesson’s rules means reasoning about which parts of this prompt are stable across requests and which vary, and ordering the request accordingly.
Step 1: identify what’s stable versus variable.

Tool definitions (e.g., a search_knowledge_base or create_ticket tool) — stable across essentially all requests, for all users, until you ship a change.
The system prompt describing the assistant’s role and behavior — stable across all requests, until you edit it.
Retrieved RAG documents — stable within a single user’s session (assuming you retrieve once and reuse the same context across a few follow-up questions), but variable across different users or different questions, since retrieval returns different chunks for different queries.
The user’s current message and recent conversation turns — variable on every single request.

Step 2: order the request so stable content comes first, and place breakpoints at the boundaries.
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[
        {
            "name": "search_knowledge_base",
            "description": "Search internal support documentation.",
            "input_schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
                "required": ["query"],
            },
            # Breakpoint 1: cache the tool definitions independently.
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        }
    ],
    system=[
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "You are a support assistant for Acme Corp. Be concise, "
                    "cite the source document for any factual claim, and "
                    "escalate to a human if you cannot resolve the issue...",
            # Breakpoint 2: cache the system prompt independently of the tools.
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        }
    ],
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    # Retrieved RAG context for this session — stable across a
                    # few follow-up turns, so it's worth its own breakpoint.
                    "text": f"Reference documents:\n{retrieved_context}",
                    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
                },
                # The actual, always-variable user question goes last, after
                # every cache breakpoint, so it never invalidates anything above it.
                {"type": "text", "text": user_question},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
Three independent breakpoints appear here: tools, system prompt, and retrieved context. Because they’re independent, refreshing the RAG documents for a new question (a very common event) invalidates only the third breakpoint — the tool definitions and system prompt, which didn’t change, continue to hit the cache. This is the payoff of the “multiple independent breakpoints” rule from the previous lesson: without it, any change anywhere in the prompt would force a full cache miss on everything.
Step 3: verify it’s actually working. Rather than assuming the above structure behaves as intended, inspect response.usage across a short sequence of requests. On the first request in a session, expect cache_creation_input_tokens to be nonzero (a cache write) and cache_read_input_tokens to be zero. On a follow-up request within the same session that reuses the same tools, system prompt, and retrieved context, expect the opposite: cache_creation_input_tokens near zero and cache_read_input_tokens large, confirming the stable prefix was read from cache rather than reprocessed.
Step 4: watch for regressions. The most common way this setup silently breaks is a well-intentioned change that touches something before a breakpoint — for example, injecting today’s date or a per-request trace ID into the system prompt text itself, ahead of the cache breakpoint. Per the previous lesson’s rule, that turns a prefix that used to be identical across requests into one that differs on every call, silently killing the cache hit rate without any error being raised. The fix is always the same: keep genuinely variable content after the last relevant breakpoint, and periodically check usage in staging to catch a regression before it reaches production traffic.
Applied consistently, this pattern is what makes prompt caching valuable in practice for RAG applications specifically: the tool definitions and system prompt (large and static) get written to cache once and read cheaply on every subsequent call, while only the retrieval-dependent and per-turn content pays full processing cost — turning what would otherwise be a linearly growing cost per request into something much closer to constant overhead for the stable portions of the prompt.
Key takeaways

Apply the caching rules by first separating a real prompt into stable pieces (tools, system prompt, session-level RAG context) and variable pieces (the current user turn).
Order the request stable-first, and place independent cache_control breakpoints at each stability boundary so unrelated updates don’t invalidate each other.
Keep genuinely variable content (dates, trace IDs, the live question) after the last breakpoint to avoid silently breaking the cache.
Verify behavior empirically via response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens rather than assuming the structure works as designed.
Done well, caching turns large static portions of a RAG-plus-tools prompt into a one-time cost, with only the variable, per-request portion paying full processing cost each time.
