claude/07-features-of-claude/08-code-exe.content:
Code execution and the Files API


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Features of Claude — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
The code execution tool lets Claude write and actually run Python code in a secure sandbox during a conversation — useful for real data analysis, calculations, or chart generation rather than Claude just describing what code would do. The Files API complements this by letting you upload a file once (like a CSV or spreadsheet) and hand Claude a reference to it, so Claude can load and analyze real data inside that sandbox instead of you pasting the data into the prompt as text.
Deep dive
Code execution is enabled like any other tool, by including it in the tools array of a Messages API request, using its dedicated type instead of a custom JSON schema:
import anthropic
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}],
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What's the standard deviation of [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]?"}
    ],
)
print(response.to_json())
When this tool is available, Claude can decide to write Python, execute it in an isolated container, observe the result, and use that result to compose its final answer — the same tool-use loop pattern as any other tool, except the “tool” here is a general-purpose code interpreter rather than a narrow, single-purpose function. This is far more reliable than asking Claude to do arithmetic or data manipulation purely by reasoning in text, since actual code execution guarantees correct computation rather than a plausible-looking approximation.
Code execution becomes especially useful in combination with real data files, which is where the Files API comes in. Rather than pasting a CSV’s contents directly into a prompt as text (wasteful, and it doesn’t scale past a certain file size), you upload the file once via the Files API and get back a file_id, then reference that ID in a container_upload content block so it’s available inside the code execution sandbox:
from pathlib import Path
 
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
 
# Step 1: upload the file once.
file_object = client.beta.files.upload(file=Path("data.csv"))
 
# Step 2: reference it by file_id, alongside the code execution tool.
response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    betas=["files-api-2025-04-14"],
    max_tokens=4096,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Analyze this CSV data and summarize the key trends."},
                {"type": "container_upload", "file_id": file_object.id},
            ],
        }
    ],
    tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}],
)
print(response.to_json())
Note the container_upload block type, distinct from the document block used for PDFs and citations — it specifically hands a file into the code execution sandbox’s filesystem so that generated Python code (e.g., pandas.read_csv(...)) can load and operate on it directly, rather than the file’s contents being inserted into the prompt as text for Claude to read. This distinction matters: document blocks put content into Claude’s context for it to reason about directly; container_upload blocks put a file onto disk inside the sandbox for code to process programmatically. The two mechanisms are complementary — a workflow might use a document block with citations to let Claude read and quote a report’s text, while separately using container_upload to let Claude compute statistics over an accompanying spreadsheet of raw numbers.
The Files API also has broader applicability beyond code execution: as covered in the citations lesson, an uploaded file can be referenced with source: {"type": "file", "file_id": ...} in a document block, letting you upload a large PDF once and reuse it across many requests by ID, rather than re-encoding and re-transmitting its base64 data on every call — a meaningful savings for frequently reused reference documents, in the same spirit as prompt caching from earlier in this module (though the two are separate mechanisms — Files API avoids re-uploading bytes; prompt caching avoids re-processing tokens).
Practical considerations and pitfalls: code execution runs in an isolated, ephemeral container, so it can’t reach your production systems or the open internet — it’s meant for self-contained computation on data you’ve explicitly provided, not for calling out to arbitrary external APIs or accessing anything beyond what’s uploaded. This is a good security property, but it also means code execution is unsuitable for tasks that require live external data. Uploaded files and their containers are also not permanent long-term storage — treat the Files API as a way to hand Claude working data for a session or a bounded set of requests, not as a general-purpose file hosting service; check current retention behavior before relying on a file_id to remain valid indefinitely. Finally, because code execution genuinely runs arbitrary model-generated code (safely sandboxed on Anthropic’s infrastructure), outputs like generated charts or computed values should still be spot-checked for correctness on high-stakes tasks, the same way you’d review any automated data analysis before acting on it.
This lesson closes out the “Features of Claude” module: extended thinking, vision, PDFs, citations, and caching each extend what a single request can perceive or reuse, while code execution and the Files API extend what Claude can actually do with data during a conversation — bringing real computation into the same agentic loop this course has built up through tool use and RAG.
Key takeaways

Enable code execution with {"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"} in tools; Claude writes and runs real Python in an isolated sandbox rather than only describing what code would do.
Upload files once via client.beta.files.upload() to get a file_id, then hand them into the sandbox with a container_upload content block so generated code can load and process them directly.
container_upload (data for code to process) is distinct from document (content for Claude to read and cite) — use whichever matches how the file should be consumed.
The Files API also supports reusing an uploaded file across multiple document/citation requests by file_id, avoiding repeated base64 re-transmission.
Code execution sandboxes are isolated with no external network access and are not permanent storage — suited to self-contained computation on provided data, with outputs still worth spot-checking on high-stakes tasks.

claude/08-model-context-protocol/01-intr.content:
Introducing MCP


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI application connect to external tools, data, and prompt templates in a consistent way, instead of every integration being built from scratch. Think of it like a USB port for AI: any MCP-compatible client can plug into any MCP-compatible server and immediately understand what it offers. This matters because it separates “who builds the AI app” from “who builds the integration,” letting both sides innovate independently.
Deep dive
Before MCP, every time you wanted an LLM application to talk to a new system — a database, a file system, a SaaS product, an internal API — you had to write custom glue code specific to that combination of app and system. If you had five AI apps and ten tools, you potentially needed fifty separate integrations. MCP solves this “M×N” problem by defining a standardized protocol: any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so you only need to build each integration once.
MCP follows a client-server architecture. An MCP host (the AI application, e.g. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or a custom app you build) contains one or more MCP clients, each of which maintains a 1:1 connection to an MCP server. The server is a lightweight program that exposes specific capabilities — tools, resources, and prompts — over the protocol. The host is responsible for managing multiple client connections, aggregating what all connected servers offer, and presenting that combined capability set to the underlying LLM.
Communication between client and server is defined by MCP’s transport layer. The two most common transports are:

stdio (standard input/output): the client launches the server as a local subprocess and they exchange JSON-RPC messages over stdin/stdout. This is the simplest option for local tools and is what you typically use during development.
HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) / Streamable HTTP: used when the server runs remotely (e.g. as a hosted web service). The client sends requests over HTTP and receives responses (including streamed events) back over the same connection.

Regardless of transport, the underlying message format is JSON-RPC 2.0, which defines requests, responses, and notifications. MCP builds a set of specific request/response types on top of this — for example tools/list, tools/call, resources/list, resources/read, prompts/list, and prompts/get.
MCP servers can expose three kinds of primitives:

Tools — callable functions the model can invoke to take an action or fetch information (e.g. “search the database,” “send an email”). These are analogous to the tool/function-calling feature already available directly in the Claude API, but now abstracted behind a standard server.
Resources — readable pieces of data addressed by a URI (e.g. a file, a database record, a config value) that the client can fetch and feed into the model’s context, similar to a GET endpoint.
Prompts — reusable, parameterized prompt templates that a server offers; the user (not the model) typically selects and fills these in through the client’s UI, and the resulting message is inserted into the conversation.

This lesson sets up the conceptual foundation for the rest of the module: subsequent lessons dig into the client side (how a host discovers and talks to servers), then walk through building an actual server from scratch — defining tools, inspecting it with a debugging tool, building a client for it, and then extending it with resources and prompts. A common early pitfall is conflating “MCP server” with “the LLM itself” — the server has no model or intelligence built in; it is purely a capability provider that the client’s LLM decides when and how to call.
Key takeaways

MCP is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools, data, and prompts through a consistent client-server protocol, solving the M×N integration problem.
The architecture has three layers: host (the AI app), client (manages one connection each), and server (exposes capabilities).
Transports are typically stdio (local subprocess) or HTTP/SSE (remote), both carrying JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.
Servers expose three primitive types: tools (callable actions), resources (readable data by URI), and prompts (reusable templates).
This lesson is purely conceptual — it sets up vocabulary used throughout the rest of the module.

claude/08-model-context-protocol/02-mcp-.content:
MCP clients


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
An MCP client is the piece of software that sits inside an AI application (the “host”) and manages a connection to one MCP server. It is what actually opens the transport, exchanges messages, and asks the server “what can you do?” This lesson explains what a client is responsible for before you build one yourself later in the module.
Deep dive
In the MCP architecture, the host is the user-facing application — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or a custom app you write using the Claude API. The host doesn’t talk to servers directly; instead it creates and owns one client instance per server it wants to connect to. This 1:1 relationship is deliberate: each client manages a single session’s handshake, capability negotiation, and message routing with exactly one server, which keeps the protocol simple and makes failures isolated (one server misbehaving doesn’t take down the others).
A client’s core responsibilities are:

Establishing the connection over whichever transport the server uses (stdio subprocess or HTTP/SSE). For stdio, this means spawning the server as a child process and wiring up its stdin/stdout as the message channel.
Initializing the session — client and server exchange an initialize handshake where they declare protocol versions and capabilities (does the server support tools? resources? prompts? does it support things like sampling or notifications?).
Discovering capabilities — calling list operations such as tools/list, resources/list, and prompts/list to learn what the server offers, since a client shouldn’t assume a server’s capabilities in advance.
Invoking capabilities — calling tools/call to execute a tool, resources/read to fetch a resource’s contents, or prompts/get to render a prompt template, and handling the responses (including errors, which MCP represents as structured results rather than transport-level failures where possible).

In Python, the mcp SDK provides ClientSession as the core client object, plus transport helpers like stdio_client (for spawning a local server subprocess) and an HTTP-based client for remote servers. A minimal shape looks like:
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client
 
server_params = StdioServerParameters(
    command="python",
    args=["my_server.py"],
)
 
async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = await session.list_tools()
            for tool in tools.tools:
                print(tool.name, tool.description)
Note the two nested async with blocks: the outer one manages the transport (the subprocess and its pipes), and the inner one manages the protocol session built on top of that transport. This lesson is conceptual — the hands-on implementation comes later in the module (see “Implementing a client”), after you’ve built a server to connect to. A host application, in practice, often manages several clients simultaneously (one per configured server) and merges their tool/resource/prompt lists before presenting them to the LLM, so the model sees one unified toolbox regardless of how many servers are actually backing it.
A common point of confusion: the client is not the LLM, and it doesn’t decide when to call a tool — that decision is made by the model based on the conversation, with the host/client layer simply executing the model’s tool-call requests against the right server and returning results. The client’s job is strictly plumbing: connect, discover, invoke, relay results back.
Key takeaways

A host application creates one MCP client per server; each client owns a single connection/session.
Clients handle four things: connecting over a transport, initializing/negotiating capabilities, discovering what the server offers (list operations), and invoking it (call/read/get operations).
Python’s mcp SDK exposes ClientSession plus transport helpers like stdio_client for local subprocess servers.
The client is plumbing, not intelligence — the LLM decides what to call; the client executes that decision against the server and relays results.
This lesson is the conceptual groundwork for the “Implementing a client” lesson later in the module.

claude/08-model-context-protocol/03-proj.content:
Project setup


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson is the hands-on checkpoint where you set up a local project to build your own MCP server and client from scratch. Rather than more theory, it’s about getting a working Python environment in place — the right packages installed, project files scaffolded — so the following lessons can focus purely on MCP concepts instead of environment troubleshooting.
Deep dive
With the conceptual groundwork from “Introducing MCP” and “MCP clients” laid, this lesson pivots to hands-on setup for the rest of the module’s project: a small MCP server you’ll build up piece by piece (tools, then resources, then prompts) plus a matching client that talks to it.
The general shape of this kind of setup, consistent with how the official MCP Python SDK project is typically bootstrapped:

Python environment: a recent Python (3.10+) with a virtual environment (venv, uv, or similar) to isolate dependencies from the rest of your system.
Installing the MCP SDK: the official Python SDK is distributed as the mcp package, installable via pip install mcp (or uv add mcp). This package provides both the server-building utilities (like FastMCP, a high-level class that turns plain Python functions into MCP tools/resources/prompts via decorators) and the client-building utilities (ClientSession, transport helpers like stdio_client).
Installing the Anthropic SDK: since the broader course goal is wiring MCP servers into Claude, you’ll also have the anthropic Python package installed alongside mcp, along with an API key set as an environment variable (commonly ANTHROPIC_API_KEY), often loaded via a .env file and a package like python-dotenv.
Project layout: typically a single project directory containing a server file (e.g. server.py) and a client file (e.g. client.py), which you’ll build out incrementally across the following lessons — first defining tools on the server, then verifying them with the MCP Inspector, then writing a client that connects to it, and later adding resources and prompts to both sides.
Running the server standalone: MCP servers built with FastMCP are typically run directly (python server.py) or via the mcp CLI’s dev helpers, which is how you’ll launch the server for the Inspector lesson that follows.

The exact package versions, folder names, and starter files used in the course’s own project template aren’t reproduced here since they depend on the specific course materials — treat this lesson as the point where you get a clean, working Python project with mcp and anthropic installed and importable before moving on to writing actual tool definitions. If something doesn’t run in later lessons, the first thing to check is usually this setup: correct Python version, the mcp package actually installed in the active virtual environment, and the API key correctly loaded.
This lesson is a pivot point in the module: everything before it (Introducing MCP, MCP clients) was conceptual, and everything after it (Defining tools with MCP, The server inspector, Implementing a client, Defining resources, Accessing resources, Defining prompts, Prompts in the client) is hands-on work inside the project scaffolded here.
Key takeaways

This is the hands-on setup lesson bridging MCP concepts and the module’s build-a-server-and-client project.
Expect a Python virtual environment, the mcp package (which includes FastMCP for servers and ClientSession/transport helpers for clients), and the anthropic package with an API key configured.
The project typically separates server code and client code into distinct files, built up incrementally across the rest of the module.
If later lessons fail to run, recheck this setup first: Python version, package installation, and API key loading.
Everything from “Defining tools with MCP” onward builds directly on top of the project created here.

claude/08-model-context-protocol/04-defi.content:
Defining tools with MCP


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson is where you write your first real MCP server: a small Python program that exposes one or more “tools” — functions the model can call. With the FastMCP helper class, turning an ordinary Python function into an MCP tool is mostly a matter of adding a decorator and writing a clear docstring.
Deep dive
An MCP tool is a callable capability a server exposes to clients — conceptually the same idea as function/tool calling already built into the Claude API, except now the tool definition and its execution both live on a separate server process rather than in your application code directly. This decoupling is the whole point: the same tool server can be reused by Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or any custom client without rewriting the tool logic.
The Python mcp SDK’s high-level server class (commonly imported as FastMCP) makes defining a server and its tools straightforward. You create one server instance, then register functions as tools using the @mcp.tool() decorator:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
 
mcp = FastMCP("Demo")
 
@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b
 
@mcp.tool()
def search_books(query: str, limit: int = 5) -> str:
    """Search the catalog by title or author."""
    return f"Found books matching {query!r} (showing up to {limit})."
 
if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
A few details matter a lot here:

The function name becomes the tool name exposed to clients, unless you override it via @mcp.tool(name="...").
The docstring becomes the tool’s description — this is what the model reads to decide whether and how to call the tool, so it should be clear and specific, just like a good tool description in direct Claude API tool use.
Type hints define the input schema. FastMCP inspects the function’s parameter types (str, int, bool, Pydantic models, etc.) and automatically generates the JSON Schema the client needs — you don’t hand-write a schema the way you sometimes do with the raw Claude API’s tools parameter.
Default values mark parameters as optional; parameters without defaults are required.
Use async def when the tool does I/O (network calls, file access, database queries) so the server doesn’t block other requests; use a plain def for fast, synchronous logic.
mcp.run() starts the server. By default this runs over the stdio transport, meaning the server expects to be launched as a subprocess by a client and communicates over stdin/stdout — this is exactly the setup used by the Inspector and by the client you’ll build in later lessons. You can also run over HTTP-based transports for remote deployment.

Once a tool is registered, it isn’t automatically “live” for a model — a client still has to connect to this server, call tools/list to discover the tool, and pass it (via its host application) into a Claude API call’s tool definitions, then relay tools/call requests back to this server when Claude decides to use it. This lesson only covers the server side of that story: writing the tool and getting the server running. The very next lesson, “The server inspector,” gives you a way to test that the tool works correctly before you write a full client for it, and the lesson after that (“Implementing a client”) closes the loop by writing the code that actually discovers and calls this tool programmatically.
A common pitfall: forgetting the parentheses on the decorator (@mcp.tool instead of @mcp.tool()) causes a confusing error, since the decorator factory expects to be called even with no arguments. Another common mistake is writing a vague docstring — because the model relies entirely on the docstring (plus parameter names/types) to know when to use the tool, a vague description leads to the tool being called at the wrong times or not at all.
Key takeaways

MCP tools are Python functions turned into callable server capabilities via the @mcp.tool() decorator on a FastMCP server instance.
The function name, docstring, and type hints directly become the tool’s name, description, and input schema — no manual JSON Schema needed.
Use async def for I/O-bound tools and plain def for fast synchronous logic.
mcp.run() defaults to the stdio transport, which is what local debugging tools and clients expect to connect to.
Defining a tool on the server is only half the story — a client still needs to discover it (tools/list) and invoke it (tools/call), which subsequent lessons cover.

claude/08-model-context-protocol/05-the-.content:
The server inspector


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
The MCP Inspector is a browser-based debugging tool that lets you connect to your MCP server and manually poke at it — list its tools, call them with test inputs, and see the raw responses — without having to write any client code yet. It’s the fastest way to check that a server you just wrote actually works before wiring it up to a real client or to Claude.
Deep dive
After defining a tool on your server in the previous lesson, you need a way to verify it behaves correctly: does it show up with the right name and description, does it accept the arguments you expect, does it return sensible output, and does it fail gracefully on bad input? Writing a full client just to answer these questions would be slow, so the MCP ecosystem provides a dedicated tool for this: the MCP Inspector.
The Inspector is a standalone Node-based application (not part of the Python SDK) typically launched with npx:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py
This command does two things: it starts your server as a subprocess (using whatever command you give it — here, running your Python server file directly), and it opens a local web UI (usually at http://localhost:6274 or similar) that acts as a full MCP client wrapped in a friendly interface. Because the Inspector itself implements the client side of the protocol, it performs the same initialize handshake and capability discovery a real client would.
Inside the Inspector UI you can typically:

See the server’s declared capabilities (tools, resources, prompts) and metadata from the initialize response.
Browse the Tools tab, which lists every tool discovered via tools/list, showing its name, description, and generated input schema (this is a good way to sanity-check that your docstring and type hints produced the schema you intended).
Select a tool, fill in a form generated from its input schema, and click to invoke it — this sends a real tools/call request to your server and displays the raw JSON response, including any errors.
Inspect logs and notifications the server sends, which is useful for debugging async tools or ones that use progress reporting.
As your server grows in later lessons, the Inspector also gains Resources and Prompts tabs for testing resources/read and prompts/get the same way.

Using the Inspector at this stage — right after defining your first tool — establishes a debugging habit you’ll repeat every time you add a new tool, resource, or prompt to the server throughout the rest of this module: define it, then immediately verify it in the Inspector before building or updating client code around it. This catches schema mistakes (like a required parameter that should have been optional) and logic bugs early, when they’re cheap to fix, rather than after they’re buried under client-side code.
Common pitfalls when using the Inspector: forgetting that the Inspector spawns its own subprocess of your server, so if your server has a syntax error or missing dependency, the Inspector will show a connection failure rather than a Python traceback — check your terminal output where you ran the npx command for the actual error. Another common issue is stray print() statements in your server code: because the stdio transport uses stdout for the actual protocol messages, any unexpected output written to stdout (rather than stderr) will corrupt the connection and the Inspector will fail to connect or show garbled data.
Key takeaways

The MCP Inspector is a browser-based tool (launched via npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector <command to run your server>) that acts as a generic MCP client for manual testing.
It lets you browse discovered tools/resources/prompts and invoke them with form-generated inputs, viewing raw protocol responses.
Use it immediately after defining any new server capability — it’s the fastest feedback loop before writing real client code.
A common failure mode is stray output on stdout corrupting the stdio transport; server errors are best diagnosed from the terminal running the server, not the Inspector UI itself.
This lesson bridges “Defining tools with MCP” and “Implementing a client” — verify the server manually here before automating access to it.

Related lessons
Previous: 04 Defining tools with MCP
Next: 06 Implementing a client

claude/08-model-context-protocol/06-impl.title: Implementing a client
claude/08-model-context-protocol/06-impl.content:
Implementing a client


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This is where you write actual Python code that connects to your MCP server the way a real application would — no more manual clicking in the Inspector. You’ll write a script that starts the server, discovers its tools, and calls them programmatically, which is the same pattern a host application uses to feed Claude a live set of tools from an MCP server.
Deep dive
Having verified your server manually with the Inspector, this lesson replaces that manual step with real client code using the mcp Python SDK. The two building blocks are a transport (how bytes move between client and server) and a session (the protocol logic layered on top).
For a local server launched as a subprocess, you use StdioServerParameters to describe how to start it, and stdio_client to open the transport:
import asyncio
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client
 
server_params = StdioServerParameters(
    command="python",
    args=["server.py"],
)
 
async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            # Required handshake before any other request
            await session.initialize()
 
            # Discover what the server offers
            tools_response = await session.list_tools()
            for tool in tools_response.tools:
                print(f"Tool: {tool.name} — {tool.description}")
 
            # Call a tool by name with arguments matching its schema
            result = await session.call_tool("add", arguments={"a": 2, "b": 3})
            print(result.content)
 
asyncio.run(main())
Walking through this: stdio_client(server_params) spawns the server process and yields raw (read, write) streams; wrapping those in ClientSession gives you the higher-level protocol methods. session.initialize() performs the MCP handshake (protocol version and capability negotiation) and must be called before any other request. session.list_tools() sends tools/list and returns the same tool metadata you saw in the Inspector’s Tools tab. session.call_tool(name, arguments) sends tools/call with a dictionary of arguments matching the tool’s input schema, and returns a result whose content holds the tool’s output (execution errors from the tool itself come back as part of this result rather than as a raised exception, so check the result before assuming success).
This is also the point where MCP connects back to the core Claude API tool-use loop you likely learned earlier in the course. In a real integration, after list_tools() you’d convert the MCP tool definitions into the tools parameter shape the Claude Messages API expects (name, description, input schema map fairly directly), send a message to Claude, and when Claude’s response includes a tool_use block, you’d call session.call_tool() with the name and input Claude provided, then feed the result back to Claude as a tool_result — the same agentic loop as native tool use, except the tool’s actual implementation now lives behind an MCP server instead of in your application code.
Common pitfalls: forgetting await session.initialize() before other calls, which causes requests to fail or hang; mismatching argument names/types against the tool’s schema (the server-side validation from FastMCP will reject bad input with a clear error, which is worth reading rather than guessing); and not using async with correctly, which can leave the subprocess running after your script exits. Because this client code mirrors what the Inspector was doing under the hood, any behavior you already validated there should also work here — if it doesn’t, suspect the client code first, since the server itself was already proven to work.
Key takeaways

A minimal client needs a transport (stdio_client + StdioServerParameters for local servers) and a ClientSession built on top of it.
Always call await session.initialize() first; then list_tools() to discover, call_tool(name, arguments) to invoke.
Tool execution errors are returned as part of the result rather than raised as exceptions — always check the result.
This client code is what a host application uses to translate MCP tool definitions into Claude API tools and to execute tool_use requests the model makes.
Behavior already verified in the Inspector should transfer directly to this client code, making the Inspector a useful sanity check when something here doesn’t work.

Related lessons
Previous: 05 The server inspector
Next: 07 Defining resources

claude/08-model-context-protocol/07-defi.content:
Defining resources


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Resources are the second MCP primitive: readable pieces of data your server exposes, addressed by a URI, rather than actions the model triggers. Think of a resource like a GET endpoint — “give me the contents of this thing” — as opposed to a tool, which is more like a POST or RPC call that does something. This lesson adds resources to the server you’ve been building.
Deep dive
So far your server only exposes tools — callable actions the model decides to invoke as part of reasoning through a task. Resources are conceptually different: they’re pieces of context data (files, database rows, config values, API responses) that a client can fetch and insert into the model’s context, similar to how you might manually paste a file’s contents into a prompt, except now it’s addressable and fetchable through the protocol instead of copy-pasted by hand.
In the Python mcp SDK, you define a resource on a FastMCP server with the @mcp.resource() decorator, giving it a URI template:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
 
mcp = FastMCP("Demo")
 
@mcp.resource("greeting://{name}")
def get_greeting(name: str) -> str:
    """Get a personalized greeting."""
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
 
@mcp.resource("config://app")
def get_config() -> str:
    """Return the current application configuration as text."""
    return "theme=dark\nlanguage=en"
A few important details:

The string passed to @mcp.resource(...) is a URI template. Static resources (like config://app) have no placeholders and represent a single fixed piece of data. Dynamic resources (like greeting://{name}) use {param} placeholders that map to the function’s parameters, letting one function serve a whole family of URIs — the client fills in the placeholder when it requests a specific resource, similar to a path parameter in a REST route.
As with tools, the docstring becomes the resource’s description, and the return value is packaged as the resource’s content (text or structured data, depending on what you return).
Resource discovery works the same way as tools: a client calls resources/list to get a listing of static resources (dynamic templates are advertised separately as resource templates), and resources/read with a specific URI to fetch a resource’s content.

The key conceptual distinction to keep straight, since it trips people up: tools are for the model to decide to call as part of reasoning through a task (they have side effects or perform computation, and the model chooses when to use them based on the conversation), while resources are typically surfaced by the client/user to explicitly attach as context — for example, a user picking “attach this file” from a UI, or an application deciding up front to always include a particular resource in the conversation. Resources are not usually offered to the model as something it can “call” the way tools are; they’re more like context the host application manages and injects deliberately.
This lesson only covers defining resources on the server side, mirroring how “Defining tools with MCP” only covered tool definitions before the Inspector and client lessons that followed. The very next lesson, “Accessing resources,” covers the client-side counterpart — how a client lists and reads resources programmatically, the same way “Implementing a client” covered calling tools. As with tools, it’s worth testing new resources in the MCP Inspector’s Resources tab before writing client code against them, to confirm the URI template and returned content look right.
A common pitfall is over-parameterizing a URI template in a way that doesn’t map cleanly to the function’s parameters, or forgetting that resource URIs need a scheme (like greeting:// or config://) — arbitrary strings without a URI-like structure aren’t valid resource identifiers under the protocol.
Key takeaways

Resources expose readable data via URIs, analogous to a GET request, and are defined with @mcp.resource("scheme://path") on a FastMCP server.
URI templates can be static (fixed data) or dynamic ({param} placeholders mapped to function parameters), letting one function serve many resource URIs.
Resources are discovered via resources/list and fetched via resources/read, mirroring the list/call pattern used for tools.
The key distinction from tools: tools are actions the model decides to invoke; resources are context data typically selected/attached by the client or user rather than called by the model mid-reasoning.
This lesson covers the server side only; the next lesson, “Accessing resources,” covers reading resources from the client.

Related lessons
Previous: 06 Implementing a client
Next: 08 Accessing resources

claude/08-model-context-protocol/08-acce.title: Accessing resources
claude/08-model-context-protocol/08-acce.content:
Accessing resources


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Now that your server exposes resources, this lesson covers how a client actually lists and reads them — the resource equivalent of “Implementing a client,” which covered discovering and calling tools. You’ll extend your client code to fetch resource content and see how that content can be fed into a conversation with Claude.
Deep dive
Mirroring the tool-access pattern from “Implementing a client,” accessing resources from a client uses the same ClientSession object, just with resource-specific methods instead of tool-specific ones:
async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
 
            # Discover available (static) resources
            resources_response = await session.list_resources()
            for resource in resources_response.resources:
                print(f"Resource: {resource.uri} — {resource.name}")
 
            # Read a specific resource by URI
            content = await session.read_resource("greeting://world")
            for item in content.contents:
                print(item.text)
session.list_resources() sends resources/list and returns the server’s advertised static resources (their URIs, names, descriptions, and MIME types). session.read_resource(uri) sends resources/read for a specific URI — including URIs matching a dynamic template you construct yourself by filling in the placeholder — and returns the resource’s content, which can be plain text or, for some resource types, binary data encoded appropriately.
The practical reason this matters for a Claude-based application: resources are how you feed external, addressable context into a conversation without hardcoding it into your prompt. A typical flow looks like: the client lists what resources are available, presents them to the user (or an application decides programmatically which ones are relevant), reads the selected resource’s content via read_resource, and then includes that content in the next message sent to Claude — for example as part of the user turn’s text, or as a dedicated context block, depending on how the host application is structured. This is different from the tool-calling loop: resources aren’t something Claude requests mid-conversation through a tool_use block by default; they’re assembled by the client/host ahead of or alongside the request. (Some MCP clients do support the model discovering and requesting resources dynamically, but the simpler and more common pattern — and the one this lesson focuses on — is the client fetching resources deliberately and attaching them as context.)
Error handling here follows a similar shape to tools: requesting a URI the server doesn’t recognize, or one that fails validation against its template, returns an error response rather than crashing the client outright, so production code should check for and handle read failures gracefully — a resource that’s temporarily unavailable (e.g. a file that was deleted) shouldn’t take down the whole conversation.
This lesson closes the resources arc of the module (define → access), the same way “Defining tools with MCP” and “Implementing a client” closed the tools arc. The next pair of lessons, “Defining prompts” and “Prompts in the client,” repeats this same define-then-access pattern one more time for the third MCP primitive.
Key takeaways

session.list_resources() sends resources/list; session.read_resource(uri) sends resources/read to fetch a specific resource’s content.
Resource content can be text or binary depending on the resource’s type, returned inside a contents list on the read result.
Unlike tools, resources are typically fetched deliberately by the client/host and attached as context, rather than requested by the model mid-reasoning via a tool-call-like mechanism.
Handle read failures gracefully — an invalid or unavailable URI returns an error result rather than crashing the session.
This lesson completes the “resources” arc of the module (define, then access), mirroring the earlier tools arc; prompts follow the same pattern next.

Next: 09 Defining prompts

claude/08-model-context-protocol/09-defi.content:
Defining prompts


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Prompts are the third MCP primitive: reusable, fill-in-the-blank message templates that a server offers, meant to be picked and completed by a user rather than called by the model. Think of them like slash commands or saved templates — “summarize this code,” “write a commit message” — that a server author writes once so every client connecting to that server can offer the same well-crafted starting points.
Deep dive
Where tools are actions the model invokes and resources are data the client attaches, prompts are templated instructions meant to be surfaced directly to the user, typically through some kind of picker UI in the client application. The user selects a prompt, fills in its arguments, and the client sends the rendered result into the conversation — the model doesn’t decide to use a prompt the way it decides to call a tool.
In the Python mcp SDK, prompts are defined with the @mcp.prompt() decorator on a FastMCP server:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
 
mcp = FastMCP("Demo")
 
@mcp.prompt()
def greet_user(name: str, style: str = "friendly") -> str:
    """Generate a greeting prompt."""
    styles = {
        "friendly": "Please write a warm, friendly greeting",
        "formal": "Please write a formal, professional greeting",
        "casual": "Please write a casual, relaxed greeting",
    }
    return f"{styles.get(style, styles['friendly'])} for someone named {name}."
 
@mcp.prompt()
def review_code(code: str) -> str:
    """Review a piece of code."""
    return f"Please review this code:\n\n{code}"
Key details, several of which mirror tools but differ in important ways:

The function name becomes the prompt’s name, and the docstring becomes its description — same as tools.
Function parameters become the prompt’s arguments, but unlike a tool’s rich JSON-Schema input, prompt arguments in MCP are structured as a flat list of named string fields — essentially form fields a user fills in through the client’s UI, not a typed schema the model reasons over.
The function’s return value becomes the message content that gets inserted into the conversation once rendered. When a client calls prompts/get, the SDK wraps the returned text as a proper message object (with a role, typically "user") — so the function itself just needs to return the templated text.
Required arguments (parameters without defaults) are validated before the function runs; calling prompts/get with a missing required argument results in a protocol-level error rather than a graceful model-facing error result, so client code should validate user input before submitting it.

Prompts solve a specific problem: prompt engineering knowledge often lives with whoever built the integration (they know the best way to phrase a request to get good results from a particular tool or dataset), but the people using the client day-to-day may not be prompt engineers. By packaging a well-tuned prompt template on the server, that expertise travels with the server to every client that connects to it — a code review prompt tuned by the server author works identically whether accessed from Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or a custom client.
This lesson is the server-side half of the module’s third and final define/access pair, following the same rhythm as tools (defined in “Defining tools with MCP,” accessed in “Implementing a client”) and resources (defined in “Defining resources,” accessed in “Accessing resources”). The next lesson, “Prompts in the client,” covers listing and retrieving prompts, and rendering their filled-in output into an actual conversation with Claude.
A common pitfall: trying to give a prompt function complex typed parameters (like a list or nested object) the way you would for a tool — because prompt arguments are user-facing form fields, they work best as simple strings with sensible defaults, not the richer types tools support.
Key takeaways

Prompts are reusable message templates defined with @mcp.prompt(), meant to be selected and filled in by a user, not invoked by the model like a tool.
Function name → prompt name, docstring → description, and parameters → a flat list of string arguments rendered as form fields in the client.
The function’s return value is wrapped as a message (typically role "user") once the prompt is rendered via prompts/get.
Prompts let integration authors package tuned prompt engineering into the server itself, so every connecting client benefits from it consistently.
This is the server-side half of the module’s third define/access pair; “Prompts in the client” covers the client side next.

Related lessons
Previous: 08 Accessing resources
Next: 10 Prompts in the client

claude/08-model-context-protocol/10-prom.title: Prompts in the client
claude/08-model-context-protocol/10-prom.content:
Prompts in the client


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson completes the prompts story by showing how a client lists a server’s available prompts, retrieves one with the user’s filled-in arguments, and turns the result into an actual message sent to Claude. It’s the same discover-then-invoke shape you’ve now used three times in this module — for tools, then resources, and now prompts.
Deep dive
Continuing directly from “Defining prompts,” this lesson adds the client-side calls needed to use prompts, via the same ClientSession object used for tools and resources:
async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
 
            # Discover available prompts
            prompts_response = await session.list_prompts()
            for prompt in prompts_response.prompts:
                print(f"Prompt: {prompt.name} — {prompt.description}")
                for arg in prompt.arguments or []:
                    print(f"  arg: {arg.name} (required={arg.required})")
 
            # Render a specific prompt with arguments
            rendered = await session.get_prompt(
                "greet_user", arguments={"name": "Ada", "style": "formal"}
            )
            for message in rendered.messages:
                print(message.role, message.content)
session.list_prompts() sends prompts/list and returns each prompt’s name, description, and its argument list (including which arguments are required) — this is what a client would use to build a picker UI or a form. session.get_prompt(name, arguments) sends prompts/get with a dictionary of argument values (all values are strings, matching how prompt arguments are defined on the server) and returns a list of rendered messages, each with a role and content, ready to be inserted directly into a conversation.
The practical integration with Claude looks like this: once you have the rendered messages list back from get_prompt, you append those messages to whatever conversation history you’re building for the Claude API’s Messages endpoint, then send the request as normal. Because the server already did the work of phrasing the instruction well, your application code doesn’t need any additional prompt engineering for that particular task — it just needs to collect the user’s argument values (through whatever UI makes sense for your host application) and pass them through.
This closes the loop on all three MCP primitives covered across this module:

Tools (defined in “Defining tools with MCP,” accessed in “Implementing a client”): callable actions the model decides to invoke mid-conversation.
Resources (defined in “Defining resources,” accessed in “Accessing resources”): readable context data fetched deliberately by the client and attached to a conversation.
Prompts (defined in “Defining prompts,” accessed here): reusable templates a user selects and fills in, rendered into ready-to-send messages.

A subtlety worth calling out: unlike a tool call, which the model itself decides to trigger based on its own reasoning, a prompt is invoked entirely outside the model’s control — by the time Claude sees the rendered message, it looks just like any other user turn, with no indication (unless your application adds one) that it came from a template rather than something the user typed by hand. This is by design, but it means prompts are best thought of as a UX convenience layered on top of the conversation, not a model-facing capability the way tools and resources (to a lesser extent) can be.
With all three primitives covered end-to-end, the module’s final lesson, “MCP review,” steps back to recap the whole protocol and how the pieces fit together.
Key takeaways

session.list_prompts() discovers available prompts and their arguments; session.get_prompt(name, arguments) renders one into ready-to-use messages.
Rendered prompt messages can be appended directly to a Claude API conversation, no extra prompt engineering needed on the application side.
This lesson completes the third and final define/access pair in the module, alongside tools and resources.
Prompts are invoked entirely by the client/user, not the model — Claude sees the rendered result as an ordinary message, not as a special protocol event.
The next and final lesson, “MCP review,” recaps the whole module.

Related lessons
Previous: 09 Defining prompts
Next: 11 MCP review

claude/08-model-context-protocol/11-mcp-.title: MCP review
claude/08-model-context-protocol/11-mcp-.content:
MCP review


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Model Context Protocol — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This final lesson of the module steps back and ties everything together: what MCP is, why it exists, and how the server and client code you built across the previous ten lessons fits into the bigger picture of building AI applications with Claude. It’s a recap, not new material.
Deep dive
The module opened with a problem statement in “Introducing MCP”: without a shared standard, every AI application needed custom, one-off integration code for every external tool or data source it wanted to use, which doesn’t scale. MCP fixes this with a standardized client-server protocol so that any MCP-compatible client can talk to any MCP-compatible server, over either a local stdio transport or a remote HTTP/SSE transport, exchanging JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.
The module then worked through the architecture layer by layer:

“MCP clients” established that a host application (like Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or your own app) owns one client per connected server, and that a client’s job is connecting, initializing, discovering, and invoking — pure plumbing, not intelligence.
“Project setup” got a real Python project running with the mcp and anthropic packages installed, ready to build against.
From there, the module worked through each of MCP’s three primitives twice — once to define it on the server, once to access it from the client:

Tools (“Defining tools with MCP” → “Implementing a client”): callable actions registered with @mcp.tool(), discovered via tools/list, and invoked via tools/call. Tools are the primitive the model decides to use mid-conversation, closely mirroring native Claude API tool use except the implementation now lives behind a reusable server.
Resources (“Defining resources” → “Accessing resources”): readable data addressed by URI, registered with @mcp.resource("scheme://path"), discovered via resources/list, and fetched via resources/read. Resources are typically fetched deliberately by the client/host and attached as context, not requested mid-reasoning by the model.
Prompts (“Defining prompts” → “Prompts in the client”): reusable templates registered with @mcp.prompt(), discovered via prompts/list, and rendered into ready-to-send messages via prompts/get. Prompts are picked and filled in by the user, packaging an integration author’s prompt engineering so it travels with the server.


Threaded through the middle, “The server inspector” introduced the MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector <server command>) as the fast manual-testing tool to validate each new server capability before writing or updating client code against it — a habit worth carrying forward into any future MCP server you build.

Put together, the pattern for building any new MCP integration is now: define the capability on the server using the appropriate FastMCP decorator, verify it in the Inspector, then update client code to discover and use it, and — when the goal is a Claude-powered application — translate what the client retrieves (tool definitions, resource content, or rendered prompt messages) into the right shape for a Claude API request.
Zooming out, MCP matters for this course specifically because it’s the standard way to extend Claude’s capabilities without cramming everything into your own application code: instead of hardcoding every database query, file operation, or API call your Claude-powered app might need, you can point it at MCP servers — ones you write, or ones published by others — and let the same client/discovery machinery handle the rest. This sets up the next module’s territory: Anthropic’s own applications (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, computer use) that already speak MCP natively, meaning the server you built in this module could, with the right configuration, be plugged directly into those tools rather than only your own hand-written client.
A good self-check before moving on: could you explain, without looking back, the difference between a tool, a resource, and a prompt, and name which side (server or client) is responsible for defining versus discovering/invoking each one? If any of those three feel shaky, revisit the corresponding define/access lesson pair before continuing.
Key takeaways

MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, data, and prompts via a client-server protocol over stdio or HTTP/SSE transports.
Tools (model-invoked actions), resources (client-fetched data by URI), and prompts (user-selected templates) are the three primitives, each defined on the server with a FastMCP decorator and accessed from the client via matching list/invoke calls.
The MCP Inspector is the fast manual-testing loop to use after defining any new server capability, before writing client code.
The overall workflow — define on server, verify in Inspector, discover/invoke from client, integrate with the Claude API — generalizes to any future MCP server you build.
This sets up the next module, where Anthropic’s own apps (Claude Code, Claude Desktop) are shown consuming MCP servers natively.

Related lessons
Previous: 10 Prompts in the client

claude/09-anthropic-apps---claude-code-a.title: Anthropic apps
claude/09-anthropic-apps---claude-code-a.content:
Anthropic apps


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Anthropic apps - Claude Code and computer use — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson surveys the applications Anthropic builds on top of the Claude API itself — Claude.ai (the chat interface), Claude Desktop, Claude Code (an agentic coding tool), and computer use (letting Claude operate a computer’s screen directly). The point is to show that everything in this course — the API, tool use, MCP — is the same foundation Anthropic’s own products are built on, not a separate simplified subset.
Deep dive
Throughout this course you’ve been building directly against the Claude API: sending messages, defining tools, and now connecting to MCP servers. This lesson zooms out to show where that same underlying technology shows up in Anthropic’s own shipped products, which is useful both as inspiration for what’s possible and as a preview of tools you’ll actually use hands-on in the rest of this module.
Claude.ai is the general-purpose chat interface most people encounter first — a conversational product with features like Projects, Artifacts, and (depending on plan) web search and file uploads. It’s built on the Messages API but wraps it in a consumer-facing UI, memory/context features, and its own tool integrations.
Claude Desktop is a native desktop application that, notably for this course, was one of the first Anthropic products to support MCP servers directly — you can configure it to connect to local or remote MCP servers (the same kind you built in the previous module) through a configuration file, giving the desktop chat interface access to custom tools, resources, and prompts without writing any client code yourself. This is a direct, practical payoff of everything learned in the MCP module: a server you already built can, in principle, be plugged into Claude Desktop’s config and used immediately.
Claude Code is an agentic command-line tool for software development. Rather than a chat window, it’s a terminal-based agent that can read your codebase, propose and make edits, run shell commands (tests, builds, git operations), and iterate based on the results — an agentic loop built on top of the same Messages API and tool-use mechanics from earlier in this course, but purpose-built and heavily tuned for coding workflows. Claude Code is also natively MCP-aware: you can register MCP servers with it via the claude mcp add command, extending what it can do beyond its built-in file/shell tools. This is the focus of the next three lessons in this module.
Computer use is a capability (available through the API and used in some Anthropic products) where Claude is given a screenshot of a computer’s screen and can respond with actions — mouse clicks, keyboard input, scrolling — that get executed and fed back as new screenshots, in a loop. This lets Claude operate general-purpose software the way a human would, when no purpose-built tool or API exists for a task. It’s a much less constrained and more experimental capability than a well-defined tool schema, since the “interface” is literally whatever’s on screen.
What ties all of these together, and what this lesson wants you to notice, is that none of them are a fundamentally different technology from what you’ve already learned: they’re all applications of the same Messages API, the same tool-calling loop, and (for Desktop and Code) the same MCP protocol, just packaged for different audiences and use cases. Understanding the API-level mechanics — as you’ve done in earlier modules — is what lets you both use these products more effectively and build your own equivalents for problems Anthropic’s off-the-shelf apps don’t address.
The rest of this module gets hands-on with one of these apps specifically: the next lesson walks through setting up Claude Code, followed by a lesson actually using it, and finally a lesson on extending it with MCP servers — connecting directly back to the previous module’s project.
Key takeaways

Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and computer use are all Anthropic products built on the same underlying Claude API and tool-use mechanics covered elsewhere in this course.
Claude Desktop and Claude Code both support MCP natively, meaning servers you build (like the one from the MCP module) can be plugged directly into them.
Claude Code is a terminal-based agentic coding tool: it reads code, proposes edits, runs commands, and iterates — the focus of the next few lessons.
Computer use lets Claude act on a screenshot-driven loop (see screen, decide action, act, see updated screen), useful when no structured tool/API exists for a task.
The rest of this module is hands-on with Claude Code specifically: setup, usage, then MCP extension.

claude/09-anthropic-apps---claude-code-a.content:
Claude Code setup


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Anthropic apps - Claude Code and computer use — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This lesson walks through installing Claude Code and getting it authenticated so you can use it in the next lesson. It’s a short, practical setup step — install the CLI globally with npm, then sign in — before moving on to actually using the tool.
Deep dive
Claude Code is distributed as an npm package and installed globally as a CLI tool. The standard installation command is:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
This requires a reasonably recent Node.js version (Node 18+, with Node 22+ recommended by current Anthropic documentation) since the npm package wraps a native binary. Anthropic also provides a standalone installer script for systems where you’d rather not depend on a global npm install, but the npm route is the most common path and the one most tutorials (including this course) walk through.
Once installed, running claude from any directory starts the tool. Before it’s useful, you need to authenticate it to your Anthropic account. The CLI provides a login flow, typically:
claude auth login
or, if you want usage billed through Anthropic Console (API credits) rather than a Claude.ai subscription plan:
claude auth login --console
This opens a browser-based OAuth flow (or prints a link if a browser isn’t available) to link the CLI to your account. Once authenticated, Claude Code remembers your session, so you don’t need to log in again on every invocation from the same machine.
A few things worth knowing at setup time, since they affect how the tool behaves once you start using it in the next lesson:

Claude Code operates within the directory you launch it from — it treats that directory as the project it has context on and permission to act within, reading files and proposing edits scoped to that folder (and subfolders) by default. Running claude from the wrong directory is a common early mistake — always cd into your project root first.
The tool has a permission system: the first time it wants to do something potentially impactful (edit a file, run a shell command), it asks for your confirmation, and you can configure broader or narrower auto-approval rules over time as you get comfortable with what it does.
Authentication is separate from any API key you might have set as an environment variable for direct SDK use earlier in this course — Claude Code’s own auth flow (via claude auth login) is what it uses, though Console-based billing does tie back to the same Anthropic Console account as an API key would.

Common setup pitfalls: an outdated Node.js version causing the npm install to fail silently or behave oddly; running the install without -g and then being unable to find the claude command on your PATH; and forgetting to authenticate before trying to use it, which produces an auth error rather than useful output. If claude --version runs successfully after installation, and a simple prompt after login gets a real response, setup is complete and you’re ready for the next lesson, which takes Claude Code for an actual hands-on spin inside a project.
Key takeaways

Install with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code, which requires a recent Node.js (22+ recommended) and installs a native binary under the hood.
Authenticate with claude auth login (or claude auth login --console for Anthropic Console/API billing) before first use.
Claude Code scopes its file access and actions to the directory you launch it from — always run it from your intended project root.
It has a built-in permission system that asks for confirmation before impactful actions like edits or shell commands.
Once installed and authenticated, the next lesson puts it to use on a real task.

claude/09-anthropic-apps---claude-code-a.content:
Claude Code in action


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Anthropic apps - Claude Code and computer use — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
With Claude Code installed and authenticated, this lesson is about actually using it — giving it a real task inside a project and watching it work through reading code, making changes, running commands, and checking its own results. It’s meant to build intuition for what “agentic coding” feels like in practice, beyond the setup steps from the previous lesson.
Deep dive
Claude Code’s defining characteristic is that it runs an agentic loop: rather than a single request/response exchange, it repeatedly reads context, decides on an action, executes that action, observes the result, and decides what to do next — continuing until the task looks complete or it needs your input. This is the same tool-use loop underlying the Claude API’s function-calling mechanics covered earlier in this course, except here the “tools” are built-in ones for interacting with a real filesystem and shell: reading files, searching across a codebase, writing/editing files, and running arbitrary commands (tests, linters, builds, git operations).
A typical hands-on session looks like this: you launch claude from your project directory and describe a task in plain language — “add input validation to the signup form,” “fix the failing test in auth_test.py,” “explain what this function does.” Claude Code then:

Reads relevant code — it doesn’t need you to paste files in; it searches and reads what it judges relevant to the task, the same way a developer would explore an unfamiliar codebase.
Plans and explains — for non-trivial tasks it typically describes what it intends to do before doing it, so you can catch a misunderstanding early rather than after changes are made.
Edits files — proposing specific changes, which (per the permission system covered in the setup lesson) it asks you to approve, especially for first-time or higher-impact actions.
Runs commands — executing tests, builds, or other verification steps to check whether its change actually works, rather than assuming it’s correct.
Iterates — if a test fails or a command errors, it reads the output and adjusts, looping back through the same read-edit-run cycle until the task is resolved or it hits a point where it needs clarification from you.

This loop is what distinguishes an agentic tool from a simple autocomplete or chat assistant: Claude Code doesn’t just suggest a diff and stop — it can verify its own work against real feedback (test output, error messages, command exit codes) and correct course, much like a developer would.
A few things to expect and watch for while using it hands-on:

Scope matters. Vague, sprawling requests (“make this codebase better”) produce vague, sprawling behavior. Specific, bounded tasks (“fix this one failing test,” “add a docstring to this function”) tend to go faster and more predictably — a good habit to build early.
Review before approving. The permission prompts exist precisely so you stay in the loop on meaningful changes; treat them as a real checkpoint, not a formality to click through.
It can run shell commands, which means it can also do destructive things (like deleting files) if instructed carelessly — the same caution you’d apply to any tool with real filesystem and command access applies here.
Context and memory: Claude Code can pick up project-specific instructions and conventions (for example, from a project-level configuration/instructions file) so it doesn’t need everything re-explained every session — useful once you move beyond one-off tasks to regular use.

This lesson is meant to be experiential — the best way to build intuition for the tool is running it on a real, small task and watching the loop play out. The next lesson connects this back to the previous module directly: it covers configuring MCP servers for Claude Code, meaning the custom tools you built earlier in this course can extend what Claude Code itself is capable of doing during this same agentic loop.
Key takeaways

Claude Code runs an agentic loop: read context, act (edit/run command), observe the result, iterate — the same tool-use mechanics from the Claude API, applied to real filesystem/shell access.
It explains its plan before acting on non-trivial tasks and asks for approval on impactful changes via its permission system.
It verifies its own work by running tests/commands and adjusting based on real output, rather than assuming a change is correct.
Specific, bounded tasks work better than vague, open-ended requests — a practical habit worth building early.
The next lesson extends this same agentic loop with MCP servers, connecting directly to the MCP module earlier in the course.

Related lessons
Previous: 02 Claude Code setup
Next: 04 Enhancements with MCP servers

claude/09-anthropic-apps---claude-code-a.content:
Enhancements with MCP servers


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Anthropic apps - Claude Code and computer use — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
This closing lesson connects the two modules of the course: it shows how to plug MCP servers — like the one you built earlier — into Claude Code (and Claude Desktop) so the agentic loop from the previous lesson gains new capabilities beyond built-in file and shell access. Instead of writing your own MCP client, these apps already act as MCP hosts, so registering a server is mostly a matter of configuration.
Deep dive
The previous lesson showed Claude Code’s built-in agentic loop: reading files, editing them, and running shell commands. That’s a fixed, general-purpose toolset. MCP servers extend it — anything you can expose as an MCP tool, resource, or prompt (as covered in depth in the MCP module) becomes available to Claude Code’s loop alongside its built-in tools, without you needing to modify Claude Code itself.
Registering a server with Claude Code is done through its CLI, using the claude mcp add command. At minimum this takes a transport type, a name for the server, and how to reach it:
# Register a remote HTTP-based MCP server
claude mcp add --transport http claude-code-docs code.claude.com/docs/mcp
 
# Register a local server (e.g. one you built in the MCP module) over stdio
claude mcp add my-server -- python server.py
Servers can be registered at different scopes, which control where the configuration is stored and who it applies to:

Local (the default) — stored privately, available only to you in the current project.
Project — written to a project-level config file (e.g. .mcp.json in the project root) so teammates get the same server automatically after cloning the repo (they’re prompted to approve it the first time).
User — stored in your user-level config, available across every project you work in, not just the current one.

Once registered, you can confirm the connection with:
claude mcp list
which shows every configured server and its current connection status — directly analogous to the discovery step (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list) you implemented by hand in the MCP module’s client lessons, except now Claude Code is doing that discovery for you and feeding the results straight into its own agentic loop.
Claude Desktop takes a slightly different configuration approach: rather than a CLI command, it typically uses a JSON configuration file (edited directly or via a settings UI) listing the MCP servers to launch and connect to on startup, using the same underlying transport concepts (commonly stdio for local servers). The effect is the same as with Claude Code — once configured, the server’s tools, resources, and prompts become available inside the chat interface.
Why this matters as a capstone to the course: everything you built in the MCP module — a server exposing tools (e.g. querying an internal system), resources (e.g. exposing config or file-backed data), and prompts (e.g. a tuned template for a recurring task) — isn’t limited to the custom client you wrote for that module. The exact same server can be dropped into Claude Code to extend its coding loop (e.g. a tool that queries your company’s internal ticket system so Claude Code can look up ticket details while fixing a bug) or into Claude Desktop to extend general chat (e.g. a resource exposing your notes so Claude can reference them). This is the practical payoff of MCP’s standardization: build the server once, and it works everywhere an MCP host exists.
Common pitfalls when connecting a server to Claude Code: forgetting that a locally-scoped server only applies to the project you were in when you ran claude mcp add (use --scope user if you want it everywhere, or --scope project if you want to share it with a team via version control); stdio-based servers failing to connect for the same reasons covered in the MCP module (stray stdout output, wrong working directory, missing dependencies) — claude mcp list and checking connection status is your first debugging step, the same instinct as using the MCP Inspector earlier in the course; and forgetting that project-scoped servers prompt for approval the first time a teammate opens the project, which is a deliberate security checkpoint, not a bug.
This lesson closes out the module and the course’s practical arc: from raw Claude API calls, to tool use, to building your own MCP servers and clients, to finally plugging those servers into Anthropic’s own production applications.
Key takeaways

MCP servers extend Claude Code’s and Claude Desktop’s built-in agentic capabilities without modifying the apps themselves — both act as MCP hosts already.
Register a server with Claude Code via claude mcp add --transport <type> <name> <target> (or a -- command for local stdio servers), then verify with claude mcp list.
Servers can be scoped local (private, current project), project (shared via a repo config file, e.g. .mcp.json), or user (available across all your projects).
Claude Desktop uses a JSON configuration file to register servers, conceptually the same idea as Claude Code’s CLI-based registration.
A server built in the MCP module works unmodified across any MCP host — the practical payoff of the protocol’s standardization, and the capstone connection between this course’s two modules.
