claude/10-agents-and-workflows/01-agents.title: Agents and workflows
claude/10-agents-and-workflows/01-agents.content:
Agents and workflows


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Agents and workflows — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
When you build something with Claude that does more than answer a single question, you have two basic ways to organize it: write code that calls Claude a few times in a fixed sequence you control (“workflow”), or let Claude decide for itself, step by step, what to do next and which tools to use (“agent”). Neither is universally better — a workflow is predictable and cheap, an agent is flexible but less predictable. This lesson introduces the vocabulary and the mental model that the rest of the module builds on.
Deep dive
This module is based on Anthropic’s “Building Effective Agents” guidance, which draws a sharp line between two ways of composing LLM calls into a larger system.
A workflow is a system where the control flow is fixed in advance by your code. You, the developer, decide the sequence of steps, which LLM calls happen in what order, and how the outputs of one step feed into the next. The LLM is invoked as a component inside a pipeline you designed — it does the “thinking” for individual steps, but it does not decide what the overall sequence of steps will be. If you diagrammed a workflow, the arrows between boxes would be drawn by you, ahead of time, and would not change at runtime.
An agent, by contrast, is a system where the LLM itself drives the process. You give the agent a goal, a set of tools, and turn it loose in a loop: the model looks at the current state, decides what to do next (call a tool, ask a clarifying question, produce a final answer), observes the result, and decides again. The control flow is not fixed by your code — it emerges from the model’s own reasoning at each step. The number of steps, which tools get called, and in what order, are all determined dynamically by the LLM as the task unfolds.
The practical difference shows up immediately in code shape. A workflow’s Python usually looks like ordinary orchestration code with LLM calls sprinkled in — if/for/asyncio.gather structures that a human wrote. An agent’s code is dominated by a while loop: keep calling the model, keep executing whatever tool calls it requests, until it signals it’s done.
# Workflow shape: YOU decide the sequence
step1 = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", ..., messages=[...])
step2 = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", ..., messages=[...step1_output...])
 
# Agent shape: THE MODEL decides the sequence
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", tools=tools, messages=messages)
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    tool_result = run_tool(response.content)  # whichever tool the model picked
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_result})
This module walks through the main workflow patterns one at a time, then moves on to agents proper.
Parallelization runs several independent LLM calls at the same time instead of one after another, then combines the results. Two flavors: sectioning (break a task into independent subtasks and run each concurrently — e.g. checking a document for four different kinds of issues at once) and voting (run the same task multiple times and aggregate the answers, useful when you want a consensus or a confidence signal). This buys wall-clock speed and, in the voting case, better answer quality through redundancy.
Chaining (prompt chaining) decomposes a task into a sequence of LLM calls where each call processes the output of the previous one. Because each step handles a simpler, more focused subtask, individual steps tend to be more accurate than trying to do everything in one shot. Chains often include a gate: a programmatic check between steps (an assertion, a validation function, or even another LLM call) that verifies the previous step’s output is good enough before continuing — this is where a workflow buys back some of the reliability that a single big freeform call would risk losing.
Routing classifies an incoming input and sends it down one of several specialized downstream paths. Rather than writing one enormous prompt that has to handle every possible kind of request, you first ask a (often cheap and fast) classification call “what kind of thing is this?”, then dispatch to a prompt or handler tuned specifically for that category. This keeps each downstream prompt focused and lets you use different models or tools per category (e.g. a cheap model for simple FAQ questions, a more capable model for complex complaints).
The lesson then turns to agents proper: what happens when you stop pre-deciding the control flow and instead give the model tools and let it decide, turn by turn, what to do. Agents combine tool use (the model’s ability to call functions you’ve defined) with a loop that keeps running until the model decides the task is complete. This is powerful for open-ended tasks where you can’t predict the right sequence of steps in advance — but it trades predictability, cost control, and latency guarantees for that flexibility. A related idea, covered later in this module, is environment inspection: giving the agent ways to actually look at its environment before acting — reading a file listing, checking a command’s exit code, inspecting the current state of a system — rather than guessing blindly and hoping. Grounding each decision in fresh observation is what keeps an agentic loop from compounding small errors into large ones.
Pitfalls to watch for across this module: a runaway agent loop that never terminates or burns far more tokens and turns than expected (mitigate with iteration caps and clear stop conditions); reaching for an agent when a two-step workflow would have solved the problem more cheaply and predictably (added complexity without added value); and, in workflows, over-chaining too many steps such that latency and cost stack up for marginal quality gains. The next six lessons work through the parallelization, chaining, and routing patterns in depth, then agents, tool use, environment inspection, and finally a direct comparison of when to choose a workflow versus an agent.
Key takeaways

A workflow has developer-defined, fixed control flow; an agent has model-driven, dynamic control flow.
Workflows compose LLM calls the way you’d compose functions — parallelization, chaining, and routing are the three core patterns.
Agents combine tool use with a loop where the LLM decides what happens next, step by step, until it’s done.
Environment inspection — letting the model observe real state before it acts — is what keeps agentic decisions grounded rather than guessed.
Neither approach is strictly better; the rest of this module is about learning to choose correctly.

Related lessons

claude/10-agents-and-workflows/02-parall.title: Parallelization workflows
claude/10-agents-and-workflows/02-parall.content:
Parallelization workflows


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Agents and workflows — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Instead of asking Claude to do several unrelated things one after another, you can fire off multiple requests to Claude at the same time and combine their answers once they all come back. This is faster (because the calls overlap in time rather than queuing up) and, when you ask the same question multiple times and compare the answers, it can also make the final result more reliable.
Deep dive
Parallelization is a workflow pattern — the control flow is still fixed by your code, but instead of a single linear chain of calls, several independent LLM calls run concurrently and their outputs are aggregated programmatically at the end. This module (based on Anthropic’s “Building Effective Agents” guidance) describes two variants: sectioning and voting.
Sectioning breaks one task into distinct, independent subtasks, each handled by its own LLM call, run concurrently. The subtasks don’t need each other’s output to run — that’s what makes them safe to parallelize. A classic example: reviewing a piece of content for four unrelated concerns (factual accuracy, tone, legal risk, formatting) as four separate calls that all fire off at once rather than four calls in sequence. Sectioning is a good fit whenever a task decomposes cleanly into independent pieces of work, and it’s also useful simply to keep each individual prompt focused — a single call trying to check four different things at once tends to do a worse job on each than four calls that specialize.
Voting runs the same task multiple times — usually with the same prompt, sometimes with slight variations — and then aggregates the results, most often via majority vote, an averaging step, or a further LLM call that synthesizes the several answers into one. Voting is useful when you want to hedge against the fact that a single LLM call is not perfectly deterministic: running it three or five times and looking for consensus can catch cases where one run went off track. It’s also useful for tasks with a natural “confidence” signal — if four out of five parallel classification calls agree, you can trust the answer more than if you’d only asked once.
Both variants share the same shape in code: kick off N independent calls concurrently, wait for all of them, then run an aggregation step. In Python this maps naturally onto asyncio.gather:
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
 
client = AsyncAnthropic()
 
async def call_claude(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
 
async def sectioning_example(document: str):
    # Independent subtasks — each checks something unrelated, run concurrently
    prompts = [
        f"Check this document for factual errors:\n{document}",
        f"Check this document's tone for professionalism:\n{document}",
        f"Check this document for legal risk:\n{document}",
    ]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(call_claude(p) for p in prompts))
    return dict(zip(["accuracy", "tone", "legal"], results))
 
async def voting_example(question: str, n: int = 5):
    # Same task, run N times, then aggregate
    prompt = f"Answer with only 'yes' or 'no': {question}"
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(call_claude(prompt) for _ in range(n)))
    yes_votes = sum(1 for r in results if "yes" in r.lower())
    return "yes" if yes_votes > n / 2 else "no"
The key mechanical point is that asyncio.gather (or the equivalent in whatever language you’re using — Promise.all in JavaScript, goroutines with a WaitGroup in Go) launches every call before waiting on any of them, so the total wall-clock time is close to the slowest single call rather than the sum of all of them. This is the entire performance win of the pattern: parallelization trades nothing in per-call cost (you still pay for every token in every call), but it can dramatically cut latency versus running the same calls sequentially, and voting can improve quality at the cost of running the same work multiple times.
Parallelization connects to the next two lessons in a specific way: it is the simplest workflow pattern because the parallel branches don’t need to talk to each other or pass state between steps — that’s exactly what chaining (the next lesson) requires, since each step in a chain depends on the previous one’s output. And where parallelization or chaining route every input through the same fixed set of calls, routing (two lessons ahead) instead picks a different single path per input based on what kind of input it is. Parallelization runs multiple paths for one input; routing picks one path per input.
Pitfalls. The most common mistake is parallelizing subtasks that actually have a dependency — if subtask B needs subtask A’s output, running them concurrently just means B runs on stale or missing context, and you should chain instead. A second pitfall with voting specifically is treating majority-vote as though it fixes any underlying quality problem — if the model is systematically wrong about something, running it five times just gets you five wrong (but consistent-looking) answers; voting only helps with inconsistency, not with bias. Third, aggregation is easy to underinvest in: a voting scheme needs a clear, well-defined way to combine N answers into one (majority vote for categorical outputs, averaging for numeric ones, or a synthesis LLM call for free text), and a sectioning scheme needs to actually reconcile results that might conflict (e.g. the tone-check flags something the accuracy-check missed). Finally, remember every concurrent call still costs money and consumes rate-limit headroom — fanning out to 20 parallel calls for a task that didn’t need it is a real cost, not a free lunch just because it’s fast.
Key takeaways

Parallelization runs independent LLM calls concurrently and combines their outputs — it trades no per-call cost for lower wall-clock latency, and (with voting) can improve reliability.
Sectioning splits one task into independent subtasks run at once; voting runs the same task multiple times and aggregates for consensus or confidence.
In code, this is asyncio.gather (or your language’s equivalent) plus an aggregation step — never parallelize subtasks with a real dependency between them.
Voting fixes inconsistency, not bias — it won’t rescue a model that’s confidently, consistently wrong.
Unlike chaining, parallel branches don’t need to share state; unlike routing, parallelization runs multiple paths for every input rather than picking one.

claude/10-agents-and-workflows/04-routin.content:
Routing workflows


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Agents and workflows — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Routing means first asking Claude (or a simple classifier) “what kind of request is this?” and then sending it to a specialized prompt, tool, or even a different model chosen for that specific category — instead of writing one giant prompt that tries to handle every possible kind of request equally well. It’s the workflow equivalent of a receptionist who directs you to the right department.
Deep dive
Routing is the third core workflow pattern covered in this module, alongside parallelization and chaining, from Anthropic’s “Building Effective Agents” guidance. The idea is simple: classify an input, then dispatch it to one of several specialized downstream handlers based on that classification. Unlike parallelization (which runs multiple paths for the same input) or a plain chain (which runs every input through the same fixed sequence), routing picks a different single path per input.
The motivation for routing is that a single, general-purpose prompt trying to handle every kind of input well often ends up mediocre at all of them. If your application handles customer support messages, some of those messages are simple account questions, some are billing disputes, and some are technical bug reports — each of those categories benefits from a differently-tuned prompt (different tone, different required fields, different escalation logic), and some categories might even warrant a different, cheaper or more capable model. Routing lets you have your cake and eat it: a first, usually cheap and fast, classification call figures out the category, and then the actual work happens in a prompt written and tuned specifically for that category.
from anthropic import Anthropic
 
client = Anthropic()
 
def classify(user_message: str) -> str:
    """Cheap, fast classification call — routes to one of a few known categories."""
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",  # a smaller/cheaper model is often enough for routing
        max_tokens=20,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Classify this support message into exactly one category: "
                "'billing', 'technical', or 'general'. Respond with only the category word.\n\n"
                f"{user_message}"
            ),
        }],
    )
    return response.content[0].text.strip().lower()
 
def handle_billing(user_message: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        system="You are a billing specialist. Be precise about charges, refunds, and account balances.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
 
def handle_technical(user_message: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        system="You are a technical support engineer. Ask for reproduction steps if the report is vague.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
 
def handle_general(user_message: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",  # simple questions don't need the most capable model
        max_tokens=512,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}],
    )
    return response.content[0].text
 
HANDLERS = {
    "billing": handle_billing,
    "technical": handle_technical,
    "general": handle_general,
}
 
def route(user_message: str) -> str:
    category = classify(user_message)
    handler = HANDLERS.get(category, handle_general)  # default fallback
    return handler(user_message)
A few design points worth noting. First, the classification step is usually deliberately cheap: it doesn’t need the most capable model, since its job is narrow (pick one of N labels), so using a smaller/faster model like Haiku for the router while reserving a more capable model for the specialized handlers is a common cost-optimization. Second, routing composes naturally with the other two patterns — a routed handler can itself be a chain (classify, then run a multi-step chain specific to that category), or a handler can itself parallelize sub-checks. Third, always include a default/fallback branch: classification isn’t perfect, and an input that doesn’t cleanly match any category needs somewhere sensible to go rather than throwing an error or silently doing nothing.
Routing also generalizes beyond picking a prompt — the same classify-then-dispatch idea can route to entirely different tools, different models (cheap model for easy cases, expensive model for hard ones), or even different downstream systems entirely (route a request to a database query tool versus a document search tool versus a calculator, based on what kind of question was asked). This is the conceptual bridge into the next two lessons: once routing gets sophisticated enough that the “router” is deciding not just which prompt to use but which tool to invoke based on the situation, and doing that repeatedly as new information comes in, you’ve essentially arrived at the core mechanic of an agent. The difference is that in a routing workflow, the developer still defines the fixed menu of categories and handlers up front; in an agent (next lesson), the model can chain together tool calls in sequences the developer never explicitly enumerated.
Pitfalls. A router with too many overlapping or ambiguous categories produces noisy misclassifications — keep categories few and clearly distinct, and test classification accuracy directly before trusting the router in production. Skipping the default/fallback case is a common bug: a KeyError (or silent no-op) on an unrecognized category is worse than routing to a sensible general-purpose handler. Over-engineering routing when a single well-written prompt could actually handle the variety is also a real risk — routing adds an extra round trip and a new failure mode (misclassification) in exchange for handler specialization, so it’s only worth it when the categories genuinely need meaningfully different treatment. Finally, watch for router/handler drift: if you update a handler’s prompt but not the classification criteria (or vice versa), inputs can silently end up in a category whose handler no longer matches what you intended.
Key takeaways

Routing classifies an input, then dispatches it to one of several specialized downstream prompts, tools, or models — one path per input, chosen dynamically.
The classification step is usually cheap (a smaller/faster model is often sufficient); the specialized handler can use whatever model or logic fits that category best.
Always include a default/fallback branch for inputs that don’t cleanly classify.
Routing composes with chaining and parallelization — a routed handler can itself be a chain or run parallel sub-checks.
When the “router” starts dynamically choosing among many tools across multiple turns rather than a fixed menu of prompts, you’ve crossed into agent territory (next lessons).

claude/10-agents-and-workflows/06-enviro.content:
Environment inspection


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Agents and workflows — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Before an agent takes its next action, it helps enormously if it can actually look around first — check what files exist, read the output of the last command, see the current state of a system — rather than guessing based only on what it assumed would happen. Environment inspection means giving the agent tools whose whole job is to observe, not to change anything, so each decision it makes is grounded in what’s actually true right now.
Deep dive
This lesson builds directly on the previous one. An agent’s loop is only as good as the information it’s reasoning over at each step. If the only tools an agent has are ones that do things (send an email, write a file, call an external API), the model has no way to check whether its previous action actually worked, or whether the world matches what it assumed — it’s making every subsequent decision on faith. Environment inspection is the practice of deliberately giving the agent tools that let it observe its environment — read a file listing, check a command’s exit code and stdout/stderr, query a database’s current row count, inspect a job’s status — so that each step in the agentic loop is grounded in fresh, real information instead of an assumption baked in at the start of the task.
The clearest illustration is a coding agent. If an agent is asked to fix a bug, and its only tool is “edit file”, it has to guess whether its edit was syntactically valid, whether it actually fixed the bug, and whether it broke something else. Give that same agent a “list files” tool, a “read file” tool, and a “run tests” tool, and its loop changes shape entirely: it can look at the directory structure before deciding where to make a change, read the actual current contents of a file before editing it (rather than trusting a possibly-stale mental model from earlier in the conversation), and — critically — run the test suite after making a change and read the real output to decide whether to keep going, try something else, or declare the task done. Each of those is an inspection tool: it changes nothing in the world, but it changes what the model knows.
from anthropic import Anthropic
 
client = Anthropic()
 
# Inspection tools: observe state, change nothing
inspection_tools = [
    {
        "name": "list_files",
        "description": "List files in a directory. Use this to see what exists before acting.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "read_file",
        "description": "Read the current contents of a file. Always check current contents before editing.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "run_tests",
        "description": "Run the test suite and return pass/fail counts plus failure output.",
        "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}},
    },
]
 
# Action tools: change the world
action_tools = [
    {
        "name": "edit_file",
        "description": "Overwrite a file with new contents.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}, "contents": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["path", "contents"],
        },
    },
]
 
tools = inspection_tools + action_tools
 
def execute_tool(name: str, tool_input: dict) -> str:
    if name == "list_files":
        return list_directory(tool_input["path"])          # observes only
    if name == "read_file":
        return read_file_contents(tool_input["path"])       # observes only
    if name == "run_tests":
        return run_test_suite()                             # observes only — the result grounds the next decision
    if name == "edit_file":
        return write_file(tool_input["path"], tool_input["contents"])  # acts
    return f"Unknown tool: {name}"
 
# The agent loop itself is identical to the previous lesson's pattern — what
# changed is the TOOL SET, which now gives the model a way to check its work
# instead of only a way to change things.
The key design idea is the split between observation tools (list, read, check status, query — no side effects, safe to call as often as needed) and action tools (write, send, delete, call an external service — has side effects, should be used deliberately). A well-designed agent prompt or system message often explicitly encourages the model to inspect before and after acting: “before editing a file, read its current contents; after making a change, run the tests to confirm it worked.” This isn’t a different loop mechanism from the previous lesson’s agent — it’s the same tool-use loop, but with a tool set that includes read-only inspection capability alongside the tools that actually do things, and often a nudge in the system prompt to actually use them.
Environment inspection matters more as tasks get longer and more open-ended, which is exactly the kind of task where agents (versus workflows) earn their keep. In a short, well-specified workflow you usually know in advance what the state will be at each step, so there’s less need for the model to check. In a long agentic loop where the model is making many sequential decisions, small errors compound — an agent that never checks its own work can drift a long way from correct before anything notices. Giving it cheap, frequent access to ground truth is one of the most effective ways to keep a long-running agent loop reliable, and it’s a natural lead-in to the final lesson’s comparison of workflows and agents: inspection tools are part of the cost of running an agent safely, and that cost is one more factor in deciding whether a fixed workflow might have been the simpler, cheaper choice for a given task.
Pitfalls. Building an agent with only action tools and no inspection tools is a common and costly oversight — it forces the model to operate blind and makes failures much harder to catch mid-task rather than at the end. The opposite failure also happens: giving the model so many overlapping inspection tools that it spends most of its turns looking around rather than making progress (burning tokens and turns on inspection with diminishing returns). Also watch for stale-state bugs — if an agent reads a file once early in a long conversation and then acts on that cached mental model many turns later without re-reading, it can act on outdated information even though a “read” tool was available; prompting the model to re-check state immediately before consequential actions (rather than relying on what it observed several turns ago) helps here. Finally, inspection tools that are slow or expensive to call (e.g. a full test suite that takes minutes) create a real tension between grounding decisions and keeping the loop fast — this is a case where you may want to give the model a cheaper, partial-inspection tool for frequent use and reserve the expensive one for key checkpoints.
Key takeaways

Environment inspection means giving an agent read-only tools (list, read, check status) alongside its action tools, so it can ground each decision in real, current state.
Splitting tools into observation (no side effects) versus action (side effects) is a useful design lens for any agent’s tool set.
Prompting the model to inspect before and after consequential actions helps catch errors mid-task instead of only at the end.
Inspection matters more as agent loops get longer — small errors compound in a long, ungrounded loop far more than in a short, well-specified workflow.
Inspection tools have real costs too (tokens, turns, latency for expensive checks) — the next lesson weighs this kind of cost against workflows more broadly.

Next: 07 Workflows vs agents

claude/10-agents-and-workflows/07-workfl.content:
Workflows vs agents


                  
                  Course context 
                  
                

Part of Agents and workflows — Building with the Claude API (Skilljar)



In plain terms
Now that you’ve seen both approaches, the question is: which one should you actually build? The short answer is to start simple — use the smallest, most predictable pattern that solves the problem (a single call, then a workflow) and only reach for a full agent when the task is genuinely open-ended enough that you can’t specify the steps in advance. This lesson closes the module by laying out that decision directly.
Deep dive
This final lesson in the module is a direct comparison, pulling together everything covered so far: the fixed, developer-controlled sequencing of workflows (parallelization, chaining, routing) versus the dynamic, model-controlled looping of agents (tool use plus an autonomous decision loop, grounded by environment inspection). Anthropic’s “Building Effective Agents” guidance is explicit that this is not a question of which approach is “better” in the abstract — it’s a tradeoff, and the right choice depends on the shape of the task.
Predictability. A workflow’s control flow is written by you, so you can reason about it, test it, and know in advance roughly what will happen for a given input — the same input reliably produces the same sequence of calls. An agent’s control flow emerges from the model’s own decisions, so the same input can, in principle, lead to a different sequence of tool calls on different runs. If your application needs guaranteed, auditable behavior — a regulated process, a step that must always happen in a specific order — a workflow’s predictability is a feature, not a limitation.
Cost and latency. A workflow’s cost is easy to estimate: you know exactly how many LLM calls a given path through the code will make, because you wrote that path. An agent’s cost is much harder to bound up front — a loop that the model controls could, in principle, take one turn or twenty, and you’re paying for tokens and latency on every turn. Workflows are generally cheaper and faster for tasks that fit them, precisely because there’s no “figuring out what to do next” overhead repeated every turn — that decision was made once, by you, ahead of time.
Flexibility and autonomy. This is where agents win decisively. Some tasks genuinely cannot be reduced to a fixed sequence of steps known in advance — open-ended research, debugging an unfamiliar codebase, or any task where the right next step depends on what was discovered in the previous step in a way too varied to enumerate. Trying to force this into a workflow means either writing an enormous number of branches to cover every case (which becomes unmaintainable) or accepting that the workflow will fail on cases it didn’t anticipate. An agent’s dynamic loop handles this naturally: it can adapt its plan based on what it learns as it goes, which is exactly the property a fixed workflow lacks.
A practical decision framework, in the spirit of the course:

































QuestionLeans towardCan you enumerate the steps and their order in advance?WorkflowDoes the task need a guaranteed, auditable sequence?WorkflowIs predictable cost/latency important?WorkflowDoes the right next step depend on what’s discovered along the way, in ways too varied to pre-specify?AgentIs the task open-ended (research, exploration, debugging) rather than a known procedure?AgentCan you afford variable cost/latency and put guardrails (turn caps, budgets) around a loop?Agent
A useful sanity check while designing: start with the simplest solution that could work, and only add complexity when you’ve demonstrated it’s needed. That usually means: try a single well-crafted LLM call first. If that’s not enough, try a workflow — chaining, routing, or parallelization, whichever fits the task’s shape (covered in lessons 2 through 4). Only if the task is genuinely open-ended enough that a workflow can’t cover the space of cases should you reach for a full agent (lessons 5 and 6) — and when you do, build in the guardrails a fixed workflow gave you for free: turn/cost caps, environment inspection so the loop is grounded rather than guessing, and — for consequential actions — human confirmation steps.
It’s also worth noting the two aren’t mutually exclusive in a larger system. A production application often nests them: a top-level router (workflow) might dispatch some request categories to a simple fixed chain, and dispatch others — the genuinely open-ended ones — to an agent loop. The agent, in turn, might use a small internal workflow (a parallel set of checks, or a short chain) as one of its available “tools.” The distinction covered across this module is a way of thinking about each individual piece of control flow in your system, not a single global choice you make once for the whole application.
Pitfalls, revisited. The two recurring pitfalls from this module are worth restating together, because they’re mirror images of each other: reaching for an agent when a workflow would have been simpler, cheaper, and more predictable (unnecessary complexity, harder to debug, unbounded cost risk); and forcing a genuinely open-ended task into a rigid workflow that can’t actually cover the space of cases it will encounter (brittle, requires constant branch-adding maintenance, silently fails on the unanticipated case). Both mistakes come from not asking, up front, whether the task’s steps can actually be enumerated in advance. That single question — “can I write down the sequence of steps, or does it genuinely depend on what’s discovered along the way?” — is the thread running through this entire module, from the very first lesson’s definitions through to this closing comparison.
Key takeaways

Workflows offer predictability, bounded cost, and auditability; agents offer flexibility and autonomy for tasks that can’t be fully specified in advance.
Default to the simplest pattern that solves the problem: a single call, then a workflow, and only an agent when the task is genuinely open-ended.
If you do build an agent, carry over the discipline workflows give you for free — turn/cost caps, environment inspection, and human confirmation for consequential actions.
Workflows and agents aren’t mutually exclusive — real systems often nest a router around an agent, or give an agent a small workflow as one of its tools.
The central question throughout this module: can you enumerate the steps in advance, or does the right next step depend on what’s discovered along the way?

Related lessons

tags.title: TAGS
tags.content:
Tagging System
Tags live in YAML frontmatter (tags: list) and optionally inline as #tag. All tags are lowercase, hyphenated for multi-word terms (e.g. claude-code, not ClaudeCode or claude_code).
Tags complement the folder hierarchy — they don’t duplicate it. Don’t tag a note engineering just because it’s already inside 40 Resources/Engineering/.
Aim for 3–6 tags per note. Fewer is fine; more is a smell.

Tag Groups
1. Structural Tags
Applied to every note. Describe what role the note plays in the vault.





















TagWhen to usemocMap of Content — an index or hub note that links to many otherstemplateA reusable note skeleton inside Templates/referenceA standalone knowledge note — the default for most content
Every note should carry exactly one structural tag.

When new folders are added to the vault, introduce the corresponding structural tag here.


2. Status Tags
Track the maturity and health of a note.





















TagMeaningdraftIncomplete or actively being written; may be inaccurateevergreenStable, well-developed, actively maintainedneeds-reviewExists but flagged as stale, uncertain, or worth revisiting
Omit the status tag when a note is just reference material with no clear lifecycle (e.g. a factual summary). Status tags are most useful on long-form notes you intend to maintain over time.

3. Domain Tags
Apply to notes in 40 Resources/. Use the broadest domain that applies, then add specific topic tags below.













TagCoversengineeringSoftware, systems, architecture, tools, languages, algorithms
Use at most one domain tag per note. If a note genuinely spans two domains, pick the primary one.

Add a domain tag here when a new Resources subfolder is created.


4. Topic Tags
More specific than domain tags. No fixed list — grow these organically as clusters form. A topic tag earns its place when three or more notes share it and you’d realistically filter by it.
Engineering examples: algorithms, architecture, systems, networking, databases, devops, languages, testing, security, ai, claude-code, react-suspense

Rules


Format: YAML frontmatter list. Prefer block style for readability:
tags:
  - evergreen
  - engineering
  - architecture
Inline style (tags: [moc]) is fine for short lists.


Casing and separators: Always lowercase. Use hyphens for multi-word tags. Never use spaces, underscores, or camelCase.


Don’t shadow the folder path. A note in 40 Resources/Engineering/ doesn’t need engineering in tags unless it helps with cross-domain discovery.


Avoid vanity tags. A tag that matches only one note adds no value. Delete or merge it.


Evolve, don’t freeze. This document defines the rules, not an exhaustive tag vocabulary. Add new topic tags freely; update this file when a structural or domain tag changes.



Quick Reference
Structural (pick one):  moc | template | reference
Status (optional):      draft | evergreen | needs-review
Domain (pick one):      engineering
Topic (1–3):            free-form, lowercase, hyphenated
